News.title: Andy Burnham blames Trump’s Iran War for rising prices impacting struggling British families
News.content:
ANDY Burnham blamed Donald Trump’s Iran War for rising prices yesterday — as Brits were warned of more pain to come.

The PM added that he would do “what I can” to help struggling families.



Inflation jumped from 2.6 to 2.9 per cent last month — its highest level since March.

It came after Ofgem’s energy price cap rose 13 per cent, adding £221 to a typical annual gas and electricity bill.



Energy experts at Cornwall Insight predict bills will rise another four per cent in October as wholesale costs remain high.

Some economists have warned inflation could climb as high as 3.5 per cent by Christmas.



Mr Burnham said: “We can’t control what is going on in the Middle East, and the effect of the conflict there is now being felt in inflation here.

“But I will do what I can to help people.”

The inflation warning came as the PM told The Times Britain was “not set up for growth”.

He said his new No 10 North operation in Manchester will take the lead on driving growth, while Chancellor John Healey and the Treasury focus on controlling the public finances.



Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane, who has advised Mr Burnham on economic policy, called for a freeze on further tax rises for the rest of Parliament.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Labour’s tax rises and business bashing have driven the cost of living higher and higher, yet Andy Burnham refuses to rule out yet more tax hikes at the Budget.”

﻿

News.title: Government’s new guide for asylum seekers shows concerned families were right to demand answers & deserve to be heard
News.content:
Basic decency

FOR months, families daring to protest about the arrival of young migrant men in their communities have been branded bigots, scaremongers and worse.

Yet now the Government is handing asylum seekers a nine-page guide explaining the most basic rules of decent British society.

It spells out that women are equal to men. That domestic abuse is a crime. That sex requires consent and that following women or blocking their path is unacceptable.



Crucially, it explains that sex with anyone under 16 is a criminal offence, even if they say yes.



Perhaps the Lefties behind the “migrants welcome” protests might care to explain why the Home Office feels it necessary to hand out leaflets telling undocumented men landing on our shores how to behave.

The answer is simple but uncomfortable: Because not all foreign cultures match British laws.

That is not to say that every asylum seeker poses a threat. Nor does it justify hostility towards migrants.



But it does justify the concerns of families living near migrant camps, hotels and houses of multiple occupation.

This leaflet proves they were right to demand answers.

They deserved to be heard — not vilified.

Rwanda losses

LABOUR’S first act after winning power was to scrap the Tories’ Rwanda scheme.



Since then, more than 50,000 migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats to claim asylum in Britain.

Worse still, 90 people have died making the journey.

So it is encouraging to learn that Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is holding talks about sending failed asylum seekers to “return hubs” in third countries.

The Sun has repeatedly warned that, without a proper deterrent, the Government is fighting a losing battle against the tide of small boats.

Better late than never.



But keeping the original plan could have spared communities much misery, saved millions of pounds and countless lives.

Inflation alert

ANDY Burnham entered Downing Street with a pledge to give families “breathing space” from the rise in living costs.

But 30 days on, all we got was a sharp intake of breath at the latest inflation figures.

Prices are rising and wages aren’t keeping pace. Hard-working families are squeezed from both sides.

The Bank of England predicts a further inflation rise this year, with energy prices and rail fares all expected to rise in the coming months — all compounded by the war in Iran.

The PM says he can’t control what’s happening in the Middle East.

But he can rein in public spending and ease off on taxes to give us all a breather.

News.title: The reason Britain is poor is obvious and should be easy to fix – so why can no one in government see it?
News.content:
GOVERNMENTS take money from the private sector and give it to the public sector. When its private sector is healthy and growing, a country is rich.

When its private sector must carry the weight of a burgeoning state machine, a country is poor.



Look no further for an explanation of why Britain is not growing. The people who generate tax surpluses (butchers, bakers, candlestick makers) are struggling to carry those who consume them (NHS managers, racism awareness counsellors, local government officials).

Our problem is that we keep hiring more and more people to work for the Government, and paying them more and more.



Public-sector salaries have risen by 6.1 per cent, according to the Office for National Statistics, private-sector salaries by just 2.8 per cent.

Given that new figures out yesterday revealed inflation is now running at 2.9 per cent — which is in itself, a scandal — private-sector workers have taken a real-terms pay cut to fund the public sector.



I am not arguing that working for a private company is more virtuous than working for the Government (though socialists sometimes seem to believe the opposite).

No, this has nothing to do with merit, and everything to do with affordability.

A government that genuinely wants the growth that politicians keep talking about would lighten the load.

It should be easy to shrink the state payroll to pre-pandemic levels.



A lot of extra officials were recruited on a supposedly emergency basis to deal with vaccination, test-and-trace and other contingencies.

And similarly, a number of extra civil servants were taken on between 2016 and 2020 to deal with the one-off adjustments of Brexit, as we put in place different trade and customs arrangements.

Both those bumps are now far in our rear-view mirror. Yet, incredibly, the public sector workforce has grown from 5.4 million in 2016 to 6.2 million now.

How can any country carry such a weight? How can we, at a time of almost no growth, increase both the number of people on the state payroll and their salaries?



I don’t believe anyone in the Government asks these questions. Their main calculation is political.

The public-sector unions believed they had an IOU from the incoming Government, and they were not wrong.

Teachers got a 5.5-per-cent pay rise, most NHS workers got 5.5 per cent with a further 3.3 per cent to come, junior doctors got the equivalent of 22 per cent.

Now, you might argue that these are good and deserving people.



As it happens, I agree. Most NHS workers are indeed public-spirited (though, by the law of averages, some of them must be lazy and useless).

If I could wave a magic wand, I would give teachers a hefty raise.

That, though, is beside the point. When there is not the money, questions of merit become irrelevant. And the plain fact is that there isn’t the money.

Our national debt just passed the £3trillion mark.

The great African-American economist Thomas Sowell liked to observe that socialists are remarkably uninterested in how wealth is created.



They assume, he would say, that its creation is a given, and that the only question is how to redistribute it. But growth does not just happen if the incentives are set wrongly.

Every redistributive tax rise is doubly bad for productivity. If you are taxed more, and keep less of what you earn, you work less hard.

If I am given benefits regardless of what I do, then I also work less hard.

Behind all the talk of “rewarding our hard-working teachers and nurses” is the reality that we are squeezing the revenue-producing part of the economy to engorge the revenue-consuming part. No country can keep doing that.

The expansion of the state payroll has not translated into greater productivity.



Indeed, civil service productivity is below where it was before the lockdown, and it is not hard to see why. Civil servants rarely come into the office.

Are ministers going to do anything about it? On the contrary.

Angela Rayner yesterday told the BBC that working from home could lead to greater productivity — which I am sure is the view of civil service trade unions, but is emphatically not the view of most private-sector bosses.

When it was put to Ms Rayner that more than 3,800 civil servants never have to go into the office at all, she replied: “Look, I’m not a Jacob Rees-Mogg, that I have to see someone in the office to know that they’re working.”

On the same day, it emerged that the former Cabinet Secretary, Chris Wormald, had been given a pay-off of around £500,000 after 14 months in the job when he was shifted to make room for the current incumbent.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Nice for him, obviously. But how much more of this can the rest of us afford?

News.title: New Rwanda-style crackdown on failed asylum seekers plotted by Home Secretary
News.content:
A RWANDA-style plan to remove failed asylum seekers to third countries is being actively cooked up by Labour, The Sun can reveal.

The Home Secretary said “live conversations” over return hubs were happening “across Europe, but in other parts of the world as well” as ministers hunt for new ways to ramp up removals.



And she revealed France has already begun deporting migrants under a separate UK-funded crackdown aimed at stopping them reaching small boats.

Watch the full video interview here



Ms Mahmood insisted Labour was right to scrap the Tories’ Rwanda scheme because it “was not working and did not work” – but confirmed ministers remain open to third-country solutions.

She told The Sun: “We are also looking at third-country hubs, returns hubs models.

“These are live conversations that are happening across Europe, but in other parts of the world as well.”

The Government has previously confirmed negotiations with a number of countries over return hubs, but no deal has yet been announced.

Return hubs would be aimed at failed asylum seekers who cannot be returned directly to their home countries – rather than replicating the axed Rwanda scheme exactly.

The Tories’ Rwanda scheme would instead have seen some asylum seekers who arrived illegally in Britain sent to the African country to have their claims processed there.



Labour scrapped the controversial plan after taking office in 2024, arguing it was hugely expensive and had failed to act as a deterrent.

Ms Mahmood said any future agreement would have to prove it was effective and legally watertight.

She said: “The most important thing I think in any deal that we strike now or in the future is about its effectiveness.

“Is it actually going to be able to do the thing that it says it’s going to do? Can it do so in a way that is compliant legally as well?



“That is the test hurdle. Those are the same challenges that other countries in Europe are grappling with. There’s no easy answers here, but I’m confident that whatever decisions we make, the main test will be: is it going to work, and can it be effective?”

Meanwhile, France has begun removing migrants under a separate £662million three-year deal bankrolled by British taxpayers.

The agreement struck in April includes plans for a detention centre in northern France to hold migrants before they can make the Channel crossing, with funding partly dependent on results.

Ms Mahmood said “They have actually done some deportations already, so some have begun.”



But she stopped short of confirming the long-awaited detention centre would be operational by the end of this year, saying: “We’re obviously working with them. It’s not operational yet.”

She insisted the French were nevertheless “doing their bit”, saying they had also increased prosecutions and were bringing more people to justice under their system.

And she warned Britain would stop funding parts of the French crackdown if they failed to deliver, saying: “If actually, you know, later this year, in the next year, we’re thinking some sort of bits are not working, we won’t fund them anymore.

“We’re going to fund the things that work.”

The deal is also set to boost the number of French law enforcement officers deployed against Channel crossings by 40 per cent, with Ms Mahmood saying the increase was already being rolled out.



She also defended French cops amid criticism over officers failing to stop packed dinghies once they reach the water.

She said French officers have “much fewer options” at the water’s edge because of the risk to migrants’ lives.

Ms Mahmood said: “If you only look at activity that’s happening at the water’s edge, actually that’s the last point at which anything can be done because at that point you’ve got an operational risk of people being in the water, and then obviously French officials have to make a decision based on operational risk to life.

“If you just go a few 100 yards up from water’s edge, you will see a lot of disruption activity. There is a huge amount of work happening with French law enforcement that is literally stopping people from actually getting to water’s edge in the first place.”

Her comments came as she visited Heathrow Immigration Removal Centre to mark the number of criminals and immigration offenders returned from Britain hitting its highest level since 2016.



Some 80,286 people have been returned since the election in July 2024, including foreign criminals, immigration offenders and failed asylum seekers.

But just 6,103 were migrants who had arrived in Britain by small boat, while only 19,622 of the overall total were enforced returns.

A further 11,733 were foreign national offenders, including 5,995 removed under the early removal scheme.

Ms Mahmood vowed to go “further and faster” against Channel crossings, declaring: “We’re going to bear down on small boats relentlessly.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And as smugglers turn to “mega-dinghies” carrying hundreds of migrants at once, she warned: “Rest assured, the very fact of them changing their tactics is because they’re finding it more difficult to operate, and now they’re thinking of new ways of getting around the changes that we’re making with the French.



“We will find ways to stop them.”

News.title: Ex-Death Row Records security chief hits back over claim he is REAL Tupac murder suspect after Keefe D’s wild allegation
News.content:
THE former security chief at Death Row Records has hit back at claims that he is the real suspect behind Tupac Shakur’s murder following wild allegations by the Compton gangbanger on trial.

Reggie Wright Jr., a former Compton police officer and associate of Marion “Suge” Knight, scoffed at accusations made by Duane “Keefe D” Davis, calling the claims a desperate bid to survive prosecution.



Davis, 63, has repeatedly alleged that Wright Jr. was the mastermind behind the drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, that resulted in Shakur‘s death.

“Evidence points to Reggie Wright Jr. He brought up my name from day one. He basically started some bulls**t,” Davis told CBS affiliate KLAS from jail days before the start of jury selection.



Wright Jr., the former head of security at Death Row Records, scoffed at Davis’ allegations, calling him a “pathological liar.”

“I laugh, I mean, to be accused of murder is not a laughing matter, but it’s because I know he’s a pathological liar,” Wright Jr. told The U.S. Sun.

“[That’s] his attorney’s own admission. They tell you can’t believe anything he said.

“Now, they’re trying to say that because they want to discredit everything that he said when he’s facing 25 years to life, which you don’t play with the government when they got something on you already.



“That you’re trying to get off because you piss them off or get caught in one lie and that deal is gone,” he added, referring to the proffer agreement between Davis and a federal task force in Los Angeles for information about Shakur’s and rapper Biggie Smalls’ murders.

Wright Jr. continues, “It’s funny to me. I used to watch a TV show with my father when I was growing up, it’s called The Practice.

“And they used that law firm, they used to defend people and they say, always have a plan B, have somebody else to blame it on when your client is in trouble. So, I guess I’m just plan B.”

Wright Jr. was in Las Vegas at the time of the shooting, but he was several miles away at the since-shuttered Club 662, setting up the venue for Knight and Shakur’s arrival.

Knight and Shakur were scheduled to attend the club for an after-party following the Mike Tyson boxing match at the MGM Grand Casino Hotel.



Wright Jr. recalled the tumultuous environment that surrounded the Death Row crew nearly 30 years ago.

“We were chaotic, but that was normal for Death Row, for us. We was always unorganized, with a bunch of young guys, had too many people around us,” he said.

“It’s strange. I guess I was strange back then and didn’t see nothing wrong. It was like common practice.



“I didn’t look at it like a fear or a hazardous work condition or anything like that. I just looked at it as a normal hip-hop community.”

Wright Jr. recalled that nearly two dozen associates of Knight and Shakur arrived at the Luxor Hotel in Las Vegas, all eager to attend the boxing match.

“When they came out of the fight, they all hooked up, more pumped up, popped,” Wright Jr. said, referring to the body language of Shakur, Knight, and their crew in the MGM Grand Casino Hotel surveillance footage.

The infamous moment captured the vicious beatdown of Orlando Anderson, Davis’ nephew and a member of the South Side Compton Crips, by the Death Row crew in the casino’s lobby.

Wright Jr. said he would have beefed up security for Knight and Shakur had he known the MGM Grand incident involved a gang-affiliated person.



“You never expect that to happen. You saw it on TV and stuff like that, but if I would have known of the beatdown, the incident that happened at the MGM, and [had I] knew that it was gang members, not just a regular citizen, then yes, I would have been on a different type of alert,” he added.

“But, quite frankly, I don’t even think I would have thought that they would have retaliated that quick in Vegas.

“I thought that was pretty ballsy now to mount up, arm themselves, which they probably already was armed, but to go in and round out people to retaliate that quick.

“I thought that was pretty ballsy on their part, but not uncommon.

“Unfortunately, in our society that’s like crazy, unheard of. You go to the police if something like that happened,” Wright Jr. said of the aftermath of the brawl at the MGM Grand.



“[In] their society and their culture, they were supposed to do that. They had to do that.

Prosecutors said the murder of Shakur, 25, was a retaliatory hit orchestrated by Davis, who sought revenge for the beating of his nephew at the hands of the rapper and his entourage.

The prosecution has repeatedly said that Davis did not fire the shots that killed Shakur, but that he plotted the shooting and provided the firearm.

Davis, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, has pleaded not guilty and argued that he was not in Las Vegas at the time of the drive-by shooting in September 1996.



In recent interviews, Davis claimed that his past comments about his involvement in Shakur’s death, in interviews and in his memoir, Compton Street Legend, were all exaggerated for royalties.

Michael Sanft, Davis’ defense attorney, told jurors in his opening statement that his client was known to “bulls**t” and argued that the state has failed to compile hard evidence linking him to Shakur’s murder.

Wright Jr. believes Davis’ latest claims are a desperate attempt to save himself after years of “poking the bear.”

“What are you expecting him to say? The only other option for you to do is to play crazy,” Wright Jr. said.



“We rub s**t all over his face every day or something like that, trying to convince that he’s crazy because that’s the only thing. The jury is going to be a regular person on the jury.

“You’re going to be like, is he crazy? No. Well, why did he make all these statements if you’re not crazy?

“It’s a done deal. Mr. Davis is the one that kept running his mouth, poking the bear, poking his nose at the state of Nevada.

“You keep doing that, of course. You keep talking about a situation that you got a pass on.

“You’re going to have younger people come aboard. I’m sure the old DAs and all them, they were cool, but then you get some young DAs or assistant DAs that come in and be like, hey, hey, this guy is out here still running his mouth.



“Can we open this investigation and solve it? And I really believe that’s what happened because he wants to write books. He wanted to go and do all the interviews, and they decided they got a motivated young assistant DA that convinced his boss to give him a shot.”

As Wright Jr. gets set to take the stand in Davis’ murder trial, he hopes the outcome puts to rest the wild conspiracy circulating on social media about Shakur’s death.

“I’m hoping for all of these unanswered questions to get answered, did Orlando [Anderson] ever go to the hospital. Just questions out there on YouTube,” he said.

“I done heard stuff that a helicopter landed and picked up Tupac and took him away to Cuba. The guy in the autopsy report was 6’2, Pac was only 5’8, 5’9.

“Just all of this stuff that’s on social media to get put to rest. And if it turns out that Keefe did do what he said he do, then justice.



“I know ultimately, and I don’t know most people’s religion, but mine is God. So, we definitely gotta ask God for forgiveness.

“And we’re going to be judged for that. But the main thing is we also got man-made justice.

“I believe in law enforcement and the law, the criminal justice system still for right or wrong. So justice for Tupac is my outcome. That’s what I hope for the final outcome.”

Davis’ trial is expected to last four to five weeks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He’s facing life in prison if convicted.



You can watch our full interview with Reggie Wright Jr. on our YouTube channel.

News.title: Reform plots 600,000 new apprenticeships for young Brits by axing ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees and foreign student loans
News.content:
JOBS BOOST Reform plots 600,000 new apprenticeships for young Brits by axing ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees and foreign student loans

YOUNG Brits will have 30 per cent of their apprentice wages covered by the taxpayer under Reform plans for a major “skills revolution”.

Nigel Farage‘s party say they will save small businesses employing 16-18 year-olds around £4,000 per year.



It will cost taxpayers’ around £1.5billion over five years with Reform insisting the bill will be clawed back elsewhere.

The cash will come partly from scrapping taxpayer funded loans for foreign students and funding for “Micky Mouse” degrees.



It will create an extra 600,000 apprenticeships for young Brits by the end of Reform’s first term in government, the party claimed.

Reform’s education spokesperson Suella Braverman said: “I want an economic and social renaissance, not because it fills me with jingoistic pride but because this country needs it.

“We need a restoration and renewal of this country, so that once again, we are training up our own with the skills that we all need to be a functioning country.”



There are 140,000 fewer apprenticeships being undertaken compared to 2017, according to Reform analysis.

Apprenticeship levels have fallen to their lowest levels since 2011-12, just three years after the global financial crash.

Opportunities for young Brits have fallen 40 per cent in manufacturing, engineering and plumbing, 60 per cent in painting and decorating and 75 per cent in health and social care.



Ms Braverman said the ambitious target will be fulfilled by the end of Reform’s first term in Government.

She added: “My message to young people is simple, your success is our country’s success and we want a stake in it. We are on your side and that is why we are willing to invest in you right at the beginning of your career.”

McLoughlin Group Holdings managing director Kevin McLoughlin said the target showed Reform were “serious about investing in young people.”

He said: “We need an apprenticeship policy that will incentivise the SMEs that keep Britain running.

“I was an apprentice myself and now as a business owner I know a 30% reduction in the cost of employing an apprentice shows Reform are serious about investing in young people and lowering the cost of running a business.



“The Apprenticeship Wage Credit shows Reform UK are prepared to invest in young people and the skills this country needs.”

Reform also says it will save taxpayers millions by slashing funding for “Mickey Mouse” degrees at third-rate universities.

News.title: Man charged with murder after woman, 52, killed and second victim, 32, injured in double stabbing inside home
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MURDER CHARGE Man charged with murder after woman, 52, killed and second victim, 32, injured in double stabbing inside home

COPS have charged a man with murder after the death of a 52-year-old woman while another victim was injured in a double stabbing.

Officers were called at 8.19am on August 18 to an address on Askew Road in Shepherd’s Bush, West London, following reports of a stabbing.



A woman, aged 52, was sadly pronounced dead despite the best efforts of emergency services at the scene.

The victim has now been named as Samantha Turner.



Her family have been informed and continue to be supported by specialist officers.

A second woman, aged 32, suffered non-life threatening stab injuries.

She remains in hospital and continues to be assessed.

A murder investigation was launched, and a man was arrested at the scene.



Alan Dore, from Shepherd’s Bush, was charged on August 19 with murder and attempted murder.

He is due to appear at Hendon Magistrates’ Court on August 20.

Detective Inspector Richard MacKenzie, who is leading the investigation, said at the time: “Our enquiries continue at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances of this deeply tragic incident.

“Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the victim and injured woman.

“We believe this to be an isolated incident within a residential address, but we know it will cause concern locally.



“Our officers will remain in the area throughout today.

“We will update the community when we can, and I encourage anyone with any information, CCTV or doorbell camera footage which could support the investigation to contact us.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101 quoting reference 1673/18AUG.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Body found after fire rips through factory as murder detectives launch investigation
News.content:
Body found after fire rips through factory as murder detectives launch investigation

West Yorkshire Police said a body was found inside a factory at the centre of a major fire in Batley and have urged anyone who may have 'witnessed anything unusual' to come forward

View 2 Images A body was found following a 'large fire' at the factory (Image: Yorkshire Live)

A body has been found in the wreckage of a major fire that tore through a factory in West Yorkshire.

‌



West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service raced to the derelict building on Warwick Road in Batley in the early hours of Saturday, August 15. Police also attended the scene and later confirmed they had found cannabis at the address.

‌



West Yorkshire Police say work is ongoing to identify the deceased individual.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector James Entwistle, of the Homicide and Major Enquiry Team, said: "Our enquiries at the scene remain ongoing and, as part of those investigations, officers have sadly located a body within the building.

"I understand this development will be concerning for local residents and the wider community.

"I would like to reassure the public that a dedicated team of officers and specialist investigators are working diligently to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire and determine exactly what has taken place."

‌



View 2 Images Emergency services at the scene on Warwick Road (Image: Yorkshire Live)

Det Ch Insp Entwistle said officers will provide further updates to the public as soon as it is in a position to do so, reports Yorkshire Live.

"This remains a complex investigation and I would urge anyone who may have witnessed anything unusual, has information about the incident or location, or possesses CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage from the area, to contact us," he added.

‌



"What may seem like a small piece of information could prove vital in helping us establish the facts."

A West Yorkshire Police spokesman said: "Officers investigating a fire in Batley from earlier this week have sadly found a body.

"Police were alerted to reports of a large fire at a building on the corner of Warwick Road and Mount Street by West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service just after 3am on Saturday 15 August.

"The cause of fire has not yet been established, and a scene remains in place while enquiries are ongoing."

Anyone with any information is urged to contact police on 101, or online here, quoting reference 13260464916. Any footage can be uploaded here. Alternatively, report anonymously to Crimestoppers by calling 0800 555 111.

News.title: Deportations hit 10-year high as Shabana Mahmood says change 'sends a message'
News.content:
Deportations hit 10-year high as Shabana Mahmood says change 'sends a message'

New Home Office figures reveal more than 80,000 foreign criminals and failed asylum seekers have been removed since the general election, with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood hailing the 52% increase

View 2 Images Shabana Mahmood says the increase in deportations sends a message to criminal gangs (Image: Getty Images)

Deportations of foreign criminals and failed asylum seekers have reached their highest level in a decade.

‌



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said new figures "send a message" that those who come to the UK illegally, or break the law, will be removed. Home Office data released today shows returns have gone up by 52% since the general election compared to the last two years under the Tories.

‌



More than 80,000 people have been removed since July 2024 - the highest level since 2016. Ms Mahmood said: "This is a vital step in our effort to restore control to our border and make our migration system fairer for all. These new statistics send a message.

‌



"We will always welcome those who come here legally and seek to build a better life. But if you come here illegally, or you break our laws, we will send you home. I know there is more to be done.

Reform civil war erupts as top supporter suspended after scathing Farage and Yusuf criticism READ MORE :

View 2 Images More than 6,000 who arrived by small boat have been removed (Image: CPS/PA Wire)

"That is why we are pursuing new legislation that will more swiftly remove those here illegally, and we are doubling funding to our Immigration Enforcement teams by 2028."

‌



Home Office data shows there were 80,286 returns recorded between July 1, 2024, and July 31 this year - including 19,622 enforced returns of people with no legal right to remain in the UK. This included over 6,000 who arrived by small boat.

And nearly 12,000 were foreign national offenders were removed from the UK, the data shows. There were 163 charter flights for returns to countries in Africa, Asia, Europe and South America in that time.

The government has ramped up immigration returns and has put forward controversial plans to speed up the appeals process. Under legislation making its way through Parliament a new Independent Immigration Appeals Authority (IIAA) - made up of trained members of the public - will rule on appeals rather than judges. This will speed up removals, the Home Secretary said.

‌



And new measures will prevent last-minute modern slavery claims. The Home Office is also looking at how much force officers should use while removing families with children.

This includes whether the use of handcuffs should be authorised, with officials saying removals attempts are being regularly frustrated. But the proposal has sparked an outcry, with more than 150 charities branding it a "sustained attack on children's rights".

Ms Mahmood has said the government is prepared to bring in visa sanctions to countries who fail to take back citizens facing removal from the UK.

Article continues below

And she has announced the Immigration Enforcement budget will be doubled by 2028/29, with staffing increased by 60%. The Home Office said this will result in tens of thousands more raids, arrests, and removals.

It comes as Labour faces pressure from Nigel Farage's Reform, which has focused on immigration and removals. It has claimed it would remove 600,000 people over a five-year period, and send prisoners to jails overseas.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle plan move back to UK in matter of weeks

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, are set to return to Britain with Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, for an extended period

View 6 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are pictured at an event this month (Image: The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are planning a major return to Britain – with their two children set to attend school in the UK.

‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are understood to be preparing to return to Britain with Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, for an extended period.

‌



The family is expected to arrive by the end of August, with the children due to begin the new school year in September. The move comes six years after Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties and relocated to the US.

‌



The couple are understood to have secured a private, non-royal home in Britain, although details of their new residence and the children's school have not been disclosed for security and privacy reasons.

View 6 Images King Charles is said to be aware of the plans

King Charles is said to be aware of the plans, with the move potentially giving the monarch more opportunities to spend private time with his grandchildren. Charles and Harry had an emotional reunion last month, which the Mirror told would likely pave the way for Harry's return to the UK.

‌



Despite making millions since leaving his role as a working royal in 2020, and arranging his own private security team, Harry has claimed he remains a target for terrorists in the UK and needs protection from the Metropolitan Police when he returns.

A 40-page risk assessment suggested he faced an “elevated risk” in the UK, where five of the six known terror plots against him originated. At least four individuals responsible for those threats are thought to be out of prison, and their whereabouts are unknown.

View 6 Images Prince Harry shares World Cup pictures of Princess Lilibet and Prince Archie

‌



The Home Office has always maintained that Harry’s security is considered on a case-by-case basis and if he informs the department of his travel plans at least 28 days in advance.

The Duke has spent years challenging the decision over his security arrangements after losing taxpayer-funded protection when he ceased to be a working royal and moved overseas. His return could therefore reignite questions over what security arrangements will be put in place for the Sussexes and who would pay for them.

Harry and Meghan have retained their home in Montecito, California, meaning their reported British move does not necessarily signal a permanent abandonment of their US base.

‌



View 6 Images Before this year, Prince Harry last saw the King in late 2025 (Image: PA)

The return does not mean Harry and Meghan are becoming working royals again. The Sussexes are expected to remain financially independent and continue their commercial and charitable work, while Harry is not expected to undertake official royal duties.

The decision is particularly striking given Harry's previous concerns about bringing his family back to Britain. It comes after it was reported this week that the Prince could return to the UK "every few months".

‌



The report followed the Prince's July return to the UK, during which he met with the King and Queen for a strictly under-wraps visit with his children, and he teed up a battle with the Home Office over his taxpayer-funded security.

View 6 Images Harry and Meghan's children are reportedly starting school in the UK this September (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

The Prince is determined to reconcile with his family and won’t do anything to jeopardise it, a source told the Mirror, as he places far greater importance on repairing family ties than at any point since he and his wife Meghan stepped back as working royals in 2020.

‌



On the cards, the source said, could even be a public reunion with the King at his Invictus Games in Birmingham next year, with the Prince having visited the major city a year ahead of the competition during his visit in July.

They said: "There's no doubt he [Harry] enjoyed his time in the UK with his family, especially getting the opportunity to see his father with his wife and children.

View 6 Images Prince Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

Article continues below

"The last few years have been incredibly emotional for him, and now he's reached a place where he wants to not only visit his home country more, but also would really like to be with his family. If the King were to attend the Invictus Games next year, and appear in public with him, it would be a huge moment for all of them. He wants the Birmingham Games to be the best ever, and it would be extra special to have all his family by his side, and that means the King as well.

"He's said before that he would like reconciliation with his family, so undoubtedly he's determined to make things work, and that means not doing anything to jeopardise that."

The Telegraph reports that sources have told them the family will set up their main home in the UK and see how it goes before making any permanent decisions.

News.title: Hayden Panettiere dies aged 36: Unexpected death triggers criminal investigation
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere has died at the age of 36, with the initial investigation from police finding there was 'no foul play' and autopsy results confirming 'no signs of trauma'

US actress Hayden Panettiere, who was best known for her roles in Heroes and Nashville, has died aged 36. Her death was confirmed by her representatives and followed by a statement.

The statement from her father, Skip, read: “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

Meanwhile, her mother spoke the first time on Tuesday, firing shots at ex Brian Hickerson. She said: "I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry -- it is a struggle and it's a very challenging industry and it's not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path."

She also added: "This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death, and that was Brian Hickerson."

The Coroner's office confirmed that Hayden's autopsy showed 'no signs of trauma' at the time of her death. It had been reported that the police were responding to a call about a suspected "cardiac arrest". A police report later revealed that both her ex Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the scene at the time of her death.

911 audio footage also heard dispatchers discuss a suspected overdose. Both Narcan and Epinephrine were reportedly brought to the scene by emergency services Panettiere's cause of death has not been announced at this time.

A preliminary police investigation has confirmed there were no signs of "foul play or suspicious circumstances" when they arrived at her home after a 911 emergency call from an acquaintance of Panettiere's.

News.title: Murder probe launched after woman dies and eight others injured in fire
News.content:
Murder probe launched after woman dies and eight others injured in fire

Police have said they believe the fatal fire in Hounslow, London, may have been started deliberately.

View 2 Images Forensics at the scene of a fire on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow, in which a 48-year-old woman died and a further eight people were taken to hospital. (Image: Ben Whitley/PA Wire)

A murder investigation is under way after a 48-year-old woman died and a further eight people were taken to hospital following a fire at a property in Hounslow early on Wednesday, the Metropolitan Police has said.

‌



Officers were called to a property on Berkeley Avenue at just after 1am following reports of a fire. A woman died in hospital, while another woman, 40, remains in a life-threatening condition.

‌



The force said six men and one woman who were taken to hospital have since been discharged with minor injuries. Police said a murder inquiry is now under way, but no arrests have been made.

‌



View 2 Images Police have said a murder inquiry is now underway, but no arrests have been made. (Image: Ben Whitley/PA Wire)

Detective chief inspector Neil John, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured.

Article continues below

“Our enquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire, which we believe may have been started deliberately.

“We understand this to be an isolated incident within a residential address; however, we understand it will cause concern within the local community.”

News.title: Family left 'broken' after dad dies in car park as police launch investigation
News.content:
Family left 'broken' after dad dies in car park as police launch investigation

Ben Gough, 41, was discovered after emergency services were called to a car park in Truro, Cornwall, with police launching a probe into the 'unexplained' death

View Image Ben Gough was found dead in a car park in Truro (Image: Leanne Gough/ Family issued )

The grieving sister of a man who was found dead at a car park in Cornwall says the discovery has "broken their family," and that they will "never recover" from their loss.

The body of Ben Gough, 41, was discovered after emergency services were called to Moorfield Car Park in Calenick Street, Truro, at around 10.45am on Monday, August 17.

Devon and Cornwall Police are probing the "unexplained" death with significant enquiries ongoing to establish what happened.

The force said a 44-year-old man from Truro was arrested on assault, grievous bodily harm, administering a noxious substance, and theft.

Ben's sister, Leanne Gough, said their family has "nothing but love" for him, reports Cornwall Live. "Ben was loved by all of his family more than he can ever imagine," she said.

"Losing him has broken our family and we will never recover from this. People may have certain views on Ben but his family know the real Ben and he had nothing but love in him".

Multiple others have taken to social media to pay tribute to Ben, who one friend said "always had a smile" on his face.

"Fly high Ben, thinking of your family, children and true friends! You always had a smile on your face when I saw you," Amanda wrote.

Melissa said: "So sad for you Ben you will be missed absolutely gutted for your family and your true friends R.I.P buddy xxx".

Kirsten added: "RIP thanks for always bigging my son up. You were like a brother to him xx." Mark said: "Rip terrible tragedy thoughts are with his family".

Steven also commented: "That is so sad my thoughts [are with] him and his family. R. I. P."

Katie said: "So upset even writing this!! I generally am heartbroken. Can't believe this is true, can't believe you're gone!! I was only talking to you early Sunday morning!!

Article continues below

"You have been one of my closest besties for many many years!! Will be missed always - love you always!!".

John wrote: "Young life ended so tragically RIP mate" and Richard said: "Can't believe it [...] RIP bruv, some cracking memories with you".

Multiple other tributes read: "Rest in eternal peace Ben, thoughts are with your family" and "Condolences to the family."

News.title: Distressing photos show critically endangered orca with gunshot wounds in fins
News.content:
Distressing photos show critically endangered orca with gunshot wounds in fins

WARNING: DISTURBING IMAGES: Conservationists fear Toñi, the oldest known female in the tiny Iberian orca population, may have been deliberately shot

View 2 Images Toñi is the oldest known female in the endangered Iberian orca population (Image: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org / SWNS)

A critically endangered orca known for damaging boats has been found with suspected shotgun wounds.

‌



Spanish officials have opened an investigation after Toñi, the oldest known female in the endangered Iberian orca population, was seen with a series of injuries across her dorsal fin in the Strait of Gibraltar. Spain’s Ministry for Ecological Transition has confirmed the injuries, with ministry sources indicating several projectiles may still be lodged in the whale’s fin, raising fears she could develop an infection.

‌



The discovery has alarmed conservationists who have closely followed Toñi and say she appeared uninjured when they saw and photographed her only weeks earlier.

‌



The WeWhale team said: “The sudden appearance of these injuries within a matter of weeks, together with their number, size and distribution, clearly leads to believe that they are the result of a shotgun discharge."

View 2 Images Scientists have warned that the behaviour may not have been deliberate attacks (Image: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org / SWNS)

Toñi had recently travelled with her pod from waters near Faro, and Spanish authorities are now working with officials in Portugal as they try to establish how she was injured. The whale is well known to WeWhale and the Iberian Orca Guardians Foundation, which have monitored members of the small population over a number of years.

‌



Janek Andre Founder and president of WeWhale and the Iberian Orca Guardians Foundation: “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there. Now we are seeing multiple impact wounds across her dorsal fin and back which, in our assessment, are consistent with her having been shot with a shotgun.

“For us, these aren’t anonymous animals. We know them individually, we know their families. Seeing Toñi like this is devastating. If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.”

The Iberian orcas have attracted international attention in recent years following repeated encounters with boats off the coasts of Spain and Portugal. Since 2020, crews have reported the animals making contact with rudders, turning vessels and causing extensive damage. At least four boats have reportedly sunk following encounters with the whales.

‌



But scientists have warned against interpreting the behaviour as deliberate attacks, with theories ranging from social play to the animals practising hunting behaviour.

The encounters have nonetheless caused growing frustration among some sailors, with controversial attempts to keep the animals away previously caught on camera. Footage emerged in 2023 showing people throwing firecrackers into the water as orcas approached a boat’s rudder.

There are estimated to be just 30 to 40 Iberian orcas left, and conservationists say the population already faces a number of pressures including food shortages, pollution and heavy shipping traffic.

‌



WeWhale warned that the loss or serious injury of even a single whale could have a significant impact on such a small population.

Their statement reads: “Losing or seriously harming even one animal has significance far beyond the individual when dealing with a population this small."

Andre said: “Whatever someone’s opinion about vessel interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be acceptable. These orcas need protection, not retaliation.”

Article continues below

Spanish marine protection agencies have appealed to sailors and boat operators for any information which could help investigators establish what happened to Toñi. WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians said they will continue documenting the whale’s condition and behaviour while the investigation remains ongoing.

News.title: EasyJet cancels all flights from UK airport - full list of destinations scrapped
News.content:
EasyJet cancels all flights from UK airport - full list of destinations scrapped

EasyJet has confirmed flights from Leeds Bradford Airport (LBA) will cease from January 2027 as the airline focuses on 'maintaining and developing' its 'most popular' routes

View 2 Images EasyJet says it will be focusing on its 'most popular' routes (Image: Jam Press)

EasyJet has announced it will no longer be running flights from Leeds Bradford Airport (LBA).

‌



The budget airline said it was withdrawing from the airport next January to "focus on maintaining and developing" its "most popular" routes.

‌



Passengers travelling from LBA were able to fly to Barcelona, Paris, Belfast, Malaga, Mallorca and Geneva - but these journeys will cease from January 5, 2027.

‌



Anyone with EasyJet bookings beyond that date have been offered a free transfer to flights from an alternative airport or a refund, the airline said.

EasyJet has not yet confirmed whether all scheduled flights to its destinations from Leeds Bradford Airport will go ahead.

View 2 Images Leeds Bradford Airport offered EasyJet flights to Barcelona, Paris, Belfast, Malaga, Mallorca and Geneva (Image: SWNS)

‌



But its website showed no available flights from Leeds Bradford to Geneva. Flights to Malaga and Mallorca meanwhile appeared to stop running after November.

Flights to Barcelona, Paris and Belfast still appeared to be available until January.

An EasyJet spokesperson said: "Following a review of our routes from Leeds Bradford Airport, we have made the decision to no longer operate flights from the airport after 5 January.

‌



"Our focus is on maintaining and developing routes which prove most popular with customers."

"We have contacted customers with bookings beyond this date to provide them with advance notice and inform them of their options, including a free transfer to flights from an alternative airport or a refund, and we are very sorry for the inconvenience caused.

"We value the relationship we have built with Leeds Bradford Airport and we always keep options for our network under review, with the aim of providing more choice and connectivity where we see demand."

Article continues below

EasyJet began flights from Leeds Bradford Airport in 2010.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to UK
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to move back to the UK, the BBC understands.

As first reported by the Daily Telegraph, external and the Sun,, external Prince Harry and Meghan intend to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside of London.

The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.

King Charles was told of the move on Sunday. There are no current plans for either of Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working Royals.

The Sussexes and their children visited King Charles at Highgrove in July this year, but it is understood the move was not discussed.

The BBC understands the King was unaware of the move before last weekend but he welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.

But there will be no expected change to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Prince William and Princess Catherine have also been informed of their plans.

The couple's move from California comes after they left the UK and royal duties in early 2020.

Family relations had been strained since, with July's visit to the King and Queen Camilla being a key development in their relationship.

The Palace described the meeting at the King's private home in Gloucestershire as a "private family occasion".

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years.

Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since 2022, when they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II.

Security for the couple has long been a point of tension, with the July visit being reconsidered because the Duke of Sussex's request for police protection was rejected.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

The Duke had sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after he stopped being a working royal and moved to the US with the Duchess.

Prince Harry had previously said that worries about safety have prevented him from coming to the UK and bring his wife and children.

News.title: Couple and teenage daughter who died in water off Shoreham named by police
News.content:
Three members of the same family who died after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham have been named by police.

Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara El-Khawas are thought to have gone into the water near Shoreham Fort on Tuesday, Sussex Police said.

A younger girl from the same family, who was pulled from the water with them, remains in hospital in a critical condition.

Police said the family had travelled from their London home to visit Shoreham and after reviewing CCTV footage investigators say they believe the deaths were a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.

The Palestinian Forum said the family were British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in the Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon. Earlier, the Palestinian embassy in London told the BBC that Hassan El-Khawas had been a refugee.

Adnan Hmidan, chairman of the Palestinian Forum in Britain, said the community was "deeply shocked and saddened" by what had happened.

He said two other children were on the shore at the time of the incident.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the entire family, particularly the children, who are facing an unimaginable loss," he said.

The Palestinian Embassy in London said it was closely monitoring the incident and contacting British authorities to establish the circumstances and check on the condition of the girl in hospital.

A statement issued by the embassy sent condolences to the family and the UK's Palestinian community and wished the girl a speedy recovery.

News.title: Track defect found on approach to site of Lewes derailment, initial report says
News.content:
A defect was found on railway tracks in East Sussex at the site where a train derailed leaving 30 injured, a report says.

Initial findings from the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) found an "irregularity" with the tracks near Lewes where three carriages tumbled down an embankment last Thursday.

The RAIB, which is continuing to investigate the derailment, said it had received "several reports of rough riding at the location of the derailment from passengers on other trains".

Network Rail and Greater Thameslink Railway, whose Southern Rail train was involved in the crash, said in a joint statement they were "sorry this happened on our railway".

Investigators from the RAIB have said CCTV from a train which passed through the crash site at 14:04 BST showed the "irregularity" with the track geometry just before the point where the train came off the tracks.

The 14:24 service from London Victoria to Eastbourne derailed in the Landport area of Lewes at about 15:54 BST.

The derailment left two people seriously injured, and 18 were taken to hospital with less serious injuries. The 18 have since left hospital.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Salmonella outbreak: What we know so far
News.content:
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has recently declared a national outbreak, external of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill with the bug.

Although not yet proven, imported eggs or dishes containing them are the leading suspects as to the cause.

Evidence also suggests people caught the bug while eating out, rather than at home - with catering and food services such as restaurants, cafes or take-aways likely to play a part.

But there is still a lot to be discovered.

What do we know and what questions remain?

News.title: Vaccine breakthrough stops cancer returning in trial
News.content:
A new personalised vaccine given in combination with a drug has stopped skin cancer returning in patients during a trial, representing a potentially watershed moment in cancer treatment.

The vaccine, developed by drug companies Merck and Moderna, was given to patients with high-risk melanoma, a type of skin cancer, after they had surgery.

Early results show this new jab extended the length of time these patients were cancer free, but it's unclear for how long, according to an announcement by the two firms.

Cancer experts say this is a breakthrough, but emphasise caution as the full results have not been released or peer-reviewed whereby independent experts examine and check the trial findings.

And even after the trials process has finished, the treatment would still need to be approved by regulators and then go through another approval process before it was made available on the NHS.

The vaccine, called Intismeran, was given in combination with Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug already used in cancer treatment.

Compared with taking the Keytruda on its own, the companies said taking the drug and vaccine together significantly increased the time patients remained cancer free and reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other organs.

The phase three trial involved more than 1,000 patients who had high-risk stage two, three or four melanoma - meaning they ranged from having large tumours in a specific area to cancers which had already spread to other parts of the body.

News.title: 'Incredible': SpaceX rocket spotted off Christmas Island coast
News.content:
A SpaceX rocket has made an unexpected appearance off Christmas Island after touching down in the Indian Ocean following a test flight from Texas on 24 July.

David Watchorn, chair of the Christmas Island Tourism Association said he initially thought he was looking at ships on his way to work, before realising it was "a rocket, a space rocket" being towed.

The 52-metre long rocket has caused a stir among locals, with some "sneaking out" of work for a glimpse, and others preparing their boats for a closer look at the debris.

"It's really incredible to think about what it's been through," Watchorn told the BBC.

"The more and more you look at it, the more fascinating it's becoming".

News.title: Male prisons in England and Wales have fewer than 1,800 spaces
News.content:
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it was building more prisons while exploring early release options and expanding electronic tagging.

The figures come after Prime Minister Andy Burnham made more prisoners exempt from the upcoming early release scheme following backlash from victims.

Burnham came under further pressure after the killers of PC Andrew Harper would still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Last week, Burnham said he was "confident" PC Harper's killers could be excluded from the government's early release scheme

On August 3, Burnham said in a written article, external he had "wanted to go even further" but had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

A spokesperson for the MoJ said "public safety will always be our priority".

"We are fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most serious offenders behind bars, on top of murderers, anyone on life sentences and those in prison for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences who are already blocked from any changes," they said.

"We share the public's anger that these options are even being considered, after we inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse."

News.title: Behaviour guidelines for life in UK published for asylum seekers
News.content:
New behavioural guidance for asylum seekers has been published by the Home Office.

A nine-page booklet covering issues including respect in public, sex and consent, and gender equality, has gone online, with guidance on how laws and customs in the UK may be different from the home country of asylum seekers.

The Conservatives said any asylum seekers breaking UK law should be deported and Reform UK claimed the publication of the document meant the government "knows that they are a menace".

A Home Office spokesman said: "We expect everyone who comes to the UK to abide by our laws. If they do not, they will face consequences, including the refusal of their asylum claim and removal from the UK."

According to the latest Home Office figures, a total of 93,525 people applied for asylum in the UK from April 2025 to March 2026, which was down by 12% on the same period in the previous year.

The booklet sets out how asylum seekers must understand UK law, because the consequences of breaking the law mean "you could get in trouble with the police, lose your asylum support, or it could affect your asylum claim."

A section on gender, external explains that women in the UK have equal rights to men, and do not need the permission from a husband, father, brother or any other man to do things like work, study, travel, or make decisions.

Another section on sex and consent sets out how both people must agree to sex or sexual contact of any kind, and consent cannot be given if someone is asleep, drunk, or unable to respond.

And a section headed Respect in Public outlines how it is not acceptable to whistle or make kissing noises at people on the street, nor "make sexual comments to someone, even if you think it is a compliment".

The guidance also contains contact details for organisations for victims and those seeking help with the issues raised.

The Home Office spokesman added: "Returns of failed asylum seekers have reached their highest level since 2010 under this government."

The latest government figures show nearly 70,000 illegal migrants and foreign criminals have been returned or deported from the UK since Labour came to power in July 2024.

The BBC understands nearly 10,000 foreign criminals, including murderers and rapists, have been removed since the last election â a 36% increase on the previous 21 months.

News.title: Students wait for GCSE and BTec  grades as app launches for 750 schools in England
News.content:
Pupils in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive GCSE, BTecs and other Level 2 results on Thursday, with some grades in England available through an app that is rolling out for the first time.

Schools and colleges will distribute grades in person, but from 11:00 BST pupils at more than 750 schools in England will also be able to see their grades on their phones.

Results this year come as the government in England plans to boost technical education and address a growing number of English and Maths GCSE resits.

Last year, 67.4% of all GCSE entries were graded 4/C or above.

News.title: Jump in energy bills drives UK inflation to highest rate for four months
News.content:
Higher energy bills drove UK inflation up to 2.9% in the year to July, the highest level in four months, according to new figures.

Gas prices soared at the sharpest pace in almost four years, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, leading to an increase in the cap on household energy bills in July. Energy costs surged after US-Israel war with Iran began, which has restricted global oil supplies.

July's reading is the highest since March but some price growth slowed. Food inflation, at 1.3%, is at its lowest rate for close to five years.

Experts said the inflation figure is unlikely to influence the Bank of England to change its key interest rate at its next meeting in September.

Energy costs for households rose on 1 July after Ofgem, the energy regulator, increased the price cap on gas and electricity costs by 13%, which added Â£221 a year to the typical bill.

Homes are forecast to see a 4% rise in energy bills from October, according to Cornwall Insight, which would take them to the highest level since July 2023.

There is ongoing uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, which has seen effective closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key trading passage for ships carrying oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities.

Cornwall Insight, an independent energy consultancy, added that energy price pressures were being compounded by the ongoing heatwave across Europe "increasing gas demand for power generation to meeting air conditioning and cooling demand".

News.title: Two accused of drug trafficking after UK-Nigeria investigation
News.content:
A man and a woman have been charged with international drugs trafficking offences as part of an investigation involving police in the UK and Nigeria.

Oladipupo Atandare, 50, from Dagenham and Latifat Yusuf, 44, from Hornchurch were arrested following the seizure of more than 180kg (397lb) of cocaine in the UK on 5 August.

They appeared at Barkingside Magistrates Court on 8 August and were remanded in custody. They will next appear at Snaresbrook Crown Court on 7 September.

The Metropolitan Police said the arrests related to solely the UK drugs seizure, but inquiries are continuing into the discovery of a similar-sized amount of cocaine in Nigeria.

On Tuesday Nigerian authorities said they had discovered 184.5kg of cocaine, worth about Â£20m, in brown boxes at a courier facility in Lagos.

There have been a series of arrests in Nigeria, including a logistics company employee and a social media influencer with nearly 700,000 followers on Instagram.

News.title: Emma Barnett reveals she 'had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have'
News.content:
BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed she had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

Barnett, 41, returned to Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday morning, explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

She told listeners: "I made a programme on endometriosis on BBC Two and ended up being in hospital for endometriosis.

"So yes, I've been recuperating, shall we say, from surgery for endometriosis and a hysterectomy to boot. So that's been less fun than the Today programme, but it is lovely to be back."

Barnett's announcement came soon after she published a blog about the "hysterectomy I never wanted to have", external.

The presenter, who has two children, said it was "totally surreal" to be in hospital on the night her documentary was broadcast in June, only well enough to watch the final 10 minutes.

"Some 48 hours before the documentary aired - I had undergone a near-5 hour surgery and somehow found myself lying in bed recovering from extensive endometriosis surgery, a hysterectomy and a gallbladder removal," she wrote.

"Triple threat. Go big or go home. Life imitating art."

She added: "I felt blind-sided and robbed, even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.

"But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have."

Endometriosis is where cells similar to those in the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body, resulting in what Barnett has described as "bone-grinding, life-altering pain". It affects one in 10 women and there is no known cure.

A hysterectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the womb (uterus). A hysterectomy alongside removal of endometriosis can reduce the risk of recurrence, according to Endometriosis UK, external.

In her blog, Barnett also said she suspected most of her pain may have been down to another condition, adenomyosis, which can be treated by a hysterectomy.

Her surgery was necessitated after she had an ultrasound while filming the final scene of the documentary, and a problem in her gallbladder was found. "Suddenly things became urgent and non negotiable."

The broadcaster added that she was hopeful that the surgery had helped.

She wrote: "Early indications are that the pain is very much improved - although I am still healing from the surgery itself so that also feels uncertain and frightening to admit - even to myself."

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings issued for parts of UK with flash flooding expected
News.content:
Yellow thunderstorm warnings have been issued across the UK, with heavy showers expected to lead to flash flooding and travel disruption.

The Met Office warnings will come into force across northern England, Northern Ireland and eastern Scotland later in the day on Wednesday. The warning for northern England will remain in place until Thursday morning.

The downpours follow almost two months of dry weather, with parts of the country experiencing their first rain in weeks on Tuesday.

People in areas impacted by thunderstorms have been told by the Met Office to expect that businesses and homes could flood, transport services could be delayed and power cuts are likely.

The yellow weather warnings are in place for:

Northern Ireland from 12:00 until 23:59 BST on Wednesday

Parts of North East Scotland, including Aberdeen, from 14:00 until 21:00 on Wednesday

Parts of the North of England, including Manchester and Newcastle upon Tyne, from 19:00 until 10:00 on Thursday

The Met Office said lightning, hail and thunder were expected in the areas affected by warnings, with up to 30mm of rain expected within a few hours in parts of North East Scotland and across Northern Ireland.

Parts of northern England could see up to 50mm of rain within six hours.

Much of the UK has seen a mixture of sunshine and scattered showers already on Wednesday.

In Wisley, Surrey, a 62-day long dry spell was broken on Wednesday morning, with the remarkable run ending after 1.6mm fell before 10.00.

News.title: PM unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas
News.content:
Every rough sleeper in England will be offered accommodation this winter, the prime minister has said.

Andy Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July and now says he wants "to get everyone in for Christmas".

Emergency accommodation will be provided to end the need for rough sleeping alongside practical support for any health needs, as part of a Â£442m package.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Burnham promised to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester when mayor of the area but "failed because he didn't do the hard work necessary".

Burnham's pledge seeks to build on the success of Everyone In, a Covid pandemic-era scheme that saw thousands of rough sleepers housed in hotels and temporary accommodation.

About 37,000 people were helped by that scheme, following its launch in March 2020. The charity Shelter found that about a quarter of them had found settled accommodation, in the form of housing lasting at least six months., external

The PM's announcement comes with an additional Â£102m in new funding, taking Burnham's total commitment to tackling rough sleeping to Â£442m since becoming prime minister.

The money is said to be "fully funded" within the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

As well as providing immediate support to get people off the streets, the funding is also designed to deliver more than 1,000 homes over the next three years to provide rough sleepers with permanent accommodation.

The funding will also provide "intensive wraparound support", typically psychiatric and drug and alcohol services to help people rebuild their lives.

Burnham said he did not believe "anybody should be forced to sleep rough".

He added: "And actually when you do leave people sleeping rough it can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, in and out of hospital beds and sometimes in contact with the police."

The prime minister said the government funding "may not fully get us there" as he appealed to charities and faith organisations to help ensure an offer is made to everybody who needs it.

He added: "We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again."

Rooms in shared flats or houses, B&B accommodation, warm spaces for short-term refuge and supported lodgings are among the types of accommodation mentioned in the government's guidance that could be used to bring people in off the streets.

Burnham also told The Big Issue, external he would commit to donating 15% of his prime minister's salary to tackle homelessness, which follows his decision to give 15% of his MP salary to causes in his Makerfield constituency.

A prime minister is entitled to an additional salary of Â£83,837 on top of their salary for being an MP. Recent PMs have claimed Â£75,440, with the previous government of Sir Keir Starmer continuing the freeze on ministerial salaries.

News.title: Single guilty verdict in Palestine Action trial
News.content:
A jury has been discharged after reaching a single guilty verdict in the trial of eight Palestine Action activists who were accused of helping to organise a raid on the UK site of an Israel-based defence firm

The jury at the Old Bailey spent more than 37 hours considering evidence, but failed to reach verdicts on 14 of 15 charges relating to the raid at the Elbit Systems Ltd factory in Filton, near Bristol, in August 2024.

One guilty verdict, for criminal damage, was passed on Tuesday, but the defendant cannot be named for legal reasons.

Prosecutors will now consider seeking a retrial for the unresolved charges - but any trial could be a year away due to backlogs in the Crown Courts.

Palestine Action members broke into the Elbit Systems Ltd factory on 6 August 2024 and their own footage shows they began destroying equipment, including drones, which they believe were destined for use by the Israeli Defence Forces in Gaza.

The firm has contracts with the British military and other Nato members and has previously said that claims that its Bristol factory supplies Israeli forces is "completely false".

The defendants, who must now wait to see if they face a retrial, are:

Ian Sanders, 47, of Leamington Spa

Aleksandra Herbich, 42, of Brent in north-west London

Teuta Hoxha, 30, of Southwark in south-east London

Sean Middleborough, 34, of Liverpool

Julija Brigadirova, 34, from Chorlton in Manchester

Hannah Davidson, 53, of Edinburgh

Madeleine Norman, 31, of Edinburgh

William Plastow, 35, of Manchester

The Old Bailey trial was opened on 22 June and all eight defendants had denied charges of criminal damage and violent disorder.

During the case, Plastow, 35, was cleared of violent disorder.

The court heard none of the defendants were at Elbit during raid, but were alleged to have helped to plan it, including by compiling an equipment list, carrying out reconnaissance, purchasing tools and weapons used by others, and co-ordinating other elements of the break-in - such as filming the incident.

Four people have already been convicted and jailed for their roles in the break-in and the eight defendants in this second trial were not part of that on-the-ground team.

Judge Patrick Field KC discharged the Old Bailey jury on Wednesday, the day after it convicted one of the defendants of criminal damage by a majority of nine to one, but reached no other decisions.

The jury was first sent out on 6 August.

The Crown Prosecution Service will now need to decide whether to seek a retrial.

A hearing has been set for 14 September to decide the future of the case.
