While I met plenty of people who had been to San Miguel before I left, most had never even heard of it, let alone Guanajuato or Querétaro, which get far fewer American visitors.

Americans tend to like to enjoy places where they can be more comfortable, which usually means they flock to where Americans already are. Massive European hubs that have been recommended by countless American tourists to their friends and family will rake in visitors, while Central Mexican destinations — for better or worse — go unnoticed.

Central Mexico will never appear in as many movies (in a positive way, at least) as France or England. It will never be considered as romantic as Italy. So Americans will keep going to Europe.

I’ve been to Europe several times and now I’ve been to Mexico for nine weeks. The lack of familiarity, which is both real and exaggerated, is what made traveling in Mexico so great. I was never craving uniquely American experiences in Mexico. Why would I come to Mexico if I wanted everything to be like the United States?

So yes, there is sometimes a lack of familiarity. I noticed people wearing different clothes and eating different foods. They had different phrases that sometimes made me uncomfortable and they had different customs. But now I understand them and can go back to the U.S. having learned new things. I would not have gotten that if I just went to a place where every person I saw was a tourist.

3. Logistical and language issues

Americans like to speak English. In Central Mexico it’s far more common for people to lead with Spanish, unlike in Cabo or Cancún. For many American travelers, that’s enough to dissuade a visit.

Airport announcements are exclusively in Spanish, as well as signs at bus terminals. Sometimes asking for directions or ordering at a restaurant can be difficult. It can be hard to make conversation or meet acquaintances.

That’s part of the reason why San Miguel gets so many American tourists. You can easily get around with English and the town is relatively well-integrated to Americans. It may sometimes make for a less authentic trip, but one that is much easier to navigate and is more familiar while still having all the charm that Central Mexico provides.

As someone who speaks very limited Spanish, I was worried about the language barrier. Staying in San Miguel made it more seamless, but it was harder to get by when I traveled to Querétaro or Oaxaca. But that discomfort is part of traveling and part of becoming integrated in the culture. I had translation apps on my phone and tried to make an effort to speak in Spanish when I could. That was more than enough to get by.

It often was not easy but it was never that hard. If Spanish is stopping you from taking a trip to Mexico, I’m here to tell you that it shouldn’t. I struggled at times, but without trying to speak Spanish, I would not have been able to experience some of the rewarding experiences that I had.

What you’re missing out on

Colorful cities. Colonial streets. Winding mountain passes and waterfalls. Ancient ruins and cactus gardens. Tacos, tlayudas and empanadas.

Central Mexico truly has it all. I have been grateful to discover it during my nine-week internship. There were many times that I was grateful for streets that felt devoid of Americans, and there were times I was wishing for more familiarity. But that is the beauty of studying abroad.

Americans are missing out on many of the same experiences they can get in Europe. In Mexico, they can travel on a shorter flight and at lower prices. It also comes with learning what the real Mexico is like, which is ever-important as the two countries have been increasingly linked for decades. Over 38 million people of Mexican origin live in the U.S., and nearly two million Americans live in Mexico.

As these two countries seemingly grow apart over political tensions, meeting Mexicans in person and seeing how they truly live their lives has never been so fulfilling. It has also never been so maddening as they continue to be vilified in the United States. I can confidently say that coming to Mexico will be one of the greatest experiences of my college years and one that I will never forget.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups
World.content:
Thank you to everyone who completed the Mexico News Daily “Mexico and My Money” survey, which sought to gather information about the financial practices and experiences of foreigners living in Mexico.

Almost 700 of you responded to the survey and we have now analyzed the results, which are presented in this article.

Before we get to them, let us remind you that we conducted this survey to help guide and define the topics of a new MND series called “Mexico and My Money.”

The first article in the series, which was introduced by MND CEO Travis Bembenek earlier this month, will be published next week.

The MND ‘Mexico and My Money’ survey results

Who responded?

By our cutoff time, 680 people living in 25 of Mexico’s 32 states had responded to the survey.

The top 10 states where respondents live are Jalisco, Guanajuato, Nayarit, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Mexico City, Yucatán, Oaxaca, Baja California and Sinaloa.

Around 44% of respondents have lived in Mexico for 11 years or longer, while the remaining 56% have lived here for 10 years or less.

The respondents are both full-time (70%) and part-time (30%) residents of Mexico.

Almost eight in ten respondents (79%) are retired, while the remainder work either part-time (11%) or full-time (10%).

More than seven in 10 respondents (73%) own their primary home, while the remainder rent.

10 Key Takeaways

7 in 10 respondents think their money is safe or very safe in banks in Mexico

More than four in 10 respondents (44%) think their money is “safe” in a bank in Mexico while an additional 28% believe their money is “very safe” in a bank in Mexico.

Almost one-quarter of respondents (23.5%) chose the “neutral” option in response to the question about the safety of their deposits in banks in Mexico.

Only 5% of respondents think their money is “unsafe” (4.5%) or “very unsafe” (less than 0.5%) in a bank in Mexico.

One factor that may have influenced people’s perceptions about the safety of their money in banks in Mexico is that federal Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora promptly reassured CIBanco and Intercam account holders that their money was “absolutely” safe after the U.S. Department of the Treasury last year accused the banks of laundering millions of dollars for drug cartels, prompting the government to take control of them. For the vast majority of CIBanco and Intercam customers that proved to be the case, although account holders who responded to a previous Mexico News Daily survey did face a range of inconveniences linked to the U.S. accusations.

8 in 10 respondents don’t have a Mexican credit card

Almost 37% of respondents don’t have a checking account based in Mexico, 58% don’t have a savings account with a bank in Mexico and a striking 79% don’t have a credit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

A strong majority of respondents (72%) do, however, have a debit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

The results suggest that many foreigners in Mexico use credit cards issued by banks in their countries of origin.

One possible reason why many foreigners opt not to get a credit card from a bank in Mexico is that credit card interest rates are typically very high.

8 of 10 respondents have made some kind of investment in Mexico

Only 21% of respondents have not invested in at least one of real estate, stocks, bonds or a business in Mexico. The remaining 79% of surveyed foreigners have invested in at least one of those assets.

The purchase of a home in Mexico was easily the most popular investment. Seven in 10 respondents (71%) own a home in Mexico, while 14% have a property in which they don’t currently live. Just over 12% of respondents receive rental income from a property they own in Mexico.

One in 10 respondents (10%) has invested in a business in Mexico, while 8% of surveyed foreigners have bought stocks and 9% have purchased bonds.

A strong majority of respondents have not had ‘money issues’ with contractors or other service providers in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (83%) of respondents have not had “money issues” with contractors in Mexico.

Almost nine in 10 surveyed foreigners (87%) have not had “money issues” with people who provide regular services to them in Mexico, such as landlords, cleaners or gardeners.

* Read about some of the money issues respondents have experienced with contractors and other service providers in the final section of this article.

Most respondents have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (82%) have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico, whereas 18% of survey respondents have been a victim of such an offense.

* Read about some of the financial crimes respondents have suffered in the final section of this article.

The vast majority of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico

Almost 97% of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico. Just over 3% of surveyed foreigners have borrowed money in Mexico.

This result suggests that the vast majority of respondents purchased real estate, vehicles and other assets in Mexico with their own funds or took out loans abroad.

As is the case with credit cards, the high cost of credit in Mexico is a deterrent to taking out loans in Mexico for many foreigners.

Rising prices in Mexico have negatively affected the lifestyles of 4 in 10 respondents

The increase in prices in Mexico in recent years has negatively affected the lifestyles of around four in ten (38%) respondents.

The lifestyles of the remaining 62% of surveyed foreigners have not been adversely affected by rising prices.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, the lowest level in more than six years. However, inflation in Mexico was much higher in earlier years of this decade, peaking at an annual headline rate of 8.7% August and September of 2022.

Inflation, combined with other factors such as the strength of the peso, has made life in Mexico considerably more expensive in recent years.

Respondents are, on average, ‘somewhat concerned’ about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate

MND asked survey respondents to rate their concern over fluctuations in the value of the Mexican peso or the US dollar on a scale of 0 to 100.

On the scale, 0 meant “unconcerned”; 50 signified “somewhat concerned”; and 100 denoted “always concerned.”

The average response among respondents was 53, indicating that the surveyed foreigners are, collectively speaking, “somewhat concerned” about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate.

In general, fluctuations in the exchange rate are more of a concern now for foreigners in Mexico than in years gone by because, over a period spanning decades, the value of the peso against the US dollar trended down. However, in recent years the peso has bucked that trend, appreciating more than 10% against the greenback between 2021 and 2025, and continuing to strengthen this year.

A majority of respondents have loaned money in Mexico

Over half of the survey respondents have loaned money locally while living in Mexico.

Around 22% of respondents have loaned an amount under US $500, while 20% have lent between $500 and $3,000. About 11.5% of respondents have lent over $3,000 to someone in Mexico. Those three percentages add up to about 53.5%.

The remaining 46.5% of surveyed foreigners haven’t lent money to anyone while living in Mexico.

15% is the most common restaurant tip rate among respondents

Almost 48% of respondents typically tip “roughly 15%” of their total bill at restaurants in Mexico.

Almost 30% of surveyed foreigners usually tip “roughly 20%” when eating out, while 18.5% typically leave gratuities of “roughly 10%” of their total bill.

Just over 2% of respondents typically tip more than 20% of their total restaurant bill, while just under 2% usually tip less than 10%.

Your say

We asked survey respondents to provide additional information if they have experienced money issues with contractors and/or service providers in Mexico or if they have been a victim of a financial crime here. Many of the survey respondents who said they have been a victim of a financial crime recounted stories of being mugged, pickpocketed or having money stolen from their homes.

Below is a (lightly edited) selection of the comments we received.

Money issues with contractors

I paid for materials I didn’t get.

The price changed during the project due to the number of man-hours worked.

I had disagreements over what was included with certain construction costs. The disagreements arose from familiarity with what is typical in the U.S. versus what is typical in Mexico.

I paid for products and services I never received.

I didn’t receive reimbursement for a shoddy job.

I paid upfront for work that never happened or was executed poorly.

The contractor demanded more money than we agreed on.

The contractor failed to complete work and stole building materials.

Money issues with contractors and providers of regular services

A cleaning lady we had for eight years was stealing money from our purse and wallets during the whole time she was working for us.

A landlord kept my 20,000-peso security deposit without cause.

In order to continue having hot water in the apartment, I had to purchase equipment and pay for the installation because the landlord would not.

My rent increased above the agreed-upon rate. The increase was much higher than the standard rate increase in San Miguel de Allende.

The gardener wanted more money and simply stopped working until he got his raise.

I’m a former timeshare owner and the maintenance fee was immediately doubled after I was informed it was being adjusted because it was unfair. This was almost 20 years ago. It was extremely intimidating and I was threatened. Now that we know about cartel involvement in timeshares, I am so glad we got out even though we had to pay US $10,000.

My landlord insisted on me paying rent in US dollars, then stopped when the dollar weakened. The landlord greatly increased my rent, specifically saying, “My expenses have gone up because of inflation and the dollar isn’t worth as much.” She then converted the rent from dollars into pesos, increasing it by 20%.

I have had minor issues but have always been able to work them out. That’s life anywhere.

Financial crimes in Mexico

I was a victim of fraud when purchasing a car.

I was mugged. I lost my phone and wallet.

I was robbed of money, jewelry and a tablet by a “nurse” taking care of me.

Someone hacked my virtual HSBC card and ran up unauthorized charges.

I was the victim of the fraudulent sale of a timeshare.

An employee of a Mexican bank was siphoning funds and using new deposits to cover withdrawals. She was caught. I had to testify against her in exchange for the bank honoring my account balance.

I was coerced into a timeshare purchase.

A vacation rental that I paid for in advance was not owned or managed by the guy who rented it to me.

I was a victim of a credit card scam in a taxi.

A fruit vendor gave me counterfeit money.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Peso punches below 17 to the US dollar for the second time in a week
World.content:
Listen to this article

Buoyed by a weaker greenback, the Mexican peso appreciated on Wednesday morning to trade below 17 to the US dollar.

At midday Mexico City time, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 16.97, according to Bloomberg.

Earlier on Wednesday, the peso reached 16.95 to the dollar, its strongest position since June 2024. Compared to the Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate of 17.06 on Tuesday, the peso appreciated 0.65% to reach 16.95 to the dollar.

Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote on X that the peso appreciated on Wednesday morning due to “the weakness of the dollar” as a result of the U.S. Treasury Department’s announcement that it was increasing a bond buyback operation. The dollar weakened after the Treasury Department announced in a statement that it was “increasing, by at least double, the size of liquidity support buyback operations for longer-dated nominal coupon securities (the 10-year to 20-year sector and the 20-year to 30-year sector).”

At midday, the US Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, was down 0.7% compared to the closing level on Tuesday.

Janneth Quiroz, director of economic analysis at the Monex financial group, said that the peso benefited from “the retreat of the dollar” and from the United States’ decision on Tuesday to pause planned 50% tariffs on almost $30 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The appreciation of the peso on Wednesday morning came after the currency broke the 17-unit-per-dollar floor last Friday morning. However, the peso closed at 17.03 to the dollar on Friday, according to the Bank of Mexico, and was also above 17 at the end of trading on Monday and Tuesday.

The peso has appreciated around 6% against the dollar so far this year after ending 2025 at 18.00 to the greenback.

In the most recent MND Peso Index™ analysis, which was conducted in early August when the USD:MXN rate was 17.22, the peso was found to be overvalued against the dollar by 2.4%.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Mexico keeps pressure on US over deaths in ICE custody: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 More than 16 billion pesos to be invested in Hidalgo: Governor Julio Menchaca announced two major projects: a 10.1-billion-peso “Economic Development Hub for Well-being” in Zapotlán de Juárez, and a 6.5-billion-peso “reactivation” of a cement plant in Tula de Allende.

🔥 Sheinbaum: Security operation provoked violence in Michoacán: Asked about fiery narco-blockades across the state Wednesday morning, the president confirmed an operation was underway to detain “one or several important targets.” The top target of the operation is reportedly CJNG plaza boss Heraclio Guerrero Martínez, alias “Tío Lako.”

⚖️ Velasco: Mexico wants “justice” for the 17 who died in ICE custody: Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco said that the government’s complaints, filed in July with U.S. prosecutors, seek investigations into the deaths, a “determination of responsibilities” and, if warranted, criminal charges. Sheinbaum said her government took the unusual step of filing the complaints directly, rather than leaving it to victims’ families, “because we’re now talking about 17 compatriots who have died.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

Officials spoke about a range of important issues at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference, including investment in the state of Hidalgo, violence in Michoacán and the Mexican government’s response to the deaths of 17 Mexicans in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or during ICE operations.

Sheinbaum’s confirmation that a security operation in Michoacán on Wednesday morning was the reason why various narco-blockades were set up on highways in the state was especially significant. However, she provided limited information about the events in Michoacán, saying that security officials would offer more details later in the day.

More than 16 billion pesos to be invested in 2 projects in Hidalgo

At the start of the press conference, Sheinbaum announced that Hidalgo Governor Julio Menchaca was in attendance to speak about new investment projects in the state he leads.

Menchaca announced that investment and infrastructure firm Dewa Capital would invest 10.1 billion pesos (US $595.7 million) in the development of an Economic Development Hub for Well-being in the municipality of Zapotlán de Juárez.

He also announced that cement company Cruz Azul would invest 6.5 billion pesos (US $383.3 million) to “reactivate” a plant in the municipality of Tula de Allende.

Deputy Economy Minister Ximena Escobedo said that the 10-billion-peso investment by Dewa would be divided into five stages. Among the projects in the first stage, she said, is the construction of the first two industrial buildings “that will soon house companies.” Escobedo said that construction of the two buildings would cost 2 billion pesos.

Germán Ahumada Alduncin, founder and executive director of Dewa, said that “an industrial logistics platform” will be developed across more than 910 hectares in Zapotlán de Juárez, located in southern Hidalgo near the state’s border with México state. The economic hub will be “designed to receive advanced manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceutical and medical device companies,” he said.

Nuestro titular @CarlosHenkelE acompañó al gobernador @juliomenchaca_ a la #MañaneraDelPueblo con la presidenta @Claudiashein para presentar proyectos clave de inversión para la entidad.

Impulsamos con firmeza el nuevo Polo de Desarrollo Económico para el Bienestar Reserva pic.twitter.com/sP92iSkwzG — Desarrollo Económico (@Sedeco_Hgo) August 19, 2026

“The project involves an investment of more than 10 billion pesos and will combine industrial infrastructure with clean energy, services and complementary equipment,” Ahumada said, adding that construction of the first stage will create an estimated 5,100 jobs.

Sheinbaum: Security operation provoked violence in Michoacán

A reporter asked the president about violence on Wednesday morning in Michoacán, where narco-blockades were set up on highways in various parts of the state. The setting alight of vehicles to create the blockades was reportedly a response to a security operation targeting Heraclio Guerrero Martínez, an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel plaza chief known as “Tío Lako.”

Sheinbaum didn’t mention Guerrero by name, but said there was an operation to detain “one or several important targets.”

“The Security Cabinet will provide information later,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the security operation in Michoacán provoked a violent response in “some places.”

She said that the Mexican Army is in Michoacán to support the response to the situation. Five presumed criminals were reportedly killed on Tuesday during a clash between the army and a criminal group in the municipality of Los Reyes.

Velasco: Mexico is seeking justice for Mexicans who died in ICE custody

A reporter asked the president what her government is seeking by filing complaints with prosecutor’s offices in the U.S. regarding the deaths of 17 Mexican citizens in the custody of ICE or during ICE operations. Sheinbaum referred the question to Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco.

“What we’re seeking is justice,” Velasco said.

“For there to be justice, there has to be an investigation,” he said, referring to probes into each of the deaths of Mexicans in ICE custody or during ICE operations.

“… There has to be a determination of responsibilities,” Velasco said.

“And naturally each case is different,” he added. “What we’re seeking is accountability and a determination of what happened in each case.”

Asked whether investigations could lead to criminal charges, Velasco responded, “of course.”

“This is what we’re setting out, that if there was criminal responsibility, there should be justice,” he said.

In July, the Mexican government filed a total of 20 complaints with U.S. prosecutors in states where the deaths of the 17 Mexicans occurred, namely Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri and Texas.

Sheinbaum said that the families of Mexicans who have died in ICE custody or ICE operations in the U.S. are normally responsible for filing complaints and the Mexican government “supports them.”

“However, we’re now talking about 17 compatriots who have died in the United States,” she said.

“… So we made the decision to directly file the complaints,” Sheinbaum said.

“… There are a lot of cases and our obligation is always to defend Mexicans in the United States or anywhere in the world,” she said.

World.title: Opinion: What good is a collection Mexico can’t afford to keep?
World.content:
Amigos, you’ve seen the coverage of the Gelman Collection controversy, including the open letter from our colleagues Keith Rosenblum and Jesús Ibarra asking President Claudia Sheinbaum to expropriate and nationalize the works.

As an art historian, I’ve stayed out of this and other debates about expropriating, repatriating and nationalizing Mexican art, because these cases are the symptom of a much bigger problem.

Here it is, plainly: Mexico has claimed ownership of more cultural heritage than any government could afford to look after — and then locked out the only money that might have helped. We hold one of the largest bodies of tangible heritage in the world and maintain it on one of the smallest budgets.

That’s the result of decades of policy in which art and culture served as instruments of government, useful for encouraging national pride more than as a commitment to researching and preserving what actually makes up Mexico.

How Mexican culture works

Like anywhere else, culture here has two sectors. Private companies and individuals fund major art collections — Carlos Slim’s at the Museo Soumaya, FEMSA, Jumex — and pay for concerts, touring orchestras, films and plays.

Meanwhile, everything public begins at the Secretaría de Cultura, the cabinet-level ministry that coordinates every institute, museum, school, performing company and research center beneath it.

Mexico’s federal cultural heritage structure and its 2026 budget are divided into two main branches: the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH), which safeguards, researches and teaches everything in this territory up to the 19th century; and the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL), which picks up in the 20th century.

Their budgets look similar, but the jobs aren’t: INAH covers almost four millennia of heritage across the national territory, while INBAL also runs 29 schools, the national conservatory, the ballet and the orchestras.

A dozen more agencies, from the film institute to public radio, divide what’s left.

Now the number that matters. The Carta Cultural Iberoamericana recommends countries devote 1% of public spending to culture. Mexico’s entire culture budget comes to 0.15% of federal spending.

No box office will ever be enough

INBAL’s largest program takes roughly 2.7 million pesos — 57% of the institute’s budget — with more than 95% going to salaries. INAH’s heritage protection program received 3.4 million pesos, roughly 77% of which was used for staff pay. What remains has to cover everything else, down to the electricity that keeps the air conditioning running.

You might assume that the current budget at least buys us a full accounting of what we own. Of 53,009 registered archaeological zones, INAH estimates the real number of sites holding remains at around 200,000 — we have registered a quarter of what we believe is out there.

And last October, the Auditoría Superior de la Federación found deficiencies in inventory and cataloging in more than 90% of the cultural assets it reviewed. We are not only failing to conserve our heritage; we don’t reliably know what we have.

‘But I pay for a ticket every time I go to a museum’

I learned the rule that governs all of this from Mericia Morales Curiel, one of the most important cultural managers working in Mexico and my professor: What a museum takes in at the door will never be enough to run a museum, let alone a cultural industry.

A museum is research, salaries, climate control, insurance, cataloging, conservation labs, education and security — a permanent running cost attached to objects that earn nothing on their own.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art spent more than US $402 million to operate in 2023-24. Admissions brought in US $53.3 million — 13%. The rest comes from an ecosystem that lets private industry and private citizens invest in it.

Here, there’s been a proposal to raise museum admission by as much as 223%. France ran that experiment. In January, the Louvre raised non-EU entry 45%, to 32 euros, expecting 15 to 20 million euros a year from 8.7 million visitors — barely a dent in its repair bill. France’s national auditors found the reason that bill exists: Between 2018 and 2024, the Louvre spent 105.4 million euros on art purchases and only 26.7 million on maintenance and safety compliance, allowing its security and infrastructure to decay. Their recommendation was to scrap the rule requiring the museum to spend 20% of ticket income on acquiring more art.

Back to Gelman

I feel torn writing this, but what good is owning a collection we can’t even afford to keep?

Our colleagues propose that Congress approve a budget under which, per Article 27, the state pays the collection’s holder what his property is worth: US $350 million. That is roughly 43% of Mexico’s entire annual culture budget, and more than INBAL’s total for the year. Add insurance, which recurs annually. And add a bank: The collection is pledged as collateral on a US $150 million loan from Banco Santander, which holds first claim on the paintings if the loan isn’t repaid.

They also assume no court would overturn a claim involving Frida Kahlo. In July, the Supreme Court agreed to review whether the 1984 decree protecting her work is constitutional at all, after INBAL denied Banco Ve por Más permission to permanently export “Autorretrato con medallón.” Article 16 of the 1972 law says privately owned artistic monuments may be exported with a permit. The absolute ban isn’t in the law. It’s in the decree.

What the law actually delivers

By decree, the entire body of work of 10 artists is a monumento artístico — among them Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros, Remedios Varo and Kahlo. Wherever it hangs, the state guarantees it “belongs” to all Mexicans.

Article 33 goes further: It claims the work of Mexican artists wherever in the world it was made, although it does not grant extraterritorial jurisdiction or ownership over works created or held entirely abroad under foreign law.

In practice, it delivers almost nothing. Madonna owns at least two Kahlos, among them “My Birth.” When the Detroit Institute of Arts spent more than a year trying to borrow it for a major Rivera and Kahlo show, she declined, and that was the end of it.

A work we call national heritage hangs in a private home abroad, and the country it supposedly belongs to has no standing to see it, inspect it or ask about its condition.

The decree bans permanent export from Mexico. It brings nothing home and obliges no one to show you anything. The promise is real in law and hollow in practice.

A reminder, and a lesson

How many of you have visited archaeological sites and found interpretive panels you could barely read, in Spanish only, with a guide explaining that the information is out of date? Or seen banners outside a museum because the workers are protesting their conditions? I’m not judging: For what heritage on this scale costs, these institutions perform real miracles.

And here is what makes the arithmetic absurd: In 2023, Mexico’s cultural sector generated 2.8% of national gross domestic product and employed 1.4 million people. We are not subsidizing a luxury; we are underfunding an industry.

There is a solution, and it isn’t asking the president to expropriate anything. Pago en especie, codified in 1975 from an idea that Siqueiros pitched in 1957, lets artists settle their taxes with their own work — a national collection built out of the tax code. It is 51 years old officially, and we have built nothing beside it since. Finishing what Siqueiros started would take four things:

Extend pago en especie past the artist’s studio

Let heirs and collectors settle inheritance and capital gains obligations with declared works, independently appraised and transferred to public collections.

Make giving deductible in a way that isn’t punitive

Donations are capped at a small share of the previous year’s income and sit inside an overall cap. Lift that ceiling for works given to public institutions.

Create a conservation fund

Seed it with a share of the fees the state already charges for export permits and international loans, and match it with corporate contributions. A company can sponsor a stadium; it should be able to sponsor the restoration of a Rivera and be named for it.

Turn the declaratoria into a bargain instead of a bill

Offer owners technical assistance, shared restoration costs and clear export rules in exchange for enforceable commitments to exhibit the work here.

The collectors are already here — the Soumaya, FEMSA and Jumex, as well as the ones we never see. What we have never built is a legal way for any of them to help keep the rest of it alive.

So let’s legislate again — not for a single collection, but to protect our patrimonio from looting, the black market, neglect, decay, and from failing to train the next generation of researchers, historians and restorers.

Let what makes us proud be the sharing of these works and their histories. Not merely the fact that they sit on Mexican soil, quietly falling apart in a warehouse.

Maria Meléndez writes for Mexico News Daily in Mexico City.

World.title: Mexico’s Cruz Azul Cement Cooperative Bets US$381 Million on an Idle Plant
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts — The money 6.5 billion pesos, about US$381 million at the 17.06 peso rate of August 19, 2026.

— The plant Ciudad Cooperativa Cruz Azul at Tula de Allende, in Hidalgo state, north of Mexico City.

— The payer the cooperative itself, not the federal budget. President Sheinbaum hosted the announcement.

— The promise a new kiln line running at 3 million tonnes of cement a year, and 14,200 direct and indirect jobs.

— The backstory the site was seized in 2020, went dark in 2022, and was recovered by court order in February 2026.

A ten-year civil war inside Mexico’s most famous worker-owned company left ten people dead and its founding factory silent.

Illustrative photo: the Cruz Azul cement works at Tepezala, Aguascalientes, one of the cooperative’s four plants. The idle Hidalgo plant is meant to reach 3 million tonnes a year. (Photo: Luis Alvaz, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Mexico’s Cruz Azul cement cooperative will spend 6.5 billion pesos, roughly US$381 million, to revive its founding factory. The plant sits at Tula de Allende in Hidalgo state, and it has produced nothing for years.

President Claudia Sheinbaum put the announcement on stage at her morning press conference on August 19.

What Was Announced, and by Whom

Victor Manuel Velazquez, who chairs the cooperative’s board, laid out the plan at the presidential palace on Wednesday morning. Sheinbaum and Hidalgo governor Julio Menchaca stood alongside him while he spoke.

The headline number is 6.5 billion pesos. That is about US$381 million, because the Bank of Mexico reference rate stood at 17.06 pesos to the dollar that day.

One point matters for anyone reading this from abroad. The federal government is not writing the cheque; it is hosting the news.

The cash comes from the cooperative’s own balance sheet.

Where the 6.5 Billion Pesos Goes

The cooperative broke the sum into parts. For example, more than 1.8 billion pesos, close to US$106 million, has already gone on cleaning up and refitting the existing plant.

Another 3.7 billion pesos, about US$217 million, is buying a new cement production line. That line is roughly 85 percent finished, so the spending is not a wish list.

A further billion pesos, near US$59 million, goes to the cooperative’s hospital in Tula. In addition, surgical theatres, an intensive care unit and a blood bank are on the list.

It is also involved in the cargo or mail; passenger charter; development of frequent-flyer programs; intellectual property owner; travel packages; funding: aircraft financing; and provision of maintenance and hangarage services for aircraft, engines, parts and pieces, aircraft acquisition,…

The Cruz Azul Cement Company Owns the Football Club

Outside Mexico the name means one thing: a blue-shirted football team from Mexico City. Inside Mexico, however, Cruz Azul cement is the business that pays for it.

Cooperativa La Cruz Azul is the employer, the asset and the legal person. The club is a subsidiary of the cement maker, not the other way round.

So when Sheinbaum talked about Cruz Azul on Wednesday, she was talking about kilns and clinker. As a result, the football side was not the subject at all.

A Worker-Owned Firm With a Long Memory

The story starts in 1881, after an English businessman opened a lime works at Jasso in Hidalgo. Workers took the plant over in November 1931 once the owners walked away.

In January 1934 they formally constituted a cooperative with 192 worker-owners. Nearly a century later the roll of full members sits at around 400.

Today the group runs four cement plants, in Hidalgo, Oaxaca, Aguascalientes and Puebla, while new capacity is going up in Campeche. El Economista counts about 9,500 direct jobs across the business.

Why the Hidalgo Plant Went Quiet

The Tula site was the original works and, before the trouble, supplied 35 to 40 percent of the cooperative’s cement. Then the internal war reached it.

A rival faction physically occupied the plant from 2020. Production stopped for good in August 2022, because the state power utility cut the electricity supply during the dispute.

Because the site was blocked, the cooperative suspended pay for 2,812 workers from February 2025. Local reporting says more than 5,000 people, direct and indirect, eventually lost work.

Ten Years and Ten Deaths

This was not a boardroom argument. In March the Spanish daily El Pais summed the fight up in a headline: ten years and ten dead.

The worst day came in April 2022. An attempt to retake the plant ended with eight people killed and eleven injured.

Meanwhile another clash in September 2024 brought roughly 120 arrests. The old boss, Guillermo ‘Billy’ Alvarez, resigned in August 2020 amid federal money-laundering and organised-crime investigations.

Warrants against former directors were still live into 2025.

How the Cooperative Got the Plant Back

On February 12, 2026, prosecutors acting on a judge’s order handed the site to the Velazquez faction. Since then, police have guarded the perimeter.

Velazquez was re-elected board president in May for another five years. Therefore the August announcement is both his victory lap and his bill.

Even so, nobody has published a firm restart date. The new line is nearly built, and local coverage speaks of months rather than weeks.

Hidalgo’s Wider Investment Day

The cement plan came inside a bigger package for the state worth more than 16.6 billion pesos, close to US$973 million. Cruz Azul is the smaller half of it.

The larger piece is 10.1 billion pesos, about US$592 million, from industrial developer Dewa Capital. That money builds a 910-hectare logistics and industrial park at Zapotlan de Juarez, in five phases.

For a state that usually watches investment land in Nuevo Leon or the Bajio, a single morning delivering both projects is unusual. In short, Hidalgo had a good Wednesday.

A Rough July for Mexican Retirement Savings

The same week brought less cheerful economic news. Mexico’s Afore pension managers booked paper losses of 92.763 billion pesos in July, or roughly US$5.44 billion, according to regulator Consar.

That reversed a small June gain of 7.66 billion pesos. However, El Economista blamed a slide in global markets rather than anything domestic.

Savers should keep the scale in mind, however. The funds are still up 391.3 billion pesos, about US$22.9 billion, over the first seven months of the year.

Washington Sends Mexicans to Central America

A separate row opened on August 18. CBS News reported that the United States has been deporting Mexican citizens to Guatemala and Honduras.

Two Homeland Security officials described the flights. Hundreds of people have been moved this way, although no exact tally is public.

Independent monitors put the Guatemala figure above 1,500 by mid-July. Mexico’s foreign ministry pushed back in writing.

It accepts the return of all its nationals, yet it rejects their removal to third countries and says no such agreement exists.

What to Watch From Here

The test is simple: does smoke come out of the Tula stacks, and when. After all, a finished kiln line is not the same as a running one.

Cement demand in Mexico tracks housing and public works, so the timing suits the government’s building plans. Meanwhile the cooperative still has to rehire and retrain a scattered workforce.

Watch also whether the 14,200 jobs figure survives contact with reality. Because it counts indirect work across the whole region, such numbers rarely arrive whole.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this the football club or a company?

It is the company. Cooperativa La Cruz Azul makes Cruz Azul cement and owns the football club as a subsidiary.

Is the Mexican government paying for it?

No. The money comes from the cooperative. President Sheinbaum announced it at her daily press conference, and Hidalgo’s governor backed it.

How much is 6.5 billion pesos in dollars?

About US$381 million, using the Bank of Mexico reference rate of 17.06 pesos per dollar on August 19, 2026. The wider Hidalgo package tops US$970 million.

Why was the plant closed for so long?

A leadership fight split the cooperative. A rival faction held the site from 2020, and the power supply was cut in August 2022.

Sources: El Economista; La Jornada; El Pais; Expansion; CBS News.

World.title: Boric and Matthei Reject Chile’s Kast Security Reform
World.content:
Chile · Politics

Key Facts — The bill Kast filed eight constitutional changes in the Senate on Monday, 17 August 2026, under Chile’s fastest legislative track.

— The flashpoint a new state of exception the president could declare for up to 120 days, renewable once.

— Boric on 19 August the former president called it ‘a limitation of liberties not seen before’ in Chilean democracy.

— Matthei the right’s 2025 presidential candidate said on 18 August that anyone expecting a constitutional fix is ‘completely wrong’.

— The maths a four-sevenths quorum means 89 of 155 deputies and 29 of 50 senators, and the government is short in the Senate.

— Elsewhere a trade deal with Trinidad and Tobago cleared a committee on 18 August, promising duty-free salmon and trout.

Chile’s homicide count has fallen for three years running, which is why critics keep asking why emergency powers are needed now.

Illustrative photo: the Palacio de La Moneda in Santiago, where President Kast signed the constitutional security reform on 10 August 2026 before it reached the Senate a week later. (Photo: Miguel hernandez, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Kast security reform has now united two politicians who agree on almost nothing else. Former president Gabriel Boric and veteran right-winger Evelyn Matthei both rejected it this week.

Days after the government sent it to Chile’s Senate. Their objection is the same: the bill would hand one person extraordinary powers.

What Boric Said, and Where

Gabriel Boric spoke on Wednesday, 19 August 2026, at the launch of a book by his former finance minister, Mario Marcel. He governed Chile until 11 March 2026, when José Antonio Kast took over.

Boric said he hoped for opposition that was ‘frank, respectful, but open, clear and firm’. The reform, he argued.

‘seeks to install a state of siege of 240 days with the exclusive authority of the President of the Republic’. Then came the line that travelled.

It amounted to ‘a limitation of liberties not seen before, unprecedented in Chilean democracy’, he said, according to El País and BioBioChile. In fact, that phrase belongs to Boric alone.

Matthei made a separate and rather different case a day earlier.

Matthei Attacks From the Right, Not the Left

Evelyn Matthei is not an opposition leader in the usual sense. She belongs to the UDI, the traditional Chilean right.

And ran as the Chile Vamos candidate in the 2025 election that Kast eventually won. Speaking to Radio Pauta on Tuesday, 18 August, she was blunt.

‘If anyone thinks that changing the constitution will end the security problems in Chile, they are completely wrong,’ she said. She went further on the emergency powers themselves.

‘Having a 120-day state of exception, where on top of that the president can do almost whatever he wants. What would happen if this were in the wrong hands.

However, her doubts matter more than a left-wing complaint would. Because she sits on the government’s own side of the spectrum, her words give wavering coalition senators cover.

What the Kast Security Reform Actually Contains

The reform is one piece of a package the government calls ACOT, the Agenda Against Organised Crime and Terrorism. Kast announced it in a national address on 5 August and signed the constitutional text at La Moneda on 10 August.

It went to the Senate on Monday, 17 August, with ‘suma urgencia’ — the fastest track Chilean procedure allows. The text carries eight changes to the constitution.

It does not create a new security ministry. That already exists, and Martín Arrau has run it since Kast took office.

Instead the reform writes public security into the constitution as a duty of the state. It also creates an official register of criminal and terrorist organisations.

Separate prison regimes for their leaders, and a route to seize and destroy criminal assets.

The 240-Day Question

Meanwhile, the centrepiece is a brand new state of exception, separate from the four Chile already has. A president could declare it when public security faces a grave and imminent threat, or has already been badly damaged.

It would run for up to 120 days. Under the reading published by El País and BioBioChile, the president could renew it once for the same period without asking Congress.

Which is where the 240-day figure comes from. Emol reads the text differently and says extensions follow the normal rules requiring congressional consent.

That ambiguity is itself part of the argument. Inside a declared zone the president could suspend or restrict personal liberty, movement and assembly.

He could also restrict association, intercept documents and communications, and requisition property, with a general officer placed in command.

Why the Government Says Chile Needs It

Kast’s case is that ordinary law has run out of room. In his August address he promised ‘a constitutional reform that enshrines, without ambiguity.

That protecting the security of people is a duty of the state’. Arrau, the security minister, has made the sharper argument.

‘We have to demystify the idea that the constitution is untouchable,’ he told CNN Chile on 17 August. ‘It can be touched intelligently and in a limited way.

He describes the new powers as deliberately narrow. They are meant for ‘deep, temporary interventions with accountability’ in pockets of territory where gangs operate and the state struggles to enter.

Arrau also insists the tool is a police one rather than a military one. Armed forces support, he says, would be for very specific tasks.

The Crime Numbers Both Sides Use

Chile is safer than the headlines suggest, and safer than it was. Official figures show 1,209 homicide victims in 2024, a rate near 6.1 per 100,000.

Falling to 1,091 in 2025, a rate near 5.4. That was a drop of roughly 11.5% and the third consecutive annual decline.

After the 17 August police committee, the security ministry reported homicide victims down another 17.4% so far in 2026. Supporters read that as proof the strategy works and should be deepened.

Critics read the same data as proof that emergency powers are unnecessary. Even so, fear has not fallen as fast as the body count.

Officials point to more than 200,000 violent robberies in 2025 and to international gangs now operating inside the country.

The Vote Maths Is Tight

A constitutional change in Chile needs four-sevenths of sitting members in both chambers. In practice that means 89 of 155 deputies and 29 of 50 senators.

BioBioChile counted the votes on 19 August and made it uncomfortable reading for La Moneda. The government has about 67 deputies and 23 senators, reaching roughly 26 in the Senate even with sympathetic independents.

Doubts run through the coalition itself. UDI president Guillermo Ramírez initially said his party could not back the reform.

And senators from Renovación Nacional and the Partido Nacional Libertario have voiced reservations. Still, the government won a public boost this week.

Senator María José Gatica of Renovación Nacional said on 18 August the plan had her support because ‘we need every tool to confront organised crime’.

Lawyers Are Split, and Loudly

Mauricio Duce, a criminal justice scholar, told the Associated Press on 19 August that the proposed regime ‘is right at the line. And probably crosses it, of what is admissible in a democratic system’.

Constitutional lawyer Jorge Correa Sutil made a milder criticism on 7 August. Writing security into article one is ‘completely redundant’, he told Cooperativa, because the duty is already there.

Others object to a clause restricting state benefits, including health and education access. For up to 15 years after a sentence is served.

Academic Verónica Undurraga called the draft ‘deeply worrying’. Supporters answer that constitutions are meant to be amended once reality changes.

The dispute is less about crime than about how much power one office should hold.

A Caribbean Trade Deal Moves a Step Closer

While the security fight ran, Chile’s trade agenda took a quieter step. On 18 August the foreign affairs committee of the Chamber of Deputies approved the partial scope agreement with Trinidad and Tobago.

This is a bilateral deal with a single country, not a pact with a Caribbean bloc. Trinidad and Tobago belongs to CARICOM, and the trade agency SUBREI calls it Chile’s first trade agreement with a CARICOM member.

Salmon and trout are the headline winners. Along with grapes, apples, pears, apricots and nuts.

They would enter duty-free from the day the deal takes effect, replacing tariffs that can reach 40%. The traffic runs both ways.

Ammonia and liquefied natural gas from Trinidad and Tobago. Where it is Chile’s main supplier, would drop from a 6% tariff to zero.

What Happens Next

The agreement was signed back in April 2025, after negotiations that ran from 2021 to 2024. Trinidad and Tobago has already ratified it, so Chile’s Congress is the last step before it enters into force.

Slower items are phased in. Frozen berries, prunes and some wood products reach zero in year four, while peaches, kiwis.

Fresh berries and wine take nine years, and olive oil gets a reduced 5% rate. Back on security, the Senate now starts committee work under a compressed timetable.

Because three committees are involved, the government’s hoped-for two to three months looks ambitious. Kast is negotiating from a modest position.

Cadem put his approval at 41% on 16 August, while Criteria the same day had him at 35% with 55% disapproving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is José Antonio Kast the president or the president-elect?

He is the sitting president. Kast won the runoff on 14 December 2025 and was sworn in on 11 March 2026, succeeding Gabriel Boric.

Who said the reform would bring ‘a limitation of liberties not seen before’?

Gabriel Boric, on 19 August 2026, at a book launch for former finance minister Mario Marcel. Evelyn Matthei made separate criticisms a day earlier.

Does the Kast security reform create a new security ministry?

No. Chile’s security ministry already exists and is run by Martín Arrau. The reform changes the constitution instead, adding a new state of exception and other tools.

Did Chile sign a trade deal with a Caribbean bloc?

Not with a bloc. Chile signed a bilateral partial scope agreement with Trinidad and Tobago in April 2025.

Sources: El País Chile; BioBioChile; Emol; La Tercera; El Mostrador; Cooperativa; Associated Press; SUBREI.

World.title: Escondida Wage Talks Open at the World’s Biggest Copper Mine in Chile
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts — The union Sindicato N°2 de Supervisores at Escondida, with 1,020 members, filed its contract proposal in mid-August 2026.

— The deadline the current collective contract runs out on September 30, 2026, so a new one is due by then.

— The last deal August 2023 brought a 36-month contract, a closing bonus of CLP 17.8 million (about US$19,200) and CLP 3 million (about US$3,200) in cheap loans.

— The precedent the operators’ union struck for about six weeks in 2017, and for three days in 2024 before winning roughly US$32,000 a worker.

— The copper backdrop cash copper on the London Metal Exchange hit a record US$14,912 a tonne on August 17, 2026.

— The other story Lundin Mining cut 2026 output guidance at Caserones to 120,000-130,000 tonnes after two winter storms.

Copper is trading near record highs. And a second Atacama storm has already forced Lundin Mining to cut output at its Caserones mine.

The open pit at Escondida in Chile’s Atacama Desert, the world’s biggest copper mine, which produced 1.3 million tonnes of copper in BHP’s 2025 financial year. (Photo: Bachelot Pierre J-P, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The biggest wage negotiation of Chile’s mining year has begun at Escondida, the world’s biggest copper mine. The supervisors’ union filed its demands in mid-August and asked BHP for what it calls a fair sharing of the wealth.

Because copper is near record prices and BHP has just posted bumper profits, the workers think their timing is good.

Who Is Actually At The Table

The union that opened talks is Sindicato N°2 de Supervisores de Minera Escondida. It has 1,020 active members, although it was only founded in 2014.

That matters, because the older operators’ and maintainers’ union, Sindicato N°1, has richer benefits built up over decades. The supervisors say they simply want to level the playing field.

The Demand, In The Union’s Own Words

Union president Alexis Barrera told Diario Financiero that high prices, record output and historic company results all point one way. So the union is pushing for more.

His phrase was blunt: the union wants a “fair sharing of the wealth with the workers”. Still, he framed it as a chance to settle without a fight.

The Clock On The Escondida Contract

The union handed over its proposal in mid-August, and BHP’s formal reply was due within days. The current collective contract expires on September 30, 2026.

That date is the real deadline. After it passes, Chilean labour law hands the union the right to vote on a strike.

What The Last Deal Paid

In August 2023 the two sides signed a 36-month contract after six days of mediation by the regional labour office in Antofagasta. The package included a closing bonus of CLP 17.8 million.

That is about US$19,200 at 927.5 pesos to the dollar on August 19, 2026. There were also soft loans worth CLP 3 million, roughly US$3,200.

Those are the numbers the supervisors now want to beat.

Why Escondida Strikes Move World Markets

Escondida sits in the Atacama Desert and is run by BHP, which holds 57.5%. Meanwhile Rio Tinto owns 30% and Japan’s JECO group the rest.

The mine produced 1.3 million tonnes of copper in BHP’s 2025 financial year, its best in 17 years. Chile as a whole mined about 5.4 million tonnes in 2025, close to a quarter of world supply.

The 2017 Strike Everyone Still Remembers

In February 2017 the operators’ union walked out and stayed out for roughly six weeks. Chilean accounts put it at 44 days, the longest stoppage the country’s private mining sector had seen.

Mining. com reported the mine lost more than 120,000 tonnes of copper.

In the end the union invoked Article 369 of the old labour code. That extended the old contract for 18 months, so workers returned with no new deal and no bonus.

And The Short, Expensive Strike Of 2024

The pattern changed in 2024. Sindicato N°1, with about 2,400 members, downed tools on Tuesday, August 13, and had a preliminary accord by Friday.

Reuters put the final package at around US$32,000 a worker plus US$2,000 in low-interest loans, on a three-year contract. Three days of stoppage bought far more than 44 days had in 2017.

Copper Prices Are Doing The Union A Favour

Cash copper on the London Metal Exchange set a record US$14,912 a tonne on August 17, 2026. In fact a squeeze in the London market drove it there.

The three-month benchmark was trading nearer US$13,900 a tonne by August 19. That leaves copper up around 14% so far this year.

Meanwhile BHP reported underlying attributable profit of US$13.2 billion for the year to June 2026, up 30%. In addition, copper overtook iron ore as its biggest earner for the first time.

The Awkward Part: Output Is About To Fall

BHP is not negotiating from a position of pure strength. Escondida president Alejandro Tapia said in August that the mine enters a temporary production valley.

As a result, output will be 1.0 to 1.1 million tonnes in its 2027 financial year. That is a drop of up to 300,000 tonnes, caused by falling ore grades.

A new concentrator costing an estimated US$4.4 billion to US$5.15 billion is meant to reverse it later.

Lundin Cuts Its Caserones Forecast After A Second Storm

Further south in the same desert, a very different problem hit another Chilean copper mine. Lundin Mining said on August 19 that a second severe winter storm in the Atacama region had damaged Caserones again.

The first storm knocked out power at the mine from July 18 to July 30. Then a storm that began on August 13 re-damaged a transmission tower, and power failed again on August 14.

The New Numbers From Lundin

Caserones now expects 120,000 to 130,000 tonnes of copper in 2026, down from 130,000 to 140,000 tonnes. Cash costs rise to US$2.15-US$2.35 a pound from US$2.05-US$2.25.

Company-wide guidance falls to 300,000-325,000 tonnes from 310,000-335,000 tonnes. Candelaria, Lundin’s other Chilean mine, is still expected to hit its target.

What To Watch Next

Chief executive Jack Lundin said crews were restoring power and reopening access roads, with full power expected within days. Even so, the company had kept its forecast unchanged after the first storm, and only cut once the second one landed.

For Escondida, the next milestone is BHP’s answer and then the countdown to September 30. Talks at the mine have gone to the wire before.

Both a 44-day walkout and a three-day one are live in everyone’s memory.

Background: Chile Inflation Holds Flat in June but Annual Rate Climbs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which union is negotiating at Escondida in 2026?

Sindicato N°2 de Supervisores de Minera Escondida, the supervisors’ union, which has 1,020 members. The larger operators’ union, Sindicato N°1, is not at the table this time.

When could a strike happen?

The current contract expires on September 30, 2026. Under Chilean law a strike vote only becomes possible once bargaining stalls near that deadline, so nothing can happen before then.

How much did Escondida workers win in 2024?

Reuters reported a package worth about US$32,000 per worker, plus US$2,000 in low-interest loans. The three-year contract was signed in August 2024 after a three-day strike.

How big is the Lundin Mining production cut at Caserones?

Lundin trimmed 2026 copper guidance at Caserones by 10,000 tonnes at each end of the range, to 120,000-130,000 tonnes. Two winter storms cut power to the mine.

Sources: Diario Financiero; BioBioChile; Lundin Mining; Reuters; Mining.com; BHP.

World.title: Argentina Ships First Offshore Pipes for Vaca Muerta Oil Pipeline
World.content:
Argentina · Energy

Key Facts — The shipment The vessel Navvik Launcher loaded the first 99 subsea pipes at San Antonio Este, Rio Negro, from Thursday, August 13.

— The supplier SIAT, the Tenaris welded-pipe business, provided the steel; over 10,100 tonnes moved out of Dock Sud, Buenos Aires.

— The coating Of the 721 pipes now stockpiled in Patagonia, 658 carry a concrete jacket applied at the Socotherm plant in Escobar.

— The line 437 kilometres from Allen to Punta Colorada, about US$3 billion, starting at 180,000 barrels a day and scaling to 550,000.

— The southern bet YPF is preparing a fresh exploration campaign at Palermo Aike in Santa Cruz for November or December 2026.

The buried 437-kilometre line is already finished. The sea leg and its two mooring buoys are now the part that decides when Argentina can load its first export tanker.

Illustrative photo: the subsea pipelay vessel Seven Navica, of the type used to lay offshore lines. At Punta Colorada, the specialised vessel Seminole will lay about five kilometres of concrete-coated pipe out to two mooring buoys. (Photo: JoachimKohler-HB, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The first steel for the underwater stretch of Argentina’s Vaca Muerta oil pipeline has finally left port. A supply vessel loaded 99 pipes at San Antonio Este and set course for Punta Colorada, on the Atlantic coast.

After that short hop, the country’s biggest private energy project starts building the part that touches the sea.

What Actually Left the Dock

The vessel is called the Navvik Launcher, and it is the first of nine platform supply ships booked for this job. Loading began at one in the afternoon on Thursday, August 13, at the port of San Antonio Este.

It carried 99 pipes toward the works area off Sierra Grande, in Rio Negro province. Diario Rio Negro reported on August 19 that the load was complete and the first batch had sailed.

Those 99 are a small slice of a much bigger pile. In June, the bulk carrier MV Athanasia delivered 721 steel pipes to the same port.

They have been stacked there ever since.

Why These Pipes Are Not Ordinary Pipes

Of the 721 tubes, 658 wear a thick concrete jacket. That coating was applied at the Socotherm plant in Escobar, in Buenos Aires province, before the steel went back to the docks.

Concrete does two jobs at once here. It shields the steel from the seabed.

It also adds weight, so the line will not float or shift in the currents of the Golfo San Matias.

The Long Chain Behind One Boat Trip

The pipe itself came from SIAT, the welded-pipe business Tenaris runs in Argentina from Valentin Alsina, near Buenos Aires. More than 10,100 tonnes of it was shipped out of the public wharf at Dock Sud.

Loginter handled storage and stowage at Dock Sud, while Arendal coordinated the sea transport. So a single 99-pipe sailing sits on top of months of mill work, coating and warehousing.

That matters for a country trying to build local supply chains. Because the steel, the coating and the logistics were all Argentine, the project keeps much of its spending at home.

The Vaca Muerta Oil Pipeline in Plain Numbers

The line runs 437 kilometres from Allen, in Rio Negro, to a new terminal at Punta Colorada. YPF has put the total cost of pipeline plus terminal at about US$2.98 billion, which most reports round to US$3 billion.

The buried trunk line is 30 inches across. Near the coast and out under the water, the pipe widens to 38 inches, with 24-inch branches feeding each offshore loading point.

Techint said on August 14 that all 437 kilometres were built, after a pressure test on the Rio Negro crossing. Even so, the wider project was still running at roughly 77 to 80 percent in mid-August.

What Waits at Punta Colorada

The terminal will hold six tanks of 120,000 cubic metres each. Two CALM monobuoys, moored offshore, will let very large crude carriers load without coming alongside a jetty.

The subsea line between the tanks and the buoys is only about five kilometres long. Still, it is the piece that turns a Patagonian pipeline into an export business.

The buoys themselves are built in the United Arab Emirates and shipped out through the Strait of Hormuz. YPF chief executive Horacio Marin said in August that the second unit was already at sea.

The Offshore Fleet Is Assembling

A jack-up platform, the Combifloat C7, took position off Punta Colorada in the second week of August. It will support the work of joining the pipe on the seabed.

Meanwhile the pipelay vessel Seminole is being prepared in Bahia Blanca, after arriving on a semi-submersible heavy-lift ship. Once ready, it will lay the concrete-coated line out to the buoys.

When the First Tanker Sails

YPF told a congressional committee in late July that the first cargo should leave between the end of 2026 and early 2027. Several Argentine outlets now lean toward the early-2027 end of that window.

The system starts at about 180,000 barrels a day. It is designed to climb to 550,000 barrels a day during 2027 and, on company projections, to 700,000 by 2028.

That ramp is the whole point. Vaca Muerta output has outgrown existing export routes.

So a second Atlantic outlet decides how fast Argentina can sell its crude.

Who Owns It and Who Paid

The vehicle, VMOS S.A., groups YPF with Vista, Pan American Energy, Pampa Energia, Chevron, Pluspetrol, Shell, Tecpetrol and Neuquen’s GyP. YPF holds about 30 percent.

Financing leaned on a syndicated loan of roughly US$2 billion from international banks. Argentine reports call it the largest commercial infrastructure credit in the country’s history.

The project is also registered under the RIGI incentive regime for large investments.

The Objection Nobody Has Settled

Not everyone welcomes the terminal. UNESCO has asked Argentina for more environmental information about the works, because of the protected marine area nearby.

The deadline is February 2027. The Golfo San Matias is a calving ground for southern right whales.

Therefore the offshore campaign is being watched closely by conservation groups as well as by traders.

YPF Also Turns to the Younger Sister

While the coast fills with ships, YPF is reviving a very different bet in the far south. Palermo Aike, in Santa Cruz province, is the shale formation Argentine officials call the younger sister of Vaca Muerta.

The province’s first unconventional well, MAYPA. x-1, was drilled by YPF with partner CGC.

It went 3,500 metres down and 1,000 metres sideways, and cost around US$50 million. A production test of about 180 days is under way.

ADNSUR reported on August 15 that YPF is preparing a new exploration campaign there, with work starting in November or December. CGC owner Eduardo Eurnekian has put the play’s potential at up to 10 billion barrels of oil.

He also cites more than 130 trillion cubic feet of gas. Those numbers are company estimates, not certified reserves.

Santa Cruz’s energy minister, Jaime Alvarez, prefers a softer line, calling Palermo Aike possibly half a Vaca Muerta.

What to Watch Next

The next milestones are physical and easy to track. Eight more supply-ship runs will move the rest of the 721 pipes.

Then the Seminole must start laying, and the second monobuoy has to be anchored. Only after those steps does a tanker date become real.

Until then, the finished 437 kilometres of buried steel are a very expensive line waiting on five kilometres of seabed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Vaca Muerta oil pipeline?

It is a 437-kilometre crude line, known as VMOS. It runs from Allen in Rio Negro to a new export terminal at Punta Colorada.

Who supplied the pipes for the offshore section?

SIAT, the Argentine welded-pipe business of Tenaris. More than 10,100 tonnes were shipped from Dock Sud, and 658 of the 721 pipes were concrete-coated at Socotherm in Escobar.

When will Argentina export oil through Punta Colorada?

YPF has guided to a window between late 2026 and early 2027, and recent Argentine reporting leans toward early 2027. The system starts near 180,000 barrels a day.

What is the younger sister of Vaca Muerta?

Palermo Aike, a shale formation in Santa Cruz province. YPF drilled the first unconventional well there with CGC and plans a new exploration campaign starting in November or December 2026.

Sources: Diario Rio Negro; ArgenPorts; GlobalPorts; Techint; Infobae; ADNSUR.

World.title: Argentina Beef Consumption Falls to Its Lowest in Over Two Decades
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The number 46.3 kilos of beef per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026, according to CICCRA.

— The fall down 9.4% from 51.1 kilos a year earlier, or 4.8 kilos less on every plate.

— The supply squeeze domestic beef supply between January and July dropped about 12%, some 163,400 tonnes less than in 2025.

— The price beef cost roughly 52% more in July than a year before, with butcher shops up 56.6%, per IPCVA.

— The bright spots lamb exports rose 34% by volume in the first half, and Panama opened to four Argentine citrus fruits.

Chicken has quietly overtaken beef on the national plate, while lamb exports jump and Panama opens its door to Argentine citrus.

Illustrative photo: an Argentine asado grill with beef cuts, chicken and sausages beside a stack of firewood. Beef consumption has fallen to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest in over two decades. (Photo: Robertaleotta2020, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Argentina beef consumption has slipped to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest reading in more than two decades. That figure covers the 12 months to July 2026 and comes from CICCRA, the country’s meat industry chamber.

Argentines are now eating 4.8 kilos less beef each than they did a year ago.

The Number Behind the Argentina Beef Consumption Slide

CICCRA publishes a rolling 12-month average, so the series smooths out seasonal noise. Its July 2026 reading came in at 46.3 kilos per person, against 51.1 kilos a year earlier.

That is a 9.4% drop, and the chamber called it a historic low. Argentina beef consumption has not been this thin since the early 2000s.

The wider supply picture is starker still. Between January and July, the domestic market absorbed 1.202 million tonnes of beef.

About 12% less than in the same stretch of 2025.

Why the Fall Happened So Fast

Price did most of the work. Beef in the Buenos Aires area cost around 52% more in July 2026 than in July 2025.

According to the IPCVA beef promotion institute. Butcher shops pushed hardest, at 56.6% year on year, while supermarkets rose 43.3%.

Prices did steady over four months, yet the damage to household budgets was already done. Wages have been recovering, but not fast enough to close that gap.

Because beef climbed further than almost anything else in the basket, families simply bought less of it.

Chicken Overtakes Beef on the National Plate

For a country built on the asado, this is the headline shift. Chicken consumption now sits near 49 to 50 kilos per person a year, according to figures from CEPA and industry data.

That puts poultry ahead of beef for the first time in the statistical record. Pork has climbed too, from about 6 kilos per person twenty years ago to roughly 19 kilos today.

The reason is arithmetic, not taste. Chicken prices rose about 30% over the year, barely half the pace of beef, so shoppers switched.

Total meat consumption has held up better than beef alone. Argentines still eat plenty of protein overall, so the change is about which animal, not how much.

Fewer Cattle, Less Meat

Supply tightened as well. Argentina slaughtered 7.09 million head of cattle between January and July 2026, down 9.8% from a year earlier.

Beef output over the same seven months reached 1.689 million tonnes, a 6.8% decline. Producers have been holding back females to rebuild herds, which trims short-term supply.

Carcass weights did rise, softening the blow. Even so, less meat reached the counter while demand for it was already sagging.

Exports Take a Bigger Slice

A shrinking herd is now feeding a growing export book. Shipments between January and July hit 487,200 tonnes carcass equivalent, up 8.8% year on year.

That means roughly 30% of production went abroad, against about a quarter a year earlier. In the first half alone, Argentina sold 280,140 tonnes for about US$2.26 billion.

Analysts expect full-year beef exports above US$3 billion. Since foreign buyers pay in dollars, packers naturally chase them first.

Cheaper Beef Starts Arriving From Brazil

Something unusual is happening at the same time. Argentina, a byword for beef, is importing more of it, mostly from Brazil.

Purchases of Brazilian beef reached about 13,700 tonnes in the first half, up 122% by volume. That is still only around 1.3% of domestic consumption, so the shift is a trend rather than a takeover.

Industry voices describe a slow move toward the Uruguayan model. In short, import cheaper cuts for the home market and send premium local beef overseas.

Lamb Exports Jump 34%

Away from the beef counter, one Argentine meat is booming. Sheep meat exports rose 34% by volume in the first half of 2026, the Agriculture Secretariat reported in mid-August.

Shipments totalled 4,669,757 kilos of product weight, against 3,497,311 kilos a year earlier. Export earnings climbed 46%, and average value per tonne rose 10%.

The European Union remains the main buyer, with Middle Eastern markets growing. Argentina now has 44 open destinations for sheep meat, most of it raised in Patagonia.

Sheep farming remains small next to cattle, yet the growth matters for southern provinces. Santa Cruz and Chubut supply much of the flock behind those shipments.

Panama Opens to Argentine Citrus

The other piece of good news came from Central America. Panama agreed phytosanitary terms for four fresh Argentine citrus fruits in August 2026.

The list covers lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Argentina’s Agriculture Secretariat handled the deal through SENASA, its food safety agency, with Panama’s agriculture ministry MIDA.

Panama published the rules as resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026. Tucumán, the world’s largest lemon producer, stands to gain most, although neither government published a volume target.

What This Means for Visitors and Residents

If you are eating out in Buenos Aires, the steak is still excellent. The difference is what it costs relative to everything else on the menu.

Parrillas have leaned harder on chicken, pork and cheaper cuts. Meanwhile many households now save beef for weekends instead of weekdays.

Restaurant menus tell the same story. Cheaper cuts and chicken dishes have spread, while the premium steaks increasingly target visitors paying in dollars.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether the slide continues. The first is whether real wages keep gaining ground on food prices through the rest of 2026.

The second is the cattle cycle. Once herd rebuilding ends, more animals should reach market, and that extra supply could finally cool prices at the counter.

Imports are the wild card. If Brazilian beef keeps arriving at lower prices, it could put a ceiling on what Argentine butchers can charge.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much beef do Argentines eat now?

About 46.3 kilos per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026. That is 4.8 kilos less than a year earlier, and the lowest figure in more than two decades.

Who publishes the Argentina beef consumption figure?

CICCRA, the Argentine chamber of meat industry and commerce, publishes a monthly report with a rolling 12-month per-capita average. Infobae and other outlets carried the July 2026 reading on 19 August 2026.

Is chicken really more popular than beef in Argentina?

Yes, by volume. Chicken now runs at roughly 49 to 50 kilos per person a year.

Which citrus fruits can Argentina now send to Panama?

Lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Panama approved the phytosanitary requirements in resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026, after talks between SENASA and Panama’s MIDA.

Sources: Infobae; CICCRA; La Nación; IPCVA; Agritotal.

World.title: Argentina Digital Health Plan Lands US$700 Million IDB Credit Line
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The headline number a conditional credit line of up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank, approved by Decree 757/2026.

— The date the decree was signed on August 18, 2026 and published in Argentina’s official gazette on August 19, 2026.

— The borrower the Argentine Republic, not a state bank; provinces receive the money through individual loans.

— The first loan US$85 million for Mendoza’s public hospital network, with disbursements planned over four years.

— The second loan up to US$60 million approved on August 10, 2026 for Rio Negro, aimed at about 320,000 public-system patients.

The first US$85 million goes to Mendoza, and the province has already warned the cash has not landed yet.

Illustrative photo: the Hospital Central and FUESMEN complex in Mendoza, the province set to receive the first US$85 million loan under the US$700 million credit line. (Photo: Federico Gomez Aghetta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
