We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. However, the proposals still require approval from parliament, where Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, has a majority, and President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. 📊 Nowa skala PIT będzie lepiej dopasowana do rosnących wynagrodzeń. Do 130 tys. zł pozostaje stawka 12%, między 130 a 150 tys. zł pojawi się 24%, a 32% zacznie obowiązywać dopiero powyżej 150 tys. zł. 💰 #WięcejWPortfelu pic.twitter.com/1S2MpSkVoC — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 19, 2026 The main elements of the proposed changes, which were outlined by Tusk and finance minister Andrzej Domański on Wednesday, are an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets. Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €27,800) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%. There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount. Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%. Tusk noted that, since his government took office, wages in Poland have increased by around 30%, bringing increasing numbers of people into the higher tax bracket. According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, in June this year, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,401.58 zloty, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year. “We’re not talking about millionaires here; we’re talking about a growing middle class…on whose shoulders the financing of state security, defence spending, etc. rests to a large extent,” said Domański. “We want to change this…so that those who work hard to earn their average wage can clearly feel the relief,” added Tusk. “And we want this to be financed by the wealthiest companies and the wealthiest individuals, who have the lowest tax burden.” The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Therefore, in order to finance the middle-class tax cuts, Tusk and Domański announced that the government would seek to increase corporate income tax from 19% to 22% for firms and tax capital groups that generate annual revenues above €50 million. Meanwhile, the solidarity levy for individuals earning over 1 million zloty a year would be increased by one percentage point, to 5%. “I am absolutely convinced that this will make our tax system more equitable,” declared Tusk. However, he also conceded that raising the income-tax-free amount from 30,000 to 60,000 zloty – as his Civic Platform (KO) party promised to do within its first 100 days in office – would not be possible for budgetary reasons, in particular the need to finance high defence spending. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) tax free. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build savings and channel money into the domestic financial market https://t.co/1xDHHJGYKX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 14, 2026 The prime minister said that the planned tax changes would be discussed further this week at a cabinet meeting devoted to next year’s state budget, which is currently being prepared. The relevant legislation will subsequently be submitted to parliament, with the aim of bringing it into force in 2027. However, Tusk acknowledged that there is a strong possibility of a veto by Nawrocki, who has blocked dozens of government bills, including fiscal measures. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increase in the tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. Last month, he effectively blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits by sending it to the constitutional court for review. However, he did approve a law increasing the corporate income tax rate for banks. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 Next year’s budget will be closely watched given that Poland’s fiscal situation has become increasingly problematic in recent years. In 2024, the European Union placed Poland under its excessive deficit procedure, requiring Warsaw to commit to measures to bring down the deficit. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. Given that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in autumn 2027, it is unlikely that either the government or Nawrocki – who will be supporting the right-wing opposition – will be keen on any fiscal measures that either raise taxes or reduce spending in areas such as social policy and defence. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to promote itself internationally and attract more tourists from “key European markets” and the United States. The new initiative, which has the slogan “Poland. More than you expected”, features global Polish icons such as football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, and Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, who received Polish citizenship last year. A series of videos, the first of which was released Tuesday, will aim to present Poland as “modern, safe, diverse and authentic”, as well as “defying stereotypes”, says sports and tourism minister Jakub Rutnicki. Commissioned by his ministry and launched by the Polish Tourism Organisation (POT), the campaign will be conducted in Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. The first video promotes Warsaw, Poland’s capital, and features Lewandowski, Rubik and Eisenberg appearing near the city’s landmarks. Polish actor Nikodem Rozbicki, meanwhile, plays the role of renowned 19th-century Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin. In the 30-second spot, Chopin’s character declares that Warsaw is “where my heart is” – a reference to the fact that Chopin’s heart, preserved in cognac, was brought back to the city from Paris by his sister shortly after his death in 1849 and is now immured in a pillar in the city’s Holy Cross Church. Lewandowski, who recently joined US football team Chicago Fire, tells viewers that Poland offers “more than you expected”, a reference to the campaign’s main slogan, which suggests to viewers that Poland may surprise them positively. “Research shows that people who have visited Poland rate it much more favourably than their previous perceptions or media reports suggested,” notes POT in its press release. Magdalena Krucz, the head of POT, adds that she believes the campaign “will be as surprising to audiences as Poland itself is to tourists who come to us for the first time”. However, the slogan is not new: it has been used by POT to promote Poland since 2021. The new campaign will also feature Nobel Peace Prize winner and former president Lech Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that brought down Poland’s former communist regime. POT notes that he remains “one of the most recognisable symbols in the world of the fight for freedom and democracy”. The music is arranged by Radzimir Dębski, better known as Jimek, a Polish composer and conductor who has regularly performed with US rap legend Snoop Dogg. Polish-American NBA star @JeremySochan has joined a campaign to promote Poland as a tourist destination. His appearance has been received positively, but Sochan responded directly to one commentator who said a black person shouldn't be advertising Poland https://t.co/KXDok7IAXP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2024 Poland has experienced a tourism boom in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation, behind only Malta. The biggest tourist draw is the historic city of Kraków, which was last year named the best city break destination in Europe by members of British consumer association and magazine Which? for the fifth time. This year, Time Out magazine rated Kraków the 16th best city in the world. However, the country has a wide range of tourist-friendly destinations, including long, sandy beaches on the northern Baltic coast, mountains in the south, the lake district of Masuria, as well as many historic cities and modern museums and galleries. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 The city of Lublin in eastern Poland, which will be a European City of Culture in 2029, last year welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors, including over half a million from abroad. The strategy includes creating a “Polish brand” through which internationally recognised athletes, artists, historical figures and products are showcased more prominently. World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. Today, Germany’s ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, expressed his “great sadness” at Traczyk-Stawska’s death, calling her an “advocate of dialogue in the process of Polish-German reconciliation and a passionate champion of peace, freedom, and human dignity”. „Nie stój, nie patrz, gdy się zło dzieje, tylko reaguj natychmiast, bo to jest twój obowiązek." – Wanda Traczyk-Stawska Żegnaj, Bohaterko. pic.twitter.com/MhfqlszVcI — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia. Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria. Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights. A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF. However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”. “I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region. "Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy" Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026 Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval. The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position. “If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week. “Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added. In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”. PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”. The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. World.title: Students in Czech Republic Face Higher Rents as Housing Costs Rise
World.content:
Students looking for private accommodation in Czech university cities this year are facing higher rents, with prices for some types of housing up by as much as 14 percent compared with 2025.

The increase comes as demand for student accommodation reaches its annual peak ahead of the winter semester.

Data from several Czech property platforms show that the busiest period started earlier this year, meaning students who have not yet found accommodation may face a more limited and expensive selection in September.

Those unable to secure a place in a student dormitory generally have three alternatives: renting a small apartment alone, taking a private room in a shared apartment, or renting a bed in shared accommodation.



The most expensive option is usually a small one-bedroom apartment with a kitchenette, typically around 30 square meters. According to the REMAX network, monthly rents for these apartments range from more than CZK 7,000 in Ústí nad Labem to around CZK 14,000 in Prague.

Prices have not increased evenly across the country. Brno recorded the sharpest rise, with rents for small apartments increasing by 12 percent year on year.

Prague saw a 4 percent increase, while rents in Hradec Králové and Pardubice rose by almost 9 percent. Olomouc was one of the few exceptions, with prices falling by slightly more than 2 percent.

Rent is not the only expense students need to consider. Utilities, water and maintenance charges can add another CZK 1,000 to CZK 2,000 a month, according to property platforms.

Private rooms offer a cheaper alternative

Many students instead rent individual rooms in shared apartments, with properties ranging from smaller 2+kk and 2+1 layouts to larger 4+kk and 4+1 apartments. Czech property portal Sreality.cz puts the average cost of a private room in university cities at between approximately CZK 5,700 in Opava and CZK 11,500 in Prague.

In Prague, private rooms listed on Sreality.cz were around 10 percent more expensive than during the same period last year. Prices in Brno, meanwhile, remained roughly unchanged.

Shared housing remains the cheapest option

For students on a tighter budget, sharing an apartment and renting a bed rather than an entire room remains the least expensive choice. The more people share a property, the lower the individual housing costs tend to be.

Even this option, however, has become more expensive. According to UlovDomov.cz, the cost of renting a bed has increased by several hundred Czech crowns compared with last year.

Prague remains considerably more expensive. A bed in a two-bedroom apartment costs almost CZK 5,500, about CZK 1,200 more than a bed in a three-bedroom apartment.

World.title: 58 Years Since Warsaw Pact Troops Invaded Czechoslovakia
World.content:
On August 21, 1968, Soviet troops and their Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia to bring an end to that country’s brief period of political liberalization, called the Prague Spring.

People still recall waking up on that fateful morning to find that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks had rolled into the country, crushing all hope of implementing the democratic reforms of the Prague Spring. Shocked citizens took to the streets in protest of the invasion.

About 500,000 troops were involved in the invasion and occupation, during which 137 Czechoslovaks died and some 500 were wounded.

One of the key battles was for the control of Czech Radio, similar to the one that took place at the end of the Second World War.

The invasion ended the political and economic reforms led by Alexander Dubcek and reasserted dominant Soviet and Communist authority in Czechoslovakia.

It also helped establish the Brezhnev Doctrine, which Moscow said allowed the U.S.S.R. to intervene in any country where a communist government was under threat.

Within the following year, resistance faded, Dubček was removed from office, his reforms were undone, and a more Soviet-controlled government was installed.

World.title: From Munich to Prague: Enrique Paredes on the Future of International Education
World.content:
FAST FACTS

Enrique Paredes

Marketing & Enrollment Manager, AAU

MBA – International Marketing

4 countries / 2 continents

International marketing + Customer Experience + Digital transformation

At AAU:

56.8% increase in lead-to-enrollment conversion

26% reduction in acquisition costs

53.1% increase in local enrollment

AAU #1 University in Europe based on student reviews

From Corporate Munich to Academic Prague

After building a career in international marketing, customer experience, digital transformation and commercial strategy across the US, Europe and Latin America, Enrique Paredes now leads marketing and enrollment strategy at Anglo-American University in Prague.

Having lived in four countries across two continents, Paredes believes Prague has become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for international students, not only because of its affordability, but also because of the academic, professional, and personal opportunities the city offers.

His journey into higher education was not originally planned. Originally from El Salvador, he completed his MBA in Munich with a specialization in International Marketing, an experience that gave him firsthand insight into the challenges and opportunities international students face when building their lives abroad.

After graduating, an opportunity with a major international company brought him to Prague, where he has now lived for almost eight years. He describes the move as both a significant career opportunity and a step in the direction he wanted his professional life to take.

Moving from the corporate world into higher education required a shift in mindset, but not in ambition.

“One thing that’s driven me throughout my career is ambition, purpose, and above all, determination to achieve. That’s what has kept me motivated to reach where I am today.”

Prior to entering higher education, Paredes held international marketing, project management, and customer experience leadership roles at Anheuser-Busch InBev, where he led digital initiatives across Europe. Earlier in his career, he worked on enterprise solutions at SAP and contributed to market insights and research projects for Volkswagen Group (VAG) in Germany.

That corporate background continues to influence how Paredes approaches higher education. He views recruitment not simply as marketing, but as a combination of customer experience, data, commercial strategy and long-term relationship building.

From Marketing to Enrollment Leadership

Although his title is Marketing & Enrollment Manager, Paredes’ responsibilities extend well beyond marketing and student recruitment. His role covers marketing strategy, recruitment and enrollment initiatives, decision making that shapes the organization, as well as projects that influence the broader prospective and student journey.

For him, supporting students starts long before they arrive in Prague.

“These are young people who are stepping away from home, often for the first time, to become independent. We understand how challenging that can be, and we try to support them in every way we can.”

Since joining AAU, Paredes has helped transform marketing and student recruitment into a more data-driven, commercially focused operation, redesigning elements of the recruitment funnel, digital acquisition strategy, CRM processes and cross-departmental collaboration. That shift has translated into measurable results, including a 56.8% increase in lead-to-enrollment conversion, a 26% reduction in acquisition costs, and a 53.1% increase in local enrollment, among other results.

His philosophy is simple: attracting students is only the beginning. The goal is to ensure they have a smooth transition academically, professionally, and personally, while creating an experience that stays with them long after graduation.

Recruitment Is About Fit, Not Just Volume

For Paredes, effective recruitment is not simply about generating as many leads as possible. It is about understanding what prospective students actually want and determining whether the institution can genuinely meet those expectations.

“The goal isn’t to convince everyone. It’s to understand the student, understand what they need and show them honestly whether we are the right fit. If we’re not, we should be transparent about that and focus our efforts on students where we can create real value.”

The Case for a Dual-Accredited Degree

One of the strongest advantages Paredes sees at AAU is its dual accreditation.

The university holds both US and Czech accreditation, giving students the opportunity to earn a degree recognized internationally while studying in Prague, one of Europe’s most affordable major capitals.

For students comparing the cost and experience of studying in the United States with studying in Europe, Paredes believes the model offers significant value.

AAU’s US accreditation comes through the same institutional accreditor used by universities including Stanford and UC Berkeley. This allows students to pursue an internationally recognized US-accredited education while benefiting from the lower cost of living associated with studying in Prague.

For Paredes, the dual accreditation also provides students with flexibility as they consider where they want their careers to develop.

Students who are unsure whether their future lies in Europe or the US can use their university years to explore different opportunities before making that decision.

As he puts it, students have “another three years to discover where you want your career to take you.”

Small Classes, Real-World Learning

Paredes believes universities should prepare students for the workplace, not simply help them pass exams.

He contrasts AAU’s approach with traditional university environments, where lecture halls can contain hundreds of students and learning may focus heavily on taking notes, memorizing information, and preparing for exams.

At AAU, classes average between 17 and 20 students, allowing for more direct interaction with professors, many of whom bring professional experience from industry.

Learning is centered on discussion, collaboration, and solving practical problems, including challenges sometimes presented by real companies, rather than relying solely on theoretical knowledge.

“That’s what students will encounter outside university. We want them to graduate already understanding how to solve real-world challenges.”

Paredes also points to the importance of practical experience. Every AAU student completes an internship before graduation, giving them an opportunity to gain professional experience while still studying.

A More Diverse Student Community

AAU’s recruitment strategy has also evolved in recent years.

According to Paredes, the university has intentionally expanded its visibility across multiple markets, helping create a more balanced student population between Czech and international students while welcoming students from more than 80 countries.

He sees this diversity as one of the university’s greatest strengths.

“When students work every day with classmates from different cultures and perspectives, they naturally develop communication skills, adaptability, and a global mindset that employers increasingly value.”

For Paredes, international education is therefore not only about what students learn in the classroom. The people they meet and the environments in which they study can also shape how they approach their future careers.

AI Is an Intern, Not a Replacement

Asked how universities should respond to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, Paredes offers a simple analogy.

“I personally treat it as an intern. I wouldn’t give a task to AI that I would not give an intern. It’s help. It’s not a solution.”

Rather than resisting AI, he believes universities should teach students how to use the technology effectively while strengthening the skills that remain uniquely human, among them:

Critical thinking

Leadership

Communication

Creativity

Ethical decision-making

“You can use AI to support research or analyze data, but when it comes to making important decisions, that responsibility should always remain human.”

For Paredes, the challenge for universities is therefore not simply deciding whether students should use AI, but teaching them how to use it responsibly and critically.

Why Prague?

Having lived in four countries, Paredes believes Prague offers a combination that is difficult to find elsewhere. He highlights the city’s safety, affordability, history, international atmosphere, and quality of life.

One everyday moment particularly stood out to him after moving to Prague: seeing children walking home safely at night.

“It’s something I don’t take for granted because it’s not something I’ve experienced in every country I’ve lived in.”

For international students, he believes these everyday realities matter just as much as the academic experience. Studying abroad means building a life in a new city, and factors such as safety, affordability, transport, culture, and opportunities outside the classroom can all influence that experience.

Advice to Future International Students

For students considering studying abroad, Paredes encourages them to think beyond earning a diploma.

International education, he says, is ultimately about personal growth and the experiences that come from stepping into an unfamiliar environment.

“Everything good in life happens outside your comfort zone.”

He points to his own international experiences, including building a business with a friend in Switzerland, as examples of how studying and working abroad can create opportunities that extend far beyond graduation.

For him, choosing where to study is therefore also a decision about the environment in which students will develop personally and professionally.

Final Quote

Asked to summarize what AAU represents in one sentence, Paredes offers a final thought:

“Choosing a university isn’t only about where you’ll study for the next three years. It’s about where you’ll build the skills, network, and experiences that shape the next thirty.”

World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.

World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: BREAKING NEWS! Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant avoids further shutdown – here are the next steps
World.content:
Hungary has avoided another shutdown at the Paks nuclear power plant despite the Danube approaching a critical low, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Wednesday evening. The government now expects the plant to begin restoring additional capacity from Sunday and potentially return to full operation by the end of next week.

Speaking in Paks alongside Environment Minister László Gajdos, Magyar said water management experts expect the Danube to reach its lowest point overnight on Wednesday or early Thursday morning.

However, emergency interventions carried out over the past two weeks have raised water levels sufficiently to keep the plant’s two currently operating turbines online.

Magyar said the river is now expected to bottom out at around minus 132–134 centimetres, remaining above the level at which another turbine would have to be disconnected.

“The good news is that we can now say with certainty that none of the operating turbines will have to be switched off,” the prime minister said.

Emergency construction raises water level at Paks nuclear power plant

Hungary has been racing against time to maintain sufficient water levels around the plant, which depends on the Danube for cooling.

The emergency measures include the controlled sinking of two 80-metre barges and the construction of a submerged riverbed sill near Paks. Additional water has also been released through the Ráckeve lock system. The interventions were introduced after an historic drought pushed the Danube to record-low levels and severely reduced electricity generation at Paks.

Magyar said the structure in the bay has already produced a backwater effect of around 10–15 centimetres, while the level at the cold-water channel close to the nuclear plant has risen by more than five centimetres.

Work on the riverbed sill will continue throughout Hungary’s four-day holiday weekend. With some private haulage companies unavailable during the break, the Hungarian Defence Forces will take over part of the transportation work, Index reported.

If you missed it: Russian Rosatom breaks silence as it builds Hungary’s newest nuclear reactors

Paks could return to full capacity next week

The improved situation could soon allow the plant to begin reversing some of its recent production cuts.

Magyar said the currently offline turbine could begin a gradual restart no later than midnight on Sunday. The government’s current plan is for the Paks nuclear power plant to return to full capacity around Thursday or Friday next week.

The announcement marks a significant turnaround from only days ago, when officials warned that falling water levels could force another operating turbine offline. Earlier in August, the 2-gigawatt plant – which normally generates roughly half of Hungary’s electricity – fell to just over 10% of capacity as the Danube reached record lows.

For foreign readers, the connection between the river and electricity production is crucial. Paks uses Danube water to cool the turbine condensers, requiring approximately 132 cubic metres of river water per second during normal operation. The cooling water is separated from the nuclear reactor’s primary circuit.

Full shutdown would have cost Hungary heavily

Magyar said a complete loss of production at Paks would add around HUF 50 billion (approximately EUR 137 million) per month to costs borne by the state budget and taxpayers, largely because Hungary would have to replace the missing electricity with more expensive imports.

The emergency river works were initially budgeted at HUF 6 billion (around EUR 16.4 million), although Magyar said the final public cost should be lower because companies and other organisations have contributed equipment and services.

The crisis has highlighted the vulnerability of Danube-dependent energy infrastructure during prolonged droughts. Romania was forced to shut down its Cernavodă nuclear facility this month amid similarly extreme conditions, while Hungary has so far managed to keep at least part of Paks operating.

For Hungary, the immediate danger now appears to be easing. If the Danube remains above the critical threshold and the emergency works continue as planned, the country’s most important power plant could be back at full capacity by late next week.

World.title: PM Magyar’s first 100 days: Success or failure for Hungary?
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s first 100 days as Hungary’s prime minister have produced two sharply different verdicts. The Tisza government says it has already delivered more than 100 commitments and put the country on a new course, while Fidesz, now in opposition, argues that the period has been defined by broken election promises, improvisation and “Facebook government”. So what does the first 100 days actually tell us?

The milestone has particular political significance in Hungary. Magyar’s Tisza Party came to power after the April 2026 parliamentary election, ending 16 years of consecutive Fidesz-led governments. The new administration therefore inherited not only the state apparatus but expectations of a rapid and visible break with the previous era.

Péter Magyar’s first 100 days: government points to a new direction

Magyar’s central argument is that 100 days could never be enough to repair problems accumulated over a decade and a half, but were sufficient to change Hungary’s direction.

According to the Magyar government’s official assessment, more than 100 commitments have already been fulfilled. It highlights changes to the rule of law, anti-corruption measures, public media, government spending and the handling of state assets. The government has published its own assessment on its results website, inviting voters to check its pledges against what has been implemented.

One of the government’s most significant claims concerns EU funding. In May, Magyar announced an agreement with the European Commission concerning the release of EUR 16.4 billion – around HUF 6 trillion – in previously blocked European funds. Of this, EUR 4.4 billion was earmarked for cohesion programmes, with further sums intended for education, research, the electricity grid and new railway and HÉV suburban trains.

The government also points to a change in institutional practices. It allowed the special legal order used for decree-based government to expire after six years, while the former public media news operation was abolished in July and its leadership replaced. It has also established a National Asset Recovery and Protection Office as part of its anti-corruption agenda.

On public spending, the cabinet says it has tightened controls and reviewed large state investments. It claims savings of HUF 100 billion (around EUR 274 million) on the M6 motorway project and a further HUF 59 billion (EUR 162 million) on the Mohács bridge project.

Fidesz: major election promises remain unfulfilled

Fidesz offers an almost entirely opposite assessment. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the opposition parliamentary group accused Magyar of winning the election with “false promises” and said the government had spent its first 100 days blaming its predecessor rather than delivering on its commitments.

Among the measures Fidesz says remain unfulfilled are the promised doubling of family allowance, maternity support, benefits for elderly people, GYES and GYET family benefits, a 25% pay rise for social-sector workers and a reduction of VAT on healthy food to 5%.

The party also attacked the government over the end of the interest-rate cap, its approach to the previous government’s Otthon Start housing programme and household energy subsidies. It further accused Tisza of favouring multinational companies over Hungarian businesses and of failing to deliver promises concerning fuel prices and medicine VAT. These are political allegations made in the Fidesz statement, which did not provide detailed evidence for each claim.

School support illustrates the broader dispute over delivery. Magyar has highlighted a HUF 100,000 (around EUR 274) back-to-school payment as one of his government’s social measures. During the campaign, however, Tisza said the scheme would help around 700,000 disadvantaged families, while the government’s current 100-day summary refers to assistance for around 400,000 disadvantaged children and families.

As we wrote yesterday about leaked information: Fidesz could be dismantled within weeks as its fate rests with members – and János Lázár

Success or failure? The answer depends on the benchmark

The two sides are measuring the same 100 days by different standards. Magyar emphasises structural change: relations with Brussels, institutional reforms, tighter spending controls and a break with several practices associated with the previous government. Fidesz focuses instead on household finances and campaign promises that voters could expect to feel directly.

That makes a simple success-or-failure verdict difficult. The first 100 days have brought clear changes in the machinery and direction of government, including a major agreement on EU funding. At the same time, several high-profile social commitments cited during the campaign have either not yet been implemented or remain politically disputed.

For Magyar, the larger test therefore begins after the symbolic 100-day mark. Whether the new direction translates into better healthcare, education, transport, economic growth and living standards will ultimately matter more than either side’s first political scorecard.

World.title: Xi congratulates Hungary’s new president – but what will China ties look like under the new government?
World.content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has congratulated András Baka on taking office as Hungary’s new president, stressing the long-standing friendship between the two countries. The message comes, however, at a sensitive moment for Hungary-China relations: after years of exceptionally close political and economic cooperation under Viktor Orbán, the new Hungarian government is still defining how much of that relationship it intends to preserve.

In his message on Wednesday, Xi noted that Hungary was among the first countries to recognise the People’s Republic of China and highlighted 77 years of diplomatic relations between Budapest and Beijing.

According to Xinhua, the Chinese president said the two countries had maintained relations based on “mutual respect, equality, mutual benefit and win-win cooperation”. Xi added that he was ready to work with Baka to deepen political trust and practical cooperation and advance the countries’ “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership for the new era”.

The wording is significant because that elevated partnership was agreed during Xi’s state visit to Budapest in May 2024, when relations between China and Viktor Orbán’s government were arguably closer than at any previous point. The unusually high-level diplomatic designation placed Hungary among Beijing’s closest political partners in Europe.

Hungary-China relations became a cornerstone of Orbán’s economic strategy

Under Orbán, Hungary deliberately positioned itself as one of China’s most welcoming investment destinations inside the European Union. While several EU governments became increasingly cautious about economic dependence on Beijing, Budapest pursued what Orbán described as economic connectivity and neutrality.

By late 2024, Chinese companies had pledged around EUR 9 billion in investments in Hungary, according to Reuters.

The largest projects transformed Hungary into an important European centre for the electric vehicle and battery industries. Chinese battery giant CATL announced a EUR 7.3 billion factory in Debrecen, while BYD chose Szeged for its first European passenger-car manufacturing plant, an investment expected to reach around EUR 4 billion.

Orbán’s government also backed strategic Chinese projects with public money and infrastructure. BYD’s European headquarters and research and development centre in Budapest, announced in 2025, was promised HUF 20 billion in Hungarian government assistance – approximately EUR 55 million at the Hungarian central bank’s current exchange rate.

This close economic relationship was accompanied by similarly warm political ties. Hungary repeatedly opposed a harder EU approach towards Chinese trade and objected to tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, presenting cooperation with Beijing as an alternative to economic bloc-building.

Read here Hungary news in Chinese – 点击此处阅读中文版的匈牙利新闻

The new Hungarian government has not yet broken with Beijing

The change of government in Budapest therefore created an obvious question: what happens to this strategy without Orbán?

Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government has so far given no indication that it intends to drive Chinese investors out of Hungary. Early statements have instead pointed towards a more cautious model: maintaining commercially beneficial relations with China while bringing Hungarian policy closer to common EU rules and positions. Euronews reported after the April election that Magyar was not planning a fundamental reversal of trade relations with Beijing.

Nevertheless, one recent development has complicated the relationship.

Péter Szijjártó’s move to BYD puts the old model under scrutiny

Former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó, one of the principal architects of Orbán’s China policy, resigned his parliamentary mandate in July and accepted an international executive position at BYD, responsible for external relations and developing new business areas. Details: Former FM Szijjártó quits parliament to join Chinese EV giant BYD

The move immediately raised conflict-of-interest questions because Szijjártó had personally played a major role in attracting BYD to Hungary while serving as foreign minister. He participated in negotiations over the company’s Hungarian investments and announced government support for its projects.

The new government subsequently launched a review of the BYD agreements. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said authorities would examine subsidies, tax advantages, permits, infrastructure commitments and other decisions connected to the investment. Associated Press reported that neither BYD nor Szijjártó had responded to allegations of a conflict of interest, while Szijjártó presented his new role as a prestigious professional opportunity.

The investigation does not in itself amount to a rejection of Chinese investment. It does, however, indicate that the political conditions surrounding such investment may be changing.

Xi’s congratulations to Baka can therefore be read as more than routine diplomatic protocol. Beijing is signalling continuity and emphasising the exceptional partnership built during the Orbán years. Budapest, meanwhile, has yet to demonstrate exactly what continuity will mean under a government seeking closer cooperation with the European Union.

For Hungary-China relations, the economic foundations remain substantial. The political rules governing them may now be entering a new phase.

World.title: Ukrainian gold convoy case in Hungary: here is what authorities found
World.content:
Hungary’s tax and customs authority has closed the money-laundering investigation connected to the Hungary-Ukrainian gold convoy case, finding no evidence that the large quantities of cash and gold seized from Ukrainian couriers came from criminal activity. The case drew national attention before Hungary’s parliamentary election after heavily armed counter-terrorism officers intercepted the transport near Budapest.

The Criminal Directorate-General of Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) terminated the proceedings because investigators concluded that no crime had been committed.

What happened in the Hungary Ukrainian gold convoy case?

The case began when officers from Hungary’s Counter Terrorism Centre, known by its Hungarian abbreviation TEK, stopped Ukrainian cash transporters at a rest area on the M0 motorway, the orbital road surrounding Budapest.

During the operation, authorities seized USD 40 million, EUR 35 million and nine kilograms of gold.

The timing of the raid, shortly before Hungary’s parliamentary election, quickly transformed what initially appeared to be a law-enforcement operation into a major political controversy.

The Orbán government publicly linked the incident to claims about a Ukrainian “war mafia”, while government politicians also sought to connect the case to the opposition Tisza Party, 24.hu reported.

The latest decision by NAV, however, found no evidence supporting the suspicion that the money or precious metals were linked to criminal proceeds.

If you missed it: Leaked documents point fingers to former PM Orbán’s role in raid of Ukraine’s gold convoy case

Investigators traced the assets to a bank transaction

According to NAV’s decision, presented by Lóránt Horváth, the lawyer representing the Ukrainian side, investigators established the origin of both the cash and the gold.

The assets originated from an interbank transaction between Raiffeisen Bank International AG and Ukraine’s state-owned JSC Oschadbank, the authority found.

Raiffeisen provided documentation demonstrating the origin of the banknotes and precious metals, as well as records showing that Oschadbank had paid the purchase price.

Based on the information collected during the criminal proceedings, investigators concluded that neither the banknotes nor the precious metals originated from a criminal offence.

NAV also found no doubts regarding the lawful source and ownership of the assets. As one of the legal elements required for a money-laundering offence was therefore absent, the authority concluded that no crime had taken place.

Investigators also found no indication of any other criminal offence, according to Horváth’s summary of the decision.

Why the case became politically significant in Hungary

For international readers, the importance of the case goes beyond the unusually large amount of cash and gold involved.

Relations between the Hungarian government led for years by Viktor Orbán and Ukraine have frequently been tense, particularly over the war, EU policy towards Kyiv and Hungary’s approach to military and financial support for Ukraine.

Against this background, the seizure became part of the domestic political campaign ahead of the Hungarian election. Government messaging surrounding the operation portrayed the incident as evidence of criminal networks connected to wartime Ukraine.

The closure of the money-laundering investigation means that the central allegation concerning the allegedly illicit origin of the seized assets has not been substantiated by the Hungarian authorities.

A separate criminal case remains open

While the money-laundering investigation has been terminated, the broader affair has not completely disappeared from the criminal justice system.

A separate case concerns János Hajdu, director-general of TEK, who is reportedly suspected of unlawful detention.

The investigation relates to the treatment of seven Ukrainian citizens detained during the operation. As we wrote earlier, they were allegedly kept in handcuffs for more than a day without formally being made suspects. Details: Former PM Orbán’s anti-terrorism force chief suspect in Ukrainian ‘gold convoy’ case

Hajdu previously served as a personal bodyguard to former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

The NAV decision therefore closes one of the most politically charged elements of the Hungary-Ukrainian gold convoy affair, but scrutiny of the authorities’ handling of the operation continues. The remaining investigation could now shift attention away from the origin of the money and gold and towards whether Hungarian law-enforcement officers acted lawfully during the detention of the Ukrainian nationals.
