World.title: Hungary’s wind power capacity could grow tenfold by 2030 – What to know
World.content:
Hungary’s long-stagnant wind energy sector could be on the verge of a major transformation. The government has unveiled a package of measures aimed at increasing the country’s wind power capacity more than tenfold by 2030, backed by a planned EUR 1.5 billion investment in electricity grid upgrades, the designation of new development areas for wind projects, and the launch of a multi-year programme of annual tenders that could unlock at least 4,000 MW of new grid connection capacity.

The Hungarian government has announced several measures that could give wind energy developments in Hungary an unprecedented boost. The objective is to increase the country’s wind power capacity more than tenfold by 2030, from the current installed exceptionally low capacity of approximately 330 MW, which has remained largely unchanged since 2016, to at least 4,000 MW of new grid connection capacity. Under the draft decree, the government intends to allocate at least 700 MW of new capacity with the tender being published by 31 August 2026; however, no upper limit is set on the capacity to be allocated.

According to the government’s announcement, approximately EUR 1.5 billion will be invested in the development of the electricity grid. In addition, the government announced the designation of new simplified development areas aimed at facilitating wind power developments.

At present, a comprehensive package of energy-related legislative measures – including the draft decree referred to above, which amends the rules governing the tender procedure for the allocation of available capacity on the medium- and high-voltage electricity grid – is subject to public consultation. The consultation period will close on 21 August 2026; however, the final content of the regulatory framework will only become known once the relevant legislation is published in the Hungarian Official Gazette. The draft tender documentation is also already available, although, as is customary at this stage the Hungarian Energy and Public Utility Regulatory Authority (MEKH) reserves the right to amend its content.

If you missed it: Hungarian government announces one of the country’s largest renewable energy investment programmes in decades

According to the draft decree, Hungary is not planning a one-off tender. Under the proposed framework, the MEKH will be required to launch at least one tender per year for the allocation of grid connection capacity for wind power projects between 2027 and 2030, thereby establishing a predictable, long-term tender programme for the market.

According to the current draft, applications for the first tender may be submitted between 1 September and 18 September 2026. The draft tender documentation also contains several provisions that may be particularly relevant for prospective investors. Applicants may receive a more favourable evaluation if they undertake to grant a call option for an ownership interest of up to 30% in the project company to a state-owned company designated by government decision, a local municipality, a municipally owned company or an association of such entities. Applicants may also receive a more favourable evaluation where the electricity generated by the wind power project is to be sold on a long-term basis to a municipality, a majority municipally owned company or a state-owned company as a system user. In addition, the proposed framework allows energy storage facilities, where technically justified, to be connected alongside wind power projects. Successful bidders should also be aware of the strict implementation requirements: failure by a successful bidder to submit the required construction permit to MEKH by the prescribed deadline may result in the performance security being called. Successful applicants would also be required to commence the use of their grid connection rights within 24 months from the specified grid connection date.

„While the regulatory framework is still being finalised, the draft documents already provide meaningful guidance to investors interested in the Hungarian wind energy market. With applications currently scheduled for September 2026, market participants considering investments in Hungary may wish to start preparing their projects now” – added Torsten Braner, Partner of Taylor Wessing Hungary.

World.title: Pro-Palestinian rally for Abu Safiya in Budapest draws Israeli and Jewish protest
World.content:
A Budapest pro-Palestinian protest planned for Friday has triggered growing opposition after Hungarian police said they found no legal grounds to prohibit the gathering. The demonstration is intended to express solidarity with Palestinian prisoners held by Israel and with Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, the detained former director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, whom Israeli authorities accuse of having links to Hamas.

The Community of Palestinians Living in Hungary announced the event. Its appeal calls on participants to show solidarity with Palestinian prisoners and Abu Safiya and encourages them to bring Palestinian flags, keffiyehs, photographs and posters.

Police find no grounds to ban Budapest pro-Palestinian protest

The Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) confirmed that a private individual had notified the authorities of a gathering falling under Hungary’s law on freedom of assembly.

“After examining the notification, the BRFK, acting as the assembly authority, took note of the gathering in the absence of grounds for prohibition,” police told Hungarian weekly Hetek.

The wording is significant: rather than formally “authorising” the protest, the police concluded that the legal conditions for banning it had not been met.

The decision has nevertheless prompted criticism because of the demonstration’s support for Abu Safiya and other Palestinian detainees.

Jewish organisation asks authorities to intervene

Before the police decision became public, Hungary’s Action and Protection Foundation, which monitors antisemitism and works to protect Jewish communities, had asked the Interior Ministry to examine whether the legal conditions existed to prohibit the gathering.

According to TEV, its president, Kálmán Szalai, also asked the authorities to assess possible public-security risks, potential threats to the dignity and safety of Hungary’s Jewish community and, if a ban was not legally possible, whether increased police security or restrictions should be imposed.

The organisation highlighted Israeli allegations concerning Abu Safiya, including claims that he held the rank of colonel within Hamas and that Kamal Adwan Hospital was used for Hamas activities.

If you missed it: Israeli man stabbed at Hungarian festival

Mazsihisz also condemns planned rally

The Federation of Hungarian Jewish Communities (Mazsihisz), Hungary’s largest Jewish religious organisation, has also strongly criticised the planned demonstration.

In a statement published on Tuesday, Mazsihisz said it was deeply concerned about the rally, arguing that what was being presented as solidarity with the Palestinian people was in fact support for Hamas, Abu Safiya and terrorism. The organisation stressed that this was its assessment of the event and called on the Hungarian authorities to take action within the framework of the law.

Mazsihisz said that the open or indirect promotion of terrorism and terrorists should not be protected under freedom of expression or the right of assembly. It also argued that such events could undermine the sense of security of Hungary’s Jewish community and social peace.

The federation called on the authorities to review current practice surrounding such demonstrations and to take all necessary legal and security measures to protect the Jewish community. It also urged the government to ensure that its declared policy of zero tolerance towards antisemitism is reflected in practice.

Israeli ambassador: ‘No place’ for demonstrations supporting terrorism

Israel’s ambassador to Hungary, Maya Kadosh, has also spoken out against the planned demonstration.

In a video message published on Facebook, Kadosh said demonstrations supporting terrorism had no place in Hungary. She argued that the Hungarian public should know the allegations against Abu Safiya before he is presented as a martyr or solely as a detained doctor.

“The white coat does not erase membership in a terrorist organisation,” Kadosh said.

Who is Hussam Abu Safiya?

Abu Safiya is a Palestinian paediatrician who directed Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza. Israeli forces detained him in December 2024.

Israeli authorities and the Israel Defense Forces accuse him of involvement with Hamas. The Jerusalem Post reported in February that research based on Arabic-language sources and social-media posts identified Abu Safiya as a colonel, while the IDF also described him as a ranking Hamas member.

However, his status remains heavily disputed internationally. Abu Safiya has been held without formal charges, and Israel’s Supreme Court rejected an appeal for his release in June 2026 based partly on confidential material not made public, Reuters reported. Hamas and Gaza health authorities have denied the Israeli allegations, while international human-rights organisations have called for his release.

Amnesty International described his detention as arbitrary in July and expressed serious concerns about his health and alleged treatment in custody. Israel’s prison authorities have denied allegations of mistreatment.

The solidarity demonstration will go ahead

The competing accounts surrounding Abu Safiya are therefore central to the controversy over Friday’s Budapest pro-Palestinian protest. For its organisers, the event is a solidarity action for Palestinian detainees; for its critics, including TEV and Israel’s ambassador, publicly rallying behind Abu Safiya risks legitimising a figure whom Israel considers a senior member of Hamas.

Unless the authorities reverse their position or new legal circumstances emerge, the demonstration is expected to go ahead in central Budapest on Friday afternoon.

The demonstration is scheduled for 21 August at 2 pm on Vámház körút in central Budapest, opposite the Central Market Hall, according to the Magyarországon Élő Palesztinok Közössége ( Community of Palestinians Living in Hungary ).

If the solidarity demonstration does indeed go ahead, it is likely that there will also be counter-demonstrators in the square, which will present a serious challenge for the Hungarian authorities.

World.title: How the busiest Budapest metro line cannot be extended far enough because of the Russians
World.content:
Despite having featured in plans for decades, the proposed Budapest metro line M3 extension to Káposztásmegyer is unlikely to go ahead for many years, based on the current situation. The main obstacle is no longer a lack of money or political will: both the trains operating on the line and the control system supplied by a Russian manufacturer impose serious limits on any expansion.

Even short extension of the busiest Budapest metro line is fraught with difficulties

The investment currently being prepared would extend the line by just two stations. A 1.9-kilometre section would be built from the end of Árpád út, with new stops at Rózsa utca and Rákospalota-Újpest railway station. The project would also include an intermodal transport hub and a 240-space park-and-ride car park.

Even this short section would be difficult to deliver, as several properties would have to be acquired, including social housing, a family home and commercial premises caught up in probate proceedings. In 2021, the cost of compulsory purchases was estimated at 2.8 billion forints. But after property prices rose by 75 to 90 per cent, the bill could now exceed 5 billion forints. To make matters worse, the deadlines for accounting for EU funding fall at the end of 2029 and the end of 2030, leaving very little time because of the sanctions imposed on previous governments, Népszava wrote.

Five stations are needed – but the Russians make that impossible

The full, originally planned five-station extension to Káposztásmegyer faces an even more serious problem. According to a 2025 estimate, the entire investment would cost 158 billion forints. Much of the relevant documentation has since expired, meaning that parts of the planning and approval processes would have to be started again.

The biggest difficulty, however, is the project’s dependence on the Russian company Metrowagonmash. The refurbishment of Line 3 was commissioned from the Russian manufacturer under government pressure. The old Soviet carriages were modernised, but air conditioning was not installed – nor was a modern communications-based train control system, known as CBTC. Instead, the decision was taken to refurbish the existing Russian AVR system.

The current plans are likewise based on extending that system. Yet because the necessary software licences are involved, only a very limited section of the market would be able to carry out the work – in practice, the Russian manufacturer itself.

If you missed- 20 August festivities: crucial public transport changes announced

This creates a particularly awkward situation. BKV has been locked in a legal dispute with Metrowagonmash for years, while the company also appears on the EU sanctions list as a Russian enterprise involved in the war against Ukraine. Although the Hungarian government exempted the maintenance of Budapest Metro Line 3 from the restrictions, the dependence on the Russian company remains.

The existing trains could still serve the two new stations. But the current fleet would be insufficient for the five-station extension to Káposztásmegyer. Without new trains, therefore, the full extension cannot be built, and BKK is planning on the basis that the existing metro carriages will remain in service for the next 20 years.

The Káposztásmegyer connection remains an almost unfathomably distant prospect – much like air-conditioned trains. István Tarlós, the Fidesz-backed mayor of Budapest at the time, said that air conditioning was unnecessary underground. Time and climate change have since proved him wrong: he made the wrong decision by failing to press Budapest’s case on the issue against the Orbán government.

World.title: Sziget Festival 2026 in numbers: foreigners vs Hungarians, unsatisfied organisers, the festival’s future
World.content:
The tourism and economic significance of the Sziget Festival extends beyond the money spent at the festival site: 90 per cent of foreign visitors travelled to Hungary specifically because of the event, leaving HUF 15 billion in the Hungarian economy, GKI Economic Research Co. said on Wednesday, presenting the findings of an on-site survey conducted at the festival to the Hungarian News Agency.

Sziget Festival: foreign festival-goers spend more, remain longer

GKI noted that its questionnaire-based survey, conducted among a sample of 529 people, was not representative, but was nevertheless suitable for assessing the general financial circumstances of visitors.

According to the GKI survey, a foreign festival-goer spent an average of approximately HUF 260,000 in Hungary in connection with Sziget, excluding international travel costs. This figure includes spending both at and outside the festival site, ranging from the festival ticket to accommodation and food and drink in Budapest.

By international standards, Sziget is considered to offer good value for money: only 28 per cent of foreign visitors regarded it as expensive. The survey found that Hungarian visitors spent an average of HUF 108,000.

According to a statement from Sziget, approximately 357,000 people attended this year’s event, based on the cumulative number of daily admissions. Foreign visitors accounted for 47 per cent of the total, while almost half of festival-goers were attending Sziget for the first time. Respondents spent an average of 3.2 days at the festival: 44 per cent stayed for five days, while 31 per cent attended for just one day. Foreign visitors spent an average of 3.5 days at the festival.

Economic impact of Sziget significant

The analysis found that Sziget’s economic impact was not confined to the duration or site of the festival. A significant proportion of festival-goers from outside Budapest, including foreign visitors, spent additional time in the capital and its surrounding area alongside attending the event, generating considerable additional value for the tourism economy.

Festival-goers from outside Budapest, including foreign visitors, spent HUF 98,000 outside Sziget. Of this, 38 per cent went on accommodation, 31 per cent on food and drink, 17 per cent on entertainment and 13 per cent on travel within Hungary.

According to Sziget’s own figures, approximately 58,000 foreign visitors attended the festival this year. Multiplying that figure by the average amount spent per person in Hungary, the festival’s international audience left roughly HUF 15 billion in the Hungarian economy. This was money that would not have entered the country without the festival, since 90 per cent of foreign visitors had travelled there specifically because of Sziget, MTI wrote.

Do you have an interesting story you would like to share with other readers? Write for us!

Organisers not satisfied

The revenue was distributed among accommodation providers, the hospitality sector, transport and other services, and its effects continued to be felt beyond the festival itself. In other words, Sziget’s economic significance is considerably greater than the sums spent at the festival site alone would suggest, GKI said.

“Based on feedback from the audience and the media, the direction we have outlined is good, but many circumstances were not in our favour, so the numbers did not turn out as we would have liked,” Károly Gerendai, the founder of Sziget Festival told media after the event. Last year’s six-day festival attracted 416,000 visitors, he added.

Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal

“Last autumn, we suddenly had to take over the festival from the departing foreign owners, and then political disputes almost brought Sziget to an end. In the spring, we were optimistic, but we will fall short of the hoped-for numbers,” Gerendai said.

Károly Gerendai. Photo: MTI

“The organisation and ticket sales started with a four-month delay, whereas previously we had sold a third of our tickets during this early period. The strengthening of the forint made the festival more expensive for foreigners, and the third factor was that among Hungarian ticket buyers, the extreme heatwave, drought, and questions about the power supply created a kind of disaster mentality, which dampened the mood for festival-going,” he concluded.

Gerendai added that there would be Sziget Festival in 2027, the event will be organised between 10 August and 15 August.

World.title: Colliers: Nearly third of leasing demand in Romania’s logistics market comes from manufacturing
World.content:
Approximately 28% of publicly announced leasing transactions in the first half of 2026 involved manufacturing space, almost double last year’s share and well above the typical 10-15% range, according to Colliers’ report on the real estate market’s performance in the first half of the year. At the same time, around two-thirds of demand came from new leases or relocations from less competitive premises.

Overall, publicly announced transactions reached approximately 340,000 square meters, around 20% below the level recorded in the first half of last year, but 47% above the average for the same period in 2017-2019.

The figures show that Romania is gaining ground in manufacturing, as a growing number of companies consider the country for manufacturing operations and nearshoring, according to Colliers analysts. The company’s data includes only transactions for which information is publicly available, while a significant proportion of direct agreements between landlords and occupiers, whether new leases or renewals, are not publicly announced, meaning that the actual level of activity may be higher.

“Manufacturing is gaining increasing traction; we are seeing recurring requirements that were simply not present a few years ago, as well as growing interest from Asian manufacturers, particularly Chinese companies, which are assessing Romania as a nearshoring base for the European market. This is particularly important for the industrial and logistics market, as manufacturing companies tend to be more stable occupiers and remain in their premises for longer,” explained Victor Coșconel, Partner | Head of Leasing | Office & Industrial Agencies at Colliers.

Relevant transactions in Romania in the first half of the year included Iron Mountain’s 28,000-square-meter lease renewal in Bucharest, Autonet’s 26,000-square-meter renewal, also in Bucharest, a new 15,000- square-meter lease signed by Siemens for a factory in Sibiu, as well as two new manufacturing facilities of more than 20,000 square meters, one near Bucharest and the other in Ploiești.

“These transactions confirm sustained interest in industrial and logistics space and come against a backdrop in which Romania continues to retain its competitive advantages for such activities,” Colliers analysts stated.

Romania’s logistics market contributes positively to the national economy. According to data analysed by Colliers, for every euro spent on labour in transportation and storage, Romania generates approximately EUR 2.7 in added value, compared with around EUR 1.7 across the European Union. Labour market data reinforces this advantage further. In July 2026, none of the Romanian companies surveyed by the European Commission in the warehousing and transport support activities sector cited a lack of workers as a factor limiting their activity, compared with 21% in the euro area, 49% in Poland and 38% in Hungary.

Romania is also well positioned to attract new manufacturing investment: a 2026 Colliers analysis shows that 9 out of 10 Romanian counties rank among Europe’s most competitive locations for manufacturers, alongside regions primarily in Poland, France and Spain.

Another important advantage is infrastructure, which is playing an increasingly significant role in companies’ location decisions. Bucharest’s A0 motorway is improving the attractiveness of areas that until recently were considered secondary locations, including the north of the capital around Buftea, as well as the east and south.

Romania had more than 1,400 kilometers of high-speed roads at the beginning of 2026, compared with around 900 kilometers before the pandemic, while more than 1,000 kilometers are currently at various stages of construction. Over the next five to seven years, the network could exceed 2,500 kilometers.

As infrastructure expands and companies’ requirements become more diverse, the supply of industrial and logistics space also continues to grow. Modern stock reached almost 8.3 million square meters by mid-year, after surpassing the 8 million-square-metre threshold, with most new deliveries concentrated in Bucharest. A further approximately 500,000 square meters could be added over the next two to three quarters. At the same time, competition between developers is intensifying: CTP and WDP remain the market leaders, while VGP, Element Industrial, Logicor and Industra Parks are accelerating their development pipelines, and Lion’s Head, Garbe Industrial/Fortress and Hillwood are preparing their first local projects.

For the remainder of the year, Colliers consultants expect demand to be lower than in the recent record years, while remaining at a healthy level compared with the 2015-2019 period. Over the medium and long term, the outlook remains positive, supported by competitive costs, productivity, infrastructure investment, full Schengen accession and the shortage of modern space relative to population and consumption levels. In Colliers’ view, the industrial and logistics market remains one of the Romanian real estate sectors with the strongest development potential.

World.title: Why some renewable energy projects never reach the grid
World.content:
Expert Corner

Our renewable energy market is in a new stage.



The number of MW announced, the pace of new developments and the volume of capital entering the market alone no longer tell the full story. We see investors becoming more selective, financing criteria stricter, and the market increasingly rewarding companies capable of delivering operational assets rather than ambitious pipelines.



This shift raises an important question: why do some renewable energy projects never reach the grid?



The answer is more complex than permitting delays or technical challenges. In reality, projects don't fail because of a single obstacle. More often, they fail because the entire development process has not been designed with execution in mind.

Development is only the beginning



One of the defining characteristics of the Romanian renewable energy market over the past few years has been the rapid increase in projects developed with the primary objective of being sold at Ready-to-Build (RTB) stage.



This approach has helped to attract capital and accelerate market growth. However, it has also created a disconnect between project development and project delivery.

"Many projects are structured to reach an investment milestone, rather than to become long-term operational assets. Yet the most difficult part of any renewable energy project begins after development: obtaining the final permits, coordinating multiple stakeholders, securing grid access, managing construction and ultimately energizing the asset." said Răzvan Voineagu, Head of Grid Connection & Permitting, Enexus.

We see permitting as a process of coordination, not administration



Permitting is often perceived as a sequence of approvals that simply need to be completed one after another.



In fact, permitting is one of the most complex phases of project development because every approval influences the next. Technical requirements, environmental constraints, land regulations, grid studies and institutional procedures are closely interconnected.



Successful projects are not built by collecting permits as quickly as possible. What is necessary is coordinating technical, legal and regulatory processes so that the project remains coherent from its earliest design stages through commissioning. For this you must have experts, permanent dialogue with authorities and understanding of how every decision will affect the project months or even years later.

Integration over generation



Perhaps the biggest change taking place across Europe is that renewable energy is no longer limited by generation capacity alone. Today, storage and integration have become equally important.



Global installed solar capacity has surpassed 3 TW. Across Europe, renewable energy now accounts for more than 26% (Eurostat, 2025) of final energy consumption, solar continues to expand at record levels, and negative electricity prices are becoming increasingly frequent in major markets such as Spain, Portugal, France and Greece. And in Romania, the pace of renewable project development has significantly exceeded the speed at which grid infrastructure can be expanded, with over 87,000 MW in the ANRE connection pipeline, yet only 12% having reached advanced authorization (ANRE, May 2026).

"This evolution is reshaping companies operating in the sector. At Enexus, it has reinforced our decision to expand beyond traditional EPC services by strengthening our expertise in high- and medium-voltage infrastructure, including substations and grid connection solutions. These capabilities are becoming increasingly important as the market moves from simply adding new capacity to integrating that capacity efficiently into the national energy system." underlines Răzvan Voineagu, Head of Grid Connection & Permitting, Enexus.

Regulation matters, but execution matters even more



Recent ANRE reforms (May 2026) regarding grid allocation mechanisms and project implementation timelines are reshaping how projects are financed and executed. Yes, these measures aim to improve transparency and optimize the use of available grid capacity, but also require developers to become significantly more disciplined.



The market is gradually moving away from speculative development towards projects supported by stronger technical preparation, more realistic financial assumptions and greater execution capability. This is a healthy evolution.

The next stage of the market belongs to integrated players



The evolution of the market is also changing how renewable energy companies position themselves.

"Since market entry, Enexus delivered 15 photovoltaic parks, maintained a 100% delivery rate for contracted projects and entered 2026 with more than 400 MW under construction and contract. These results supported the company's decision to expand its business model towards three strategic directions: grid infrastructure and substations, larger utility-scale projects (20-100 MW with integrated battery storage), and proprietary energy assets. These reflect the direction in which the entire market is moving." explains Răzvan Voineagu, Head of Grid Connection & Permitting, Enexus.

Renewable energy remains fundamentally a people business



To build any solar project you must combine engineering expertise with regulatory knowledge, institutional coordination and practical problem-solving. Projects become more complex, so experienced specialists are becoming one of the industry's most valuable resources. Bringing together experts and project managers who can transform investment plans into operational infrastructure is a real challenge for any company but is critical.

"We believe the human resources are already a major competitive advantage in the market. It hasn't been easy, but Enexus' growth has been matched by the growth of specialized teams, they helped us keep the 100% successful delivery rate, improve the internal processes, expand our portfolio of investors and sustain the trust of our partners." concludes Răzvan Voineagu, Head of Grid Connection & Permitting, Enexus.

As the market matures, execution becomes the new currency of trust. Investors, authorities and financial institutions all look for the same thing: certainty that a project will move from concept to operation. In the years ahead, that ability will become the industry's defining differentiator.



*This is an expert corner.

World.title: Romania had highest inflation in EU in July 2026 despite decrease
World.content:
Romania still has the highest inflation in the European Union, at 8.2% in July, even though the rate fell from 9.2% in the previous month, according to data published by Eurostat on Wednesday, August 19. Overall, inflation rose slightly to 3% at the EU level in July, from 2.9% in June.

Compared with June, annual inflation fell in 15 member states, remained stable in three and increased in nine. After Romania, the next highest inflation was recorded in Lithuania, at 5.4%, and in Cyprus and Bulgaria, both at 4.4%.

At the opposite end, Sweden had the lowest annual inflation, at 0.3%, followed by Czechia, at 1.3%, and Denmark and Hungary, at 1.6% each.

In the euro area, the rate rose from 2.8% to 2.9% in July. The largest contribution to inflation in the euro area came from services, with 1.55%, followed by energy, with 0.94%, and food, alcohol and tobacco, with 0.23%.

In Romania, the largest price increases were for services, at 13.67%. During the same period, prices of non-food goods increased by 7.93%, while food goods rose by 5.03%.

The National Bank of Romania (BNR) revised its inflation forecast for the end of 2026, from 3.9% to 6.1%. For the end of 2027, the BNR estimates an inflation rate of 2.9%. The new forecast puts inflation further above BNR's previous projection of 5.5%. BNR now expects inflation to return to its 2.5% +/-1pp target range only in the fourth quarter of 2027.

The central bank's inflation report points to the lingering effects of fiscal consolidation measures introduced in 2025 and early 2026, alongside supply shocks affecting energy prices. The report cites the US-Iran war and the extreme decline in Danube water levels among factors pushing up the prices of oil, gas and electricity.

World.title: Romanian real estate developer IMPACT appoints Iulia Iana as CEO of Finance & Sales
World.content:
IMPACT Developer & Contractor (BVB: IMP), a major Romanian builder listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, announced the appointment of Iulia Iana as CEO of IMPACT Finance & Sales, a company within the IMPACT Group specializing in sales, marketing, brokerage, commercial leasing, and IT services.

According to the press release, the appointment is part of the IMPACT Group’s strategy to strengthen its integrated business model and accelerate commercial performance, in the context of a new phase of development focused on growth and operational efficiency.

In her new role, Iulia Iana will oversee the company’s commercial activities, with responsibility for sales, marketing, IT, and the development of commercial processes across the IMPACT Group’s portfolio of projects.

Her mandate includes developing marketing and sales strategies, optimizing conversion and customer retention processes, enhancing commercial performance, and facilitating customers’ access to financing solutions for home purchases. In this position, she will contribute to the commercial strategy for projects within the IMPACT Group portfolio, including GREENFIELD Băneasa, ARIA Verdi, GREENFIELD Copou, and BOREAL Plus.

Iana has more than 14 years of experience in marketing, strategy, and management across industries including real estate, automotive, and retail. Before joining IMPACT Finance & Sales, she served as marketing director at another real estate development company, where she led the marketing and communications strategy for the company’s portfolio and contributed to the development and positioning of both the corporate brand and its residential projects.

Her expertise includes designing and implementing integrated marketing, digital, communications, and branding strategies, leading multidisciplinary teams, and managing marketing budgets, with a strong focus on linking marketing investments to lead generation, commercial opportunities, and sales performance.

In the coming period, IMPACT Finance & Sales will play a central role in supporting the IMPACT Group’s development plans by integrating marketing, sales, and financing functions into a unified commercial model.

World.title: Transilvania International Film Festival returns to Timișoara for third edition in September
World.content:
The Transilvania International Film Festival, or TIFF, is set to return to Timișoara, western Romania, from September 17 to 20, at Cinema Timiș, Cinema Studio, FABER and Capitol Summer Garden.

The event will bring award-winning films from major international festivals, Romanian premieres, a cine-concert, a special section dedicated to French filmmaker Jacques Tati, as well as a series of workshops, exhibitions and related events.

TIFF Timișoara begins at Cinema Timiș, with 3 Days in September / 3 Zile în septembrie, a comedy directed by Tudor Giurgiu, which also opened the edition in Cluj-Napoca, before an audience of more than 3,500 spectators. The film will be preceded by the exclusive screening of a fragment from NADIA, the work-in-progress documentary about the life and career of the world’s most important gymnast. 3 Days in September will enter cinemas across Romania starting September 18.

The program also brings to Timișoara the major TIFF winners: Lionel (dir. Carlos Saiz, 2025), awarded the Transilvania Trophy for the best film in the international competition, a tender exploration of unspoken memories and uncomfortable realities within a Spanish family, and Feels Like Home / Aici mă simt acasă (dir. Gábor Holtai, 2025), awarded the Audience Award, a psychological thriller about power and social complicity, which became the most-watched Hungarian film of 2026.

This Is Not Your Place / Nu e locul tău aici (dir. Florin Șerban, 2026), the recent winner of the Golden Leopard for Best Film in the International Competition of the Locarno Film Festival, will be screened in the country for the first time at TIFF Timișoara. The film tells the story of a respected doctor who discovers that his son has committed a crime and offers a bleak analysis of racism directed against Romania’s Roma community.

The selection also includes titles awarded at this year’s Cannes Film Festival. The audience will be able to see for the first time:

Grand Prix winner – Minotaur (dir. Andrei Zviaghințev, 2026), a political drama whose action takes place right at the beginning of the invasion of Ukraine;

Coward / Lașul (dir. Lukas Dhont, 2026), a queer story set against the backdrop of the First World War, which brought the Best Actor award to Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne;

Fatherland / Patria (dir. Pawel Pawlikowski, 2026), a historical drama awarded the Best Director prize, with Sandra Hüller playing the daughter of writer Thomas Mann;

Bitter Christmas / Crăciun amar, the latest film by Pedro Almodovar.

The third edition of the festival celebrates Marilyn Monroe’s centenary with a screening of the classic hit Some Like It Hot and also includes a FOCUS dedicated to French director Jacques Tati, with three of his landmark films, all presented in recently restored copies: the comedy that introduced one of cinema’s most beloved comic characters – Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot (1953), Mon Oncle (1958), which won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, and Playtime (1967), unanimously regarded as Tati’s masterpiece.

Film lovers are also expected at the cine-concert performed by GOLAN, which will perform live the original soundtrack composed for the film Meanders, an avant-garde gem from 1966, directed by Mircea Săucan.

The TIFF Timișoara program will be completed by the TIFF Talks series, exhibitions and workshops dedicated both to industry professionals and children.

World.title: Romania launches youth advisory council on climate and environmental policy
World.content:
The Environment Ministry, the Youth Platform for Sustainability, and UNICEF Romania have opened applications for a new Youth Advisory Council on Climate and the Environment. The body will comprise 20 people aged 14 to 35 who will contribute recommendations on climate and environmental policies.

The council will address topics including climate change adaptation, biodiversity, pollution, waste management, environmental education, public participation, and communication, according to the press release.

Members will participate in consultations with institutions, experts, communities, and other young people. They will also analyze current environmental issues, formulate public policy recommendations, and track how those proposals are considered in institutional processes.

Part of the council’s activity will focus on science-based public communication, source verification, and combating misinformation.

“The decisions we make today on the environment and climate directly concern young people and will influence their future,” interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said. “It is therefore important that their voices are not only heard but that they have a real and permanent framework through which they can contribute to public policy.”

Applicants must be between 14 and 35 years old, live in Romania, and be interested in climate, the environment, civic participation, communication, education, or related fields. Previous professional experience in climate, environmental, or public policy work is not required.

The selection process will assess motivation, analytical and argumentation skills, critical thinking, interest in verifying information, availability, and ability to collaborate. The final membership will seek geographical and social representation, participation from urban and rural areas, and a balance between age groups.

Applications can be submitted online until August 31 at 11:59 p.m. EEST. Applications will be assessed between September 1 and 4, followed by interviews from September 8 to 11.

The 20 selected members will be announced on September 12, while the council’s first in-person meeting is scheduled for September 14-18. Organizers will cover participants’ transportation and accommodation costs where necessary.

World.title: Balkanik Festival in Bucharest to feature monumental Brâncuși-inspired multimedia installation
World.content:
A monumental sculpture inspired by Constantin Brâncuși’s artistic principles will be presented at the 2026 Balkanik Festival in Bucharest’s Tei Park from August 28 to 30. The installation will be transformed after dark through video mapping, while a second intervention will invite festivalgoers to participate in a collective ritual of silence.

The program, titled Silent Forms / Illuminated Forms – Constantin Brâncuși at Balkanik Festival, marks 150 years since the Romanian sculptor’s birth. Rather than reproducing his works, it explores themes associated with his art, including simplified form, verticality, movement, light, and silence, the organizers said.

Scenographer Raluca Pavel’s installation The Bird (That Does Not Touch the Ground) will measure approximately 3.5 meters in height and 2.5 meters in width. Inspired by the structure of wings and the idea of ascent, it does not reproduce any of Brâncuși’s famous bird sculptures.

The work is made of sculpted polystyrene on a metal frame, finished with resin and a matte white surface. During the day, it will function as a static sculpture shaped by natural light and shadow.

However, after dark, multimedia artist Adistu will animate the installation through video mapping created specifically for its volumes and cavities. The projections will be accompanied by a sound composition using synthesizers, bird calls, and electronic textures, while the visual production will incorporate generative imagery and artificial intelligence.

The second intervention, titled The Table of Silence, will briefly interrupt the festival’s concerts, conversations, and other activities. The audience will be invited to remain silent and listen to the surrounding sounds, turning silence into a collective performance, according to the same source.

The project is part of the Brâncuși150 program and is funded by Romania’s Ministry of Culture.

The 13th Balkanik Festival will take place for the first time in Tei Park. Its lineup includes Ladaniva, Zdob și Zdub, Taraf de Caliu, Baba Zula, Bubliczki, Shiran & Bakal, Cümbüş Cemaat, and Kristijan Azirović Orkestar.

World.title: “Viennese Gala” National Tour returns to Romania for Extraordinary Christmas Concerts
World.content:
The “Viennese Gala” National Tour will return to Romania this winter, bringing together on the same stage musicians from the renowned Orchestra di Teatro D’Opera Italiana and the Vox Opera for a series of Christmas Concerts, according to a press release from the organizers.

The two orchestras are famous throughout Europe, and their collaboration brings to the stage artists who have performed alongside great names of world opera at the Verona Arena, La Scala Theatre in Milan, or the Vienna State Opera.

The musical direction is entrusted to the young conductor and soloist Bogdan Costache. Appreciated for his effervescence and dynamism, he will conduct “with the violin in his hand,” keeping alive the tradition established by Johann Strauss and revived in the modern era by André Rieu.

This year’s program proposes pieces presented for the first time nationally, emblematic works by the Strauss dynasty, Franz Lehár and Emmerich Kálmán, as well as rediscovered classic Romanian creations. The moments dedicated to the winter holidays will be completed by traditional carols performed by the Vox Opera Choir.

The stage picture will be completed by the Vox Opera Ballet Ensemble, under the choreographic direction of Vlad Sebastian, with dynamic moments of waltz, polka and can-can, culminating in the traditional invitation to dance: “Alles Walzer!”

In line with the organizers’ mission to promote the country’s young musicians, this year’s edition will bring into the spotlight the very young guitarist Gabriel Popescu, winner of numerous national and international competitions, alongside his professor and mentor, Mădălin Antonesei.

The producers promise a series of artistic surprises and special guests from Austria, Italy and Switzerland, who will be announced gradually in the period leading up to the tour.

World.title: Can a New ‘European Confederation’ Reconnect the UK with the EU?
World.content:
Nick Boles, a former Conservative MP and UK minister, made a big splash in a country still struggling to adapt to the consequences of Brexit when he published an essay this month proposing a new deal for the United Kingdom’s relationship with Europe. By Europe, Boles primarily means the European Union and European Economic Area (EEA) countries, Switzerland, Ukraine and the Western Balkans.

His proposal sparked reactions from international media and several commentators in the Western Balkans, but it also generated false claims that this was a proposal by the new UK government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Central to Boles’s proposal is the negotiation of a 'New Deal' between the UK and Europe and the establishment of a new European Confederation that would replace the European Political Community (EPC), a 47-member intergovernmental forum established in 2022 in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The diagnosis of the UK’s current predicament is accurate. Its post-Brexit relationship with Europe remains unresolved, while weakening transatlantic ties and a gradual US strategic shift away from Europe increases space for threats from Russia and China.

World.title: Suspend Officers Suspected of Beating Serb, Kosovo Police Inspectorate Says
World.content:
Kosovo Police Inspectorate. Photo: BIRN

Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate (IPK) said on Tuesday that it had recommended the suspension of two officers following an investigation into allegations made by Nenad Raskovic, a Kosovo Serb, on August 11.

Raskovic has alleged that he was physically assaulted by police officers during a raid on his home in the village of Dren, near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok. The inspectorate launched its investigation on August 12 following media reports about the incident.

Photographs shared in the media and on social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back.

“Today [Tuesday], the IPK recommended that the Kosovo Police suspend two police officers from the North Mitrovica Regional Police Directorate, suspected of being involved in this case in connection with the criminal offence of ‘mistreatment in the exercise of official duties or public authority’,” the inspectorate said in a statement.

The IPK, an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said further investigative activities will be carried out in cooperation with the Basic Prosecution in Mitrovica “to establish the full circumstances of the incident and determine the actions of the police officers involved”.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party Srpska Lista said on August 11 that Raskovic reported that police officers entered his home in Dren during a raid and, after searching the property, began beating him without explanation.

“After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medical Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” said Srpska Lista.

Raskovic also made these allegations while speaking to the media from the hospital. He was later sent to Belgrade for further treatment.

The Kosovo Police confirmed that Raskovic’s home was among the properties searched during an operation. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson, told BIRN that the searches were conducted as part of an operation related to information about weapons.

Srpska Lista called on Western embassies and international organisations, as well as NATO-led KFOR peacekeepers and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX, to examine the allegations and act within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of the public.

Civil society organisations in northern Kosovo, where Serbs form the majority, have also called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police.

World.title: ‘Terror-Free Turkey’ Process Could Boost Ankara’s International Status
World.content:
Turkey’s attempt to bring four decades of conflict with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to an end is usually discussed primarily as a domestic political question. Understandably, the process named by Ankara as “Terror-Free Turkey” is framed around internal security, disarmament and the future relationship between the Turkish state and its Kurdish citizens. Yet such a reading is incomplete.

The conflict with the PKK has never been merely an internal security challenge. For decades, it has shaped Turkey’s relations with Iraq and Syria, complicated its dealings with Washington and European governments and absorbed substantial military and intelligence resources.

The Turkish parliament’s adoption of the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration on August 10 must therefore also be understood as a development with potentially significant foreign policy consequences. Turkey will not automatically become more powerful if the process succeeds, but it could gain greater freedom to redistribute political, military and diplomatic attention across several theatres.

The central question is whether Ankara can convert a reduction in one of its longest running security burdens into greater regional room for manoeuvre. Foreign policy influence is never generated automatically by the disappearance of a single security problem. What remains decisive are economic resources, institutional quality, diplomatic credibility, military capabilities, alliance structures and the behaviour of other states.

World.title: Serbian Economy Braces for Ripple Effect of Danube Cargo Slowdown
World.content:
Severe drought has slowed cargo transport on the Serbian stretch of the Danube almost to a halt, impacting supply chains and likely driving up prices.

In July, Elixir Group, operator of one of the country’s main Danube ports, Prahovo, reported an increase of roughly 31 per cent year-on-year in the amount of cargo it handled. That all changed towards the end of the month, when the water level at Prahovo fell 45 centimetres between July 17 and August 18, forcing barge operators to drastically reduce the loads they carry.

“Due to conditions on the lower Danube, navigation has been completely suspended, directly preventing cargo vessels from reaching the Port of Prahovo,” said Dragan Stevovic, Elixir’s director of logistics and distribution, chemical division.

World.title: Russian Propaganda Thrives in Greek Media Via ‘Disinformation Laundering’
World.content:
A report splashed across Greek online media last month declared sensationally that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s parents were being investigated for corruption, after $11 million dollars was found in their bank accounts.

It wasn’t true and was debunked by Ellinika Hoaxes, a Greek fact-checking organisation. Yet the story wasn’t just published by fringe pro-Russian sites such as Pronews. It was also published by Newsbomb, a highly popular Greek-language site belonging to the DPG Digital Media Group. DPG is owned by Dimitris Giannakopoulos, a businessman and the owner of basketball club Panathinaikos BC, who is sympathetic to Vladimir Putin.

Some of the reports were accompanied by a video taken from a Russia-friendly X account which purported to be from Europe Today, a show from French pan-European TV news network, Euronews. But as Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out, the Euronews logo in the video is different from the regular one, which has a blue background and white letters and not a white background with blue letters.

In its debunking, Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out that the made-up Zelensky story was “yet another case of fabricated fake news” originating from a Russian disinformation network, Matryoshka. Also known as Operation Overload, Matryoshka is a coordinated Russian propaganda network that creates and spreads fake news and videos, deepfakes and memes using logos of well-known Western media outlets.

World.title: Serbian Media Outlets’ Management Change Sparks Suspicion Ahead of Elections
World.content:
In a move that has sparked widespread speculation across the media scene in Serbia, Portuguese media entrepreneur Pedro Vargas Santos David was registered as a director of four companies on Monday – Adria News, United Media Digital, Adria News Nova S, and Dan Graf.

The companies run the N1 and Nova S television stations in Serbia, news website Nova.rs, daily newspapers Nova and Danas, weekly magazine Radar and the Serbian edition of Forbes. These outlets’ directors were dismissed.

All of the media outlets operate within Adria News Network, owned by the Luxembourg-registered United Group. International investment group Alpac Capital and Summer Parent, the ultimate shareholder of United Group, initially confirmed back in May that an agreement had been reached for the sale of Adria News Network. Ownership changes have not been made yet.

World.title: Kosovo Opposition Snubs Acting President’s Meeting Amid Parliamentary Crisis
World.content:
Kosovo’s Acting President Albulena Haxhiu meets political leaders in Pristina on August 18, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s opposition on Tuesday disregarded an invitation from acting President Albulena Haxhiu to a meeting with the country’s political leaders aimed at defusing the ongoing parliamentary crisis.

The crisis centres around the inability of political parties to agree on a candidate for president. Under the constitution, failure to choose a new head of state will trigger new parliamentary elections.

However, attendees at Haxhiu’s meeting were mainly allies of her own party, Vetevendosje.

Instead of attending the meeting, a group of opposition MPs from the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) went to the Kosovo Assembly, as they have been doing every day, to put pressure on the provisional parliamentary speaker, Avni Dehari, to call the inaugural session of the Assembly.

The assembly’s rules require the provisional speaker to invite MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker. But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was August 8, which lasted only a few minutes.

Dehari insists he will not call a session until parties agreed on a new president.

“This situation should alarm all of us. No election victory gives anyone the right to put themselves above the constitution,” Besa Kabashi Ramaj, a PDK MP, told her opposition colleagues at a makeshift meeting in the Assembly.

Opposition MPs have been holding these makeshift meetings every day in an attempt to press Vetevendosje to call the inaugural session.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting them well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats and has insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved. The parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new assembly, otherwise a new election will be triggered.

Last week, LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku announced that his party is withdrawing its demand to hold the president’s post in order to ease the negotiations for the formation of new institutions. However, no meeting with Vetevendosje leader Kurti has been held since.

On Monday, Abdixhiku announced that he is not interested in attending Haxhiu’s meeting because opposition parties claim that Haxhiu’s role as acting president has ceased with the start of this Assembly’s session and that her role can be resumed only if she is re-elected as assembly speaker.

“The only meeting I could hold is with [Albin] Kurti. In our view, Haxhiu is only an MP, therefore we can talk only with those who are entitled to talk,” Abdixhiku said.

“[Kurti] told us that he will meet with LDK soon,” Haxhiu told media after Tuesday’s meeting.

“After all these months, we don’t need to guess what the lack of agreement would bring… If we don’t agree today, new elections do not guarantee that we will agree tomorrow,” Haxhiu said, referring to the possibility of new snap elections if the parties fail to choose a new president.

The parliamentary polls would be the fourth in less than two years.

World.title: Czech Human Rights Agenda Faces Conservative Pushback Under Babis Government
World.content:
Coordination under threat

The human rights agenda is inherently cross-sectoral. Human rights issues arise in healthcare, education, social affairs, criminal procedure and similar areas. If it were transferred to a single ministry, it would lose its inter-ministerial authority, as well as the ability to provide input on government-level work. At the same time, this area is subject to a number of international agreements and state commitments.

“Through the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups, promote dialogue and encourage their participation in public policy-making,” says former commissioner Simackova Laurencikova. “We served as a forum for dialogue among civil society, non-governmental organizations, academia and government agencies, so that these people could genuinely meet, listen to one another and work together effectively. Not just alongside one another, but together.”

In Simackova Laurencikova’s view, this society-wide coordination has been the main reason for the significant progress made on the issue of domestic and sexual violence in recent years. “We succeeded in drafting and enacting a redefinition of rape and in drafting a new, comprehensive law on domestic violence, which, for the first time ever, establishes a uniform definition of what constitutes domestic violence,” she says.

According to Simackova Laurencikova, if officials find themselves in a subordinate position within a ministry, their bargaining power will be significantly curbed. “Let’s say you’re drafting an action plan pointing out that social service facilities are failing to adequately address the protection of the human rights of clients with intellectual disabilities. If the parent ministry then tells you, ‘No, we think the system is set up properly,’ then as a rank-and-file official in that ministry, you have no chance of getting the issue off the ground.”

She also cites a specific example from the past: “When the Ministry of Regional Development was drafting the Building Code, the requirement to make buildings and government offices accessible was omitted from all regulations. From our position at the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups and set the dialogue on the right track.”

Prime Minister Babis has attempted to defend the reorganisation by citing a 2023 analysis by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that assesses the state of the public administration. “Even the OECD says to consider placing councils that do not address a government’s priorities, or are not cross-sectoral, under individual ministries,” he said.

A closer reading of the analysis, however, shows that Babis’s interpretation omitted important context. While the document does allow for the transfer of certain specific councils, it in fact calls for strengthening the coordinating role directly under the Office of the Government when it comes to cross-sectoral issues, such as the human rights agenda. Furthermore, the OECD emphasised that any changes must be preceded by an in-depth analysis of effectiveness – an analysis that Babis’s cabinet failed to conduct.

Under pressure from experts, the prime minister finally agreed to a compromise: two new offices will be established within the Office of the Government: one for human rights and the protection of minorities, and one for mental health and addiction. Experts say, however, these will be merely empty shells.

“It will be more like a secretariat. It will lack specialised teams and capacity. All that will remain are secretaries who send out invitations and take minutes at meetings, but expertise on the legislative process, policy concepts and action plans will vanish from the Office of the Government for good,” warns Simackova Laurencikova.

According to information provided to iROZHLAS, even civil servants themselves have not had their concerns raised. “We still have questions about this. Honestly, I don’t know how it’s all going to work,” said one. At the same time, however, they said they considered the current discussions at the various ministries to be constructive, even if not all of them can be so described.

The cabinet’s actions drew an immediate reaction, both from officials and from experts serving on committees and working groups.

“As for advisory bodies such as committees and working groups, we know of dozens of people who have resigned at this stage or are seriously considering standing down. Some of them resigned immediately,” says Medal, spokesperson for Straka, the trade union organisation at the Office of the Government.

Anna Smyslova, another representative of the union, says some agencies are already completely paralysed, including the Committee for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Violence Against Women. Yet this committee included key figures in the field; of 20 members, eight came directly from the non-profit sector, which provides direct assistance to victims.

Last week, Lucie Fukova, the government commissioner for Roma minority affairs, resigned from her post, citing her disagreement with the transfer of the Roma agenda to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs. Following her departure, Vice Chair Marian Dancso and member Tomas Scuka also stepped down as of the end of June. According to a statement provided to the Romea website, there are serious concerns that placing the agenda under the ministry will reduce Roma issues to a purely “social issue” and reinforce harmful stereotypes.

Towards the end of June, iROZHLAS repeatedly requested a statement from the current human rights commissioner, Tatana Mala. She did not respond to any calls, while her assistant, who could be reached by phone, stated that Mala was in meetings.

Only Justice Minister Jeronym Tejc of the ANO party replied, asserting that the equality agenda will not disappear. “The Ministry of Justice is not only in charge of criminal law legislation, but also civil legislation. I believe that where the equality agenda concerns the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, we will find common ground,” he said.

He added that when the agenda was located at the Office of the Government, the Ministry of Justice was also significantly involved in legislation related to domestic violence and the physical punishment of children.

World.title: Quiet Inheritance: Why the Croatian Diaspora Should Seek Citizenship For Their Children
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Even if you don’t plan to open a business, move, or do anything concrete, as a member of the Croatian diaspora, gaining citizenship could mean the gateway to EU education and career opportunities for generations to come.

For a growing number of American parents who happen to have Croatian ancestry, the decision to pursue Croatian citizenship is no longer mainly about their own travel plans or personal connection to the country. It’s about their children…

eu citizenship is about so much more than getting through the border more quickly…

Across the United States, parents are quietly assembling birth certificates and family records. Maybe they were fuelled by the sense of sweeping national pride the World Cup brought, or maybe the fact that that burdensome double taxation treaty between the USA and Croatia is on its way to being scrapped. Maybe it’s none of that. It could be a desire to reconnect with the roots of their ancestors as a nod to all they went through for better lives across the Atlantic Ocean.

Whatever the reason behind the move, the end goal of such a move is relatively straightforward – to secure Croatian citizenship. Even if there are zero plans to move to Croatia or anywhere else in the EU, start up a business, move a company to the EU or retire, holding Croatian (and thus EU) citizenship means that their sons and daughters can also do the same, automatically gaining full EU rights. That of course includes unfettered access to higher education and unrestricted work opportunities across 27 different countries.

This isn’t just another theoretical benefit. Once a parent becomes a Croatian citizen through descent, minor children can typically acquire the same citizenship with far less complexity involved. That single step creates a permanent legal pathway that remains open for the next generation, regardless of whether the family ever relocates.

a european education with zero barriers

One of the clearest practical advantages is university access. EU citizens generally pay the same tuition rates as local students at public universities throughout most of the European Union. In many countries those fees are substantially lower than the costs American students face at home, and in some cases they approach zero for EU nationals. Holding a Croatian passport also removes the need for student visas or complex sponsorship arrangements when applying to programmes in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Ireland, or other member states. Students can move freely for short courses, semester exchanges, or full degree programmes. The Erasmus network and similar mobility schemes become far more accessible when the student already holds EU citizenship rather than relying on temporary permissions.

For families watching American college costs rise astronomically year after year, this represents a concrete parallel option. It doesn’t require abandoning American universities. It simply expands the menu of realistic choices available to a teenager who holds both an American and a Croatian passport. It is also far easier on the pockets of parents who may only just be making ends meet.

career mobility following graduation – eu wide

The advantages continue after university is over and those famous photos are taken with diplomas in hand. An EU citizen can accept a job offer in any member state without needing a work permit or employer sponsorship. That flexibility matters in competitive fields where companies increasingly recruit across borders. Young dual citizens can take internships in Zagreb or just across the border in Ljubljana, accept graduate roles in Berlin or Amsterdam, or return home to the United States with the knowledge that EU opportunities remain permanently available to them whenever they get the itch to experience them.

Parents who secure the status of Croatian citizens while their children are still minors effectively hand them a form of professional insurance that is extremely difficult to obtain later in life. Rules can (and do) change. You only need to ask the Italian diaspora about the hurdles they now face in what was once an easy ride in getting Italian citizenship. Documentation becomes harder to locate and do anything with as older relatives pass away and time marches on. Completing the process now removes those future variables entirely and ensures flexibility that can hardly be matched in any other manner.

multi-generational safety

Many American parents with Croatian heritage say they have no intention of moving to Europe themselves. Nor do they need to. That’s totally irrelevant to the value of having Croatian citizenship for the next generation. The rights exist whether or not anyone relocates anywhere else. A family can remain fully based in the United States while still giving their children the legal ability to study, work, or live anywhere in the EU if they later choose to do so.

The same logic applies to grandchildren. Citizenship acquired today can, at least under current rules, be transmitted further down the line, creating a multi-generational safety net that requires just one single successful application at the starting point.

timing matters…

The administrative process for Croatian citizenship by descent is (in)famously document-heavy. Birth, marriage, and death records must be gathered, apostilled, and translated… The list goes on. That goes without even mentioning that much older records from the former Yugoslavia or earlier periods can take time to locate and deal with administratively. Consular and ministry processing times currently range from several months to well over a year depending on the complexity of the file.

Parents who begin while their own parents or grandparents are still able to help locate family documents often find the process smoother. Waiting until a child is already applying to universities can leave too little time for the citizenship to be finalised. For American families with verifiable Croatian ancestry, the window remains totally open. There is (at least for now) still no generational cutoff for eligible descendants in most descent-based cases, and dual citizenship with the United States is entirely permitted. The practical question is simply whether the family wants those EU education and mobility rights locked in for the next generation while the paperwork is still manageable.

The decision is less about returning to Croatia, less about business and investments, and more about giving children a permanent set of options that most of their American peers will never have. In an era of rising education costs and increasingly mobile careers, that quiet inheritance is proving more valuable than many families initially expected.

how croatianbydescent.com can help you get your hands on that trusty little blue passport

Croatian by Descent helps the diaspora to take that first step into the (sometimes choppy) waters of gaining Croatian citizenship. It acts as a complete guide to everything you might need to keep in mind when applying or just seeking more information. For total beginners with little to no knowledge of how administrative processes work in Croatia, this can be an invaluable source of guidance throughout the entire process.

Booking a free consultation with Croatian by Descent can set you on the path to securing Croatian and EU citizenship for yourself, thus making travelling to Croatia and Schengen for holidays easy and stress-free. It can also be a priceless gift to your children and grandchildren should they decide to take the leap (even temporarily) back to the country your ancestors left long ago, to attend higher education or to work, opening up a world of incredible opportunities that aren’t on the table for everyone.

World.title: Business Owners and Landlords Seek Relief After Fire in Omiš
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Business owners and private landlords are seeking relief and compensation after the fire that has ravaged the Omiš area.

The well known association Glas poduzetnika (UGP – Voice of Entrepreneurs) has proposed that the Croatian Government adopt an emergency package of measures that would temporarily relieve entrepreneurs affected by the fire in the Omiš area of tax, tourism, chamber and local charges.

Poslovni reports that the association believes that assistance must not be limited only to those whose facilities physically burned down, because damage in the affected area is also suffered by those whose facilities remained intact but who, because of the fire, were left without guests, access, income or the possibility of regular business operations.

“Such a package of assistance should not have to be reinvented every time. Croatia needs a predefined model of automatic relief and assistance to the economy in the event of fires, floods, earthquakes and other major disasters. When a catastrophe occurs, entrepreneurs must know what they can expect, and the state what it must do – without months of waiting for special decisions,” states UGP, which joined the request for urgent assistance at the initiative of the association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače – SMOi (Let’s Save Small Family Landlords).

They, for their part, are demanding exemption from payment of tax and other charges at least until the end of 2026, while for 2027 they are asking that the need to continue these measures be reassessed according to the actual situation and the speed of recovery of the affected area, noting that “one cannot expect a family from whom the fire has taken the season and income to continue paying the state as if nothing had happened.”

It should also be added that the Zagreb City Administration has announced that Zagreb will donate 130 thousand euros in aid to Omiš.
