Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Call to bail out Australia's last remaining nickel smelter
World.content:
A WA Liberal MP says Australia's only nickel smelter should be next in line for a government bailout as mining giant BHP mulls its future.

The company's Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter was mothballed in 2024 after 51 years of operations.

Rick Wilson, whose federal electorate of O'Connor includes Kalgoorlie-Boulder, is pushing for the same sort of Commonwealth support for the smelter that has been provided for metal smelters elsewhere.

In the past year, the federal government has committed a combined $1.67 billion to ensure four smelters on the east coast stay open — including a $2.5 billion deal announced last week to secure the future of Tomago Aluminium.

The Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter was officially opened by former prime minister Gough Whitlam in 1973. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Nickel was added to the government's Critical Minerals List in February 2024.

"Are jobs in the Hunter Valley worth more than in the Goldfields?" Mr Wilson said.

"No support has been offered for the nickel industry which is also classified as a strategically important mineral.

Neil Thomson, Rick Wilson, Matt Canavan and Goldfields mining industry stalwart Graham McGarry at the smelter in December. (Supplied: Facebook/Rick Wilson)

"The bigger picture is that the safeguard mechanism is destroying the viability of our heavy industries and forcing the taxpayer to subsidise industries which the government's policy have made unviable."

Taxpayer bailouts adding up

Last year, the federal opposition unsuccessfully lobbied for a Senate inquiry into Australia's metals manufacturing industry, claiming 10 smelters and refineries across Australia were in danger of closing due to high energy prices.

Last week's Tomago deal follows a string of similar bailouts the Albanese government has offered to struggling heavy industries, including Glencore's Mount Isa copper smelter and the Nyrstar smelters in Tasmania and South Australia.

The ABC asked WA-based Resources Minister Madeleine King if the federal government was working on a potential funding package to save the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter and Nickel West.

The entrance to the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter is decorated with hats and ID tags of workers who signed off for the last time in late 2024. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

In response, the ABC received a statement from the office of Industry Minister Tim Ayres, who described nickel as "an important critical mineral for Australia" with a "key role in our industrial future".

"The Commonwealth continues to work productively and collaboratively with state governments and facility owners," the statement read.

Bailouts questioned

But City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder mayor Glenn Wilson, who also chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance, said government bailouts were "sugar hits" to businesses without long-term planning to support affected communities.

"The alliance understands obviously it's important to have these facilities up and available for our communities," he said.

Glenn Wilson chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance, which comprises six local governments across the country, including the historic mining centres of Mount Isa and Broken Hill. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"But at the same time, government handouts are not the way of the future.

"Does that mean that when those government handouts finish we are just prolonging the inevitable, or are we trying to support our communities in the longer term?"

The Murrin Murrin nickel-cobalt mine in WA's northern Goldfields was officially opened in July 1999. (Supplied: Glencore/Facebook)

The future is not looking especially bright for WA's two remaining nickel mines, Glencore's Murrin Murrin mine and IGO's Nova nickel-copper mine.

Nova is set to close by the end of the year and be converted into a lithium processing facility.

Meanwhile, Glencore announced to the London Stock Exchange on August 5 it had written down the value of Murrin Murrin by $US457 million to zero in the current market.

BHP deadline approaching

The dire situation for WA's once-booming nickel industry comes six months before BHP is due to make a call on the future of its Nickel West division.

Only a tiny fraction of workers stayed on at the Kalgoorlie Nickel Smelter when it was placed into care and maintenance. (Supplied: BHP)

Only a handful of the 3,500-strong workforce stayed on at Nickel West when the smelter was mothballed.

The company declined taxpayer support in 2024 when it announced its "temporary suspension" and committed to reviewing its nickel business by February 2027.

"As part of this review, BHP is assessing the potential divestment of the Western Australia nickel assets," the company's annual report stated on Tuesday after posting a $US9.8 billion profit for the 2025-26 financial year.

"Any decision to divest will be subject to an assessment against other options, including continuing temporary suspension, restart or closure."

World.title: Woman hurt in mystery Sunshine Coast shooting
World.content:
Queensland police are investigating after a woman was shot on the Sunshine Coast.

Officers were advised a 19-year-old woman went to Nambour Hospital with a gunshot wound to her hand about 11.30pm yesterday.

Paramedics and police were not called to the incident.

Subsequent police inquiries indicate the woman and a 19-year-old man had been sitting inside a vehicle outside a residence on Image Flat Road in Nambour.

A number of unknown people in a dark coloured vehicle approached them.

Police said a single shot was fired from the car towards the 19-year-old pair, before the car sped away.

The woman's hand injury was described as non-life threatening.

Officers declared a crime scene outside the residence where the incident occurred and towed the pair's vehicle away for further investigation.

Police are asking anyone with information to come forward, but said there was any ongoing threat to the public.

World.title: FIFA vice-president withdraws support for Infantino after 'final straw'
World.content:
More national football federations and FIFA officials have withdrawn their support for the football body's president, Gianni Infantino, after the exit of chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, which one FIFA vice-president described as the "final straw".

FIFA said on Tuesday (AEST) that Lamour had left the organisation. It came weeks after he publicly criticised Mr Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other tournaments.

His exit prompted Hungary's Sandor Csanyi — one of eight FIFA vice-presidents and a member of the FIFA Council — to withdraw his support for the embattled Mr Infantino, who is under pressure from three confederations to resign.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"The final straw was the unexpected dismissal of Kevin Lamour," Mr Csanyi wrote in a letter to Infantino, seen by Reuters.

"Kevin performed his duties to a high professional and ethical standard and, as a highly competent executive, made a significant contribution to the transparent operation of the organisation.

"The fact that his dismissal was prompted by his criticism of the above-mentioned initiative — an initiative that you yourself ultimately acknowledged to have been misguided — points to serious shortcomings in professional judgement, ethical standards and leadership."

FIFA did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr Lamour had said staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Other FIFA vice-presidents who have attacked Mr Infantino's conduct are UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa, and CONCACAF president Vittorio Montagliani.

'Extremely worrying'

Dejan Savicevic has labelled recent developments at FIFA under Infantino's tenure "extremely worrying". (Getty Images: Gualter Fatia)

Montenegro's Dejan Savicevic, a FIFA Council member since 2017 and president of the country's football association, said they had also withdrawn their earlier letter of support for Mr Infantino's candidacy.

Mr Infantino is up for re-election in March and is seeking a fourth term until 2031.

Savicevic wrote a letter to FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström outlining his concerns.

"The recent developments within FIFA are extremely worrying and have shown a serious lack of communication and transparency not only to the member associations … but also to the internal members, FIFA Council included, and structures which should hold the foundations of FIFA," he wrote.

"The proposals put forward exposed concerning vulnerabilities regarding governance, not only at the political level but also within the FIFA administration.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The Football Association of Montenegro agrees with the opinion of other European national associations and UEFA and demands a thorough review of the actions of the FIFA leadership," he added.

Israel has also withdrawn its support for Mr Infantino's re-election, according to The Guardian, with the decision being taken unanimously after a meeting of the IFA's board.

Football Association of Wales (FAW) chief executive Noel Mooney told the BBC that Mr Infantino should resign after his doomed proposal to "sell off the crown jewels" to private equity investors.

Earlier this month, Wales became the first national federation to withdraw its support for Mr Infantino formally.

Despite the opposition of the three confederations, African confederation CAF and South America's CONMEBOL are currently on Mr Infantino's side.

CAF president Patrice Motsepe, who is also a FIFA vice-president, warned any attempt to remove him should be decided democratically by FIFA's 211-member associations at next year's elections, rather than through other means.

A CAF spokesperson said Mr Motsepe had nothing further to add after Mr Lamour's exit.

Reuters

World.title: Breaking: Prince Harry, Meghan and family to move back to UK, British media reports
World.content:
Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are planning to move back to the UK this month, according to media reports.

Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and his wife intend to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence outside London, the BBC reported.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, are also expected to start at a British school in September.

The news was first reported by British media, but spokespeople for ⁠Harry and Meghan had no immediate ‌comment. However, a source close to the couple confirmed the report's accuracy.

The BBC reported King Charles was told of the move on Sunday, local time.

Earlier in July, the family met with King Charles in what was widely seen as a thawing-out of frosty relations.

King hosts Harry and family at private residence The royal couple hosted the duke and duchess and their children Archie and Lilibet at a country retreat.

It was the first time in four years that the couple's seven-year-old son and five-year-old daughter have visited the UK, with Buckingham Palace describing the meeting as a "private family occasion".

Prince Harry and Meghan had previously not been in the UK together since 2022, when they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II.

It has been six years since the pair stepped down from their royal duties.

There are no public plans for either to resume those roles.

Buckingham Palace revealed in February 2024 that King Charles was undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer.

He is still receiving treatment but said last December an early diagnosis and effective intervention meant this could be scaled back.

The Harry and Meghan news coincides with a release from Queen Camilla, who spoke publicly for the first time about how hard it was to keep the King's cancer diagnosis private at first.

World.title: Olympic questions 'off limits' ahead of Rockhampton schools' rowing regatta
World.content:
Rowing Queensland has imposed new media restrictions on athletes, coaches and rowing representatives ahead of an upcoming state schools regatta at the proposed Brisbane 2032 rowing venue.

Next month's Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will bring more than 800 school-aged rowers from across Queensland to Rockhampton for three days of racing on the Fitzroy River, the controversial venue selected to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Olympics and Paralympics.

It will be the first state-level rowing event held at the venue in five years, placing a renewed spotlight on the Fitzroy River's suitability for major competition.

Rockhampton school rowers training on the Fitzroy River. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

But in a significant development, the ABC understands local rowing representatives preparing for the championships were told they could not discuss or promote the Olympics in media interviews.

Rowing Queensland has confirmed it introduced a stricter media accreditation process for the event amid heightened media interest and safeguarding concerns around school-aged rowers.

Chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin said she appreciated the increased interest in rowing in Rockhampton given its link to Brisbane 2032, but the schools' regatta should not be viewed as a test or demonstration event for the Olympics.

Tim Mander (far left) and David Crisafulli (centre) meet school rowers on the Fitzroy River, the proposed venue for rowing at the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

"Our priority is to provide an environment where school-aged athletes can train and compete safely, without additional media pressure or disruption," Ms O'Loughlin said.

She said locals were free to discuss the Olympics and events coming to Rockhampton but stressed the upcoming regatta was a school event being held on infrastructure appropriate for school sport.

The Queensland government has repeatedly defended the Fitzroy River as a suitable venue for the 2032 Games, dismissing concerns about the natural river course, flooding, crocodiles, infrastructure and racing conditions.

Members of the CQ32 Rowing Legacy Advisory Committee, which is championing the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing and canoeing at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The Olympic proposal

The proposal to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River was first championed by a Central Queensland advocacy group which included Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan.

"The Rockhampton rowing course is at the centre of everything with an airport, highway and a CBD within minutes," Senator Canavan said at the time.

"It just all stacks up. I think the Games should deliver for all of Queensland."

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart also wrote to Queensland's deputy premier advocating for Olympic rowing and canoeing to be held in Rockhampton before the venue was selected.

Australian rowers have previously used the Fitzroy River as a training venue before the Olympics. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland supports the Queensland government in hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the state but says the proposed Rockhampton venue remains subject to the technical and venue planning processes associated with hosting an Olympic event.

Ms O'Loughlin said the existing Rockhampton course and infrastructure were appropriate for a school-level competition but were not representative of what would be required for a national, international or Olympic rowing event.

"The rowing community awaits the release of information on the Olympic venue location and infrastructure, which has yet to be published by the Queensland government," she said.

A crocodile warning sign at the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Tobias Jurss-Lewis)

Scrutiny of venue

Concerns have nevertheless been raised by rowing bodies and elite Australian rowers about fairness, tidal currents and the suitability of a natural river course, including issues around flooding and crocodile management, with some advocating for dedicated facilities in south-east Queensland or interstate.

Rowing Australia said the technical assessment of the Rockhampton venue was a matter for the relevant authorities, including World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee.

It said it would continue to support key stakeholders involved in planning for Brisbane 2032.

An electronic billboard in Rockhampton has been up for several months, alternating between designs promoting the Olympics for central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Asked where Rowing Queensland believed Olympic rowing should be held, Ms O'Loughlin said the organisation was not involved in the venue-selection process.

"Rowing Queensland's position is that Olympic rowing should be held in Queensland at a venue that meets the technical requirements for Olympic competition and receives the necessary approval through the Olympic venue-assessment process," she said.

"Rowing Queensland awaits the outcomes of the relevant technical review, including the assessment by World Rowing."

Australian rowers Jess Morrison and Annabelle McIntyre competing at the 2024 Paris Olympics. (AAP via Photosport: Iain McGregor)

'Games for Queensland'

In March, the state's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority progressed its feasibility assessment for the Rockhampton Flatwater Facility to evaluate two preferred layouts, moving the high-stakes 2032 Games venue into its next detailed planning phase.

Deputy Premier and Minister for State Development, Infrastructure and Planning Jarrod Bleijie said the latest progress ensured the Rockhampton community and competitors could have confidence in the Fitzroy.

Hundreds of athletes will compete in state championship events from year 9 through to year 12 next month. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)

"The Crisafulli government promised a Games and generational legacy for all Queenslanders, including rowing and canoeing in Rocky," Mr Bleijie said.

"We're working well with the rowing and canoeing international federations, as well as the IOC and our Games delivery partners to deliver an incredible venue and competition in 2032, and a long-lasting legacy for Rockhampton."

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta will be held on the Fitzroy River from September 19 to 21, marking the pinnacle event and conclusion of the 2026 Queensland school rowing season.

World.title: Longmire reveals 'incredible deep sadness' over Swans' links to police probe
World.content:
Sydney's last premiership coach says there is a deep sense of sadness at five banned Swans players being linked to allegations of sexual assault.

John Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach, says the suspensions of five players are "flattening" for all involved.

Swans Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon are linked to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel on Monday morning.

'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad detectives are expected to soon arrive in Sydney to further their investigations.

The players are yet to be formally interviewed or charged, and it is not suggested that any of them are being accused of sexual assault.

The bans instead related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, for which they have apologised.

Longmire, who is currently the club's executive director of club performance, said the on-field ramifications of banning the players were not a priority for the Swans hierarchy.

"It was just incredible deep sadness … and that is probably where we're still sitting," he told Fox Footy on Wednesday night.

Longmire was the coach when Sydney won its most recent AFL premiership in 2012. (AAP: Joe Castro)

"Football aspirations weren't part of the discussions, they were very much in the background.

"At the forefront were other people issues — as they should have been.

"The people issues are the things that really led the discussions over the last few days … the premiership discussions were at the very back-end of anything that was talked about."

The second-placed Swans, with one home-and-away game remaining, are assured of hosting two finals as they seek to win the club's first premiership since under Longmire in 2012.

"It's flattening for a lot of people," he said.

"It's a challenge for everybody to be able to get through and be able to put one foot in front of the other and get things right.

"We feel for everybody."

Longmire was Sydney's head coach from 2011 to 2024 after being an assistant from 2002.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The culture of the footy club has taken a big hit, and it will take time for everyone to rebuild the trust in the football club," he said.

"You go from shock and disappointment, maybe a bit of anger in that. You get a bit of those emotions.

"And you also care about people, try and get that balance right, and it's very tricky."

The five players on Wednesday evening apologised in a joint statement issued by the Swans.

"We are deeply sorry to everyone involved," they said. "We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club.

"We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved."

World.title: Meet the FIFO workers keeping mining towns dancing all night
World.content:
Of the estimated 60,000 fly-in-fly-out workers in Western Australia, Benny Gee is one of a few that have nothing to do with the resources industry.

Every two months, Benny flies 1,550 kilometres north of Perth to perform at a regional nightclub in the iron ore mining hub of Karratha.

"I'd never heard of FIFO DJing until they came up and approached me," he said.

" Obviously everyone around me is FIFO doing mining jobs, and there's just me flying up and playing music. "

Benny, who is a sales representative, usually flies out on a Friday afternoon to play two nights, returning on a Sunday.

"It is a big shift, you start at 10pm and sometimes you work until 4:30 or 5am ... it's sort of preparing me for what I want to do which is tour the world with my music," he said.

DJ Benny Gee says the FIFO DJ lifestyle is special. (Supplied: DJ Benny Gee/ Good Karma Music)

Now four years into the gig, he said it has been a good opportunity to spread his music to new audiences.

"[Regional crowds] go a little bit more nuts than the city people and it's awesome," he said.

"It's just a different energy."

The DJs play shows on Friday and Saturday nights. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

'Like a holiday'

Alex Kozza, another FIFO DJ, flies to northern WA every two to three weeks and said it was like a going on a holiday.

DJ Kozza says he has developed strong relationships with the community after years of performing. (Supplied: DJ Kozza)

"I love the weather up there ... it's like a little vacation, I get to change it up from weekly DJing in Perth," the 21-year-old said.

He said many people were surprised by his job.

"People are honestly shocked — when people think of DJ they either think of club DJs in Perth or they think of the massive people playing huge festivals internationally.

" People don't realise that, at my level, people get flown across the country just to play these regional clubs. "

Karratha's night scene in full flight on a Saturday. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Three years into playing at Karratha, Alex said he has developed strong friendships.

"Every time I go up there now they will pick me up from the airport, or we will play golf," he said.

Not for everyone

Booking agent John Fraser manages about 10 FIFO DJs who work at regional clubs in various remote locations, including Broome and Port Hedland.

Mr Fraser said he started booking multiple DJs in Karratha shortly after COVID.

"Before they [venues] were just booking the same DJ from Perth who was going up every weekend back and forth and it got to a point where the owner of the club wanted just a bit more variety," he said.

"That's why we've got a group of DJs, not just one or two DJs."

DJs are flown to remote parts of Australia to give audiences a variety of entertainment. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

He said the lifestyle was not for everybody.

"I think it's a gig for a young person, while they're still single or don't have families," he said.

" It takes a certain kind of DJ to want to do it, and those that do really love it. "

While some regional pubs and clubs pubs book local talent, he said some specific venues continue to prefer to fly in DJs.

"There is definitely now some good talent in Karratha, but I guess it comes down to each venue and what they decide to do."

World.title: Wong outraged as Israel clears soldiers over strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
Israel’s ambassador to Australia has been summoned for a rebuke after the country cleared its military of any criminal wrongdoing over an attack in Gaza that killed seven aid workers, including Australian Zomi Frankcom. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) decided there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct” in the strike on the World Central Kitchen (WCK) workers in April 2024 as they delivered humanitarian aid to a warehouse. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in a 2024 airstrike while delivering aid in Gaza with World Central Kitchen. The formal IDF decision came hours after Foreign Minister Penny Wong called for “full accountability” over the deaths, as she honoured Frankcom at an event in Canberra on Wednesday to launch a humanitarian award in her name. Wong released a strongly worded statement on Thursday morning, expressing Australia’s outrage and pointing out she learnt of Israel’s decision on World Humanitarian Day moments before it was announced – a fact that was “especially insulting to Zomi’s loved ones, humanitarians and all Australians”.



“This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect,” Wong said. “Democracies seek and accept higher standards. The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues.” The foreign minister added that she will call in Israel’s ambassador – a process where a diplomat is summoned for a formal warning or dressing down – and that Australia was considering its next steps. The outcome was one of five IDF reports issued on Wednesday into separate incidents. In one case, which made global headlines, five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab died in January 2024 after pleading to be rescued from an attack that had killed her aunt, uncle and three cousins. Hind Rajab, who was killed alongside her family in an Israeli strike in 2024. Family Handout via AP



The IDF ruled there should be a criminal investigation by the military police into the death of Rajab, her family members, as well as paramedics who sought to come to her aid. In a second case, the IDF decided there should also be a criminal investigation into an ambush by Israeli forces that killed 15 Palestinians, including medical personnel, as well as a United Nations employee in March 2025. The decision on Frankcom and her colleagues outraged WCK, which condemned the outcome and called for an independent inquiry into the airstrikes on the grounds that the Israeli military could not credibly investigate its own conduct. Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues died on April 1, 2024 when the vehicle they were travelling in was fired upon while delivering aid in Gaza. The IDF said its officers had “mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”.



It claimed that attempts were made to contact WCK representatives during “the approximately half-hour period in which the convoy vehicles were tracked on the understanding that they contained Hamas operatives”, but those attempts were unsuccessful. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘We have expressed sympathy’: Israeli ambassador declines to apologise for Zomi Frankcom killing The Israeli military said the presence of armed security to accompany the convoy “was not coordinated with IDF authorities” and the vehicles had deviated from the route arranged in advance, while several people were also mistakenly identified as armed persons. “Following review of all findings of the factual assessment, it was determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said. It added that there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation”.



Two Israeli officers were dismissed from their positions and three senior officers were formally reprimanded, according to the Israeli military. WCK said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024,” the aid organisation said in a statement. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.” Wong spoke in Canberra on Wednesday at a Parliament House event attended by Frankcom’s family to launch the Zomi Frankcom Humanitarian Award.



“Two years on from Zomi Frankcom’s death, the pain of her loss remains with us,” she said. “People like Zomi are rare, and their courage deserves to be celebrated. “I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues. Zomi and her family deserve justice.” Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong with Zomi Frankcom’s brother Mal Frankcom, pictured in September 2025. Dominic Lorrimer In a report released in July 2024, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found that “a significant breakdown in situational awareness” by the Israeli military caused the strike that killed Frankcom, adding he did not believe the charity workers were deliberately targeted.



The IDF said its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM) had reviewed approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the war, then transferred them for examination by the Military Prosecution. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas Rajab and her family were trapped in a vehicle under fire in Gaza City in January 2024, while she pleaded for help by phone with her cousin Layan Hamada beside her. The IDF concluded that in the hours shortly after the firing, following a telephone call to rescue authorities, the movement of a Palestine Red Crescent ambulance was coordinated for the purpose of evacuating the casualties. “However, according to the allegations raised, upon the ambulance’s arrival at the scene of the incident, a shell was fired toward it, resulting in the deaths of the two paramedics travelling in it,” the IDF said.



“Several days later, the bodies of the seven members of the Hamada family, including the bodies of Hind and Layan, were recovered from the vehicle. In addition, the bodies of the two paramedics were recovered from the ambulance. “It has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID). In light of this decision, no further details can be provided beyond the above with respect to the aspects arising from the FFAM’s review.” The 15 Palestinian paramedics were killed as they drove in the southern city of Rafah in March 2025. The IDF decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. On Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike killed nine Palestinians at a police station in Gaza, medics said.



Medics and police sources said several officers were among those killed at what the Hamas-led interior ministry said was the headquarters of the municipal police. Fifteen others were wounded. The Israeli military said it had struck Hamas militants who “operated from the civilian police station” to advance attacks against its troops. with Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Landmark’: New mRNA vaccine could prevent skin cancer from returning, companies say
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination ‘Landmark’: New mRNA vaccine could prevent skin cancer from returning, companies say Michael Erman and Julie Steenhuysen August 20, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Moderna and Merck said a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of recurrence and spread of melanoma in a late-stage trial, a major success in a new field of cancer treatment that sent Moderna’s shares surging more than 170 per cent. The companies tested the vaccine together with Merck’s immunotherapy drug Keytruda, a widely used melanoma treatment. Thousands of patients who have undergone surgery to remove high-risk melanoma tumours could benefit as soon as next year if regulators approve the vaccine, Moderna president Stephen Hoge said in an interview on Wednesday (US time). Cancer vaccine research in Moderna’s lab in Massachusetts. Bloomberg This is the first positive late-stage trial result for an mRNA cancer vaccine, which trains a patient’s immune system to fight tumours by targeting specific mutations in those cells, and the first such study to show that adding a treatment to Keytruda worked better than that therapy alone. Merck, Moderna and other companies are testing similar approaches against lung, breast and pancreatic cancers. Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, said the Moderna results could signal a new era for treating solid-tumour cancers.



“The positive hit here leads us into truly this next phase in immunotherapy,” Knudsen said. “This is an auspicious start – this is where things begin.” The results signalled a reversal of fortune for Moderna, which has struggled to generate new products beyond its COVID-19 vaccine and faced pushback over its mRNA technology from US President Donald Trump’s administration. The Moderna headquarters in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Bloomberg US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has criticised the safety and efficacy of mRNA vaccines and cut $US500 million ($702 million) in mRNA vaccine projects. Still, the National Cancer Institute has continued to fund trials of cancer vaccines, including those based on mRNA. Moderna shares surged to multiyear highs, adding about $US40 billion to the company’s market capitalisation. Merck climbed 12 per cent on hopes the vaccine would expand its prospects in cancer as Keytruda, once the world’s best-selling drug, faces patent expiration later this decade.



The vaccine – which is a personalised treatment – could be difficult to make and scale up commercially, although Hoge said Moderna was confident it could meet demand over the next few years. Related Article Updated

World markets ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results The companies did not provide detailed results, which they said they would share at an upcoming medical meeting. They do not yet have results on overall survival, a secondary endpoint in the trial that measures whether patients who receive a treatment live longer than those who do not. Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer. Interim results of the ongoing study, released on Wednesday, found the treatment, Intismeran, met both its primary target of reducing cancer recurrence and its secondary goal of preventing tumours from spreading to other parts of the body, compared with Keytruda alone.



When the vaccine is injected into a patient, the patient’s cells produce copies of mutations for the immune system to recognise and destroy. “This is the first time that we’ve seen really clinically significant, statistically significant improvements over checkpoints like Keytruda in this population, and it is the first time we’ve done that with an individualised treatment,” Hoge said. Merck said the companies were already in talks with regulators about the treatment. Hoge said, given the vaccine’s breakthrough therapy designation, it could be available as soon as next year. He called the result a landmark. The cancer treatment combines Merck’s Keytruda with a made-to-order mRNA vaccine from Moderna that is based on an analysis of mutations found in the patients’ own tumours. The trial enrolled 1137 high-risk patients with stage IIB-IV melanoma that had been surgically removed.



Volunteers were randomised to receive up to nine doses of Keytruda plus the personalised vaccine or Keytruda alone for about one year. The companies said no new safety signals have emerged in the trial. In January, the companies announced results of a mid-stage trial of the treatment showing that it reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 49 per cent after five years. Stephane Bancel, chief executive officer of Moderna. Bloomberg Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said on CNBC the companies had not decided on pricing, saying the data had only become available a couple of days ago. William Blair analyst Myles Minter said the interim results position both companies well to seek regulatory approval, while also reading positively for the vaccine’s studies in other types of cancer.



Last month, Barclays analysts said they expected the therapy could generate annual sales of about $US3 billion for treating melanoma by 2035. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results Stan Choe Updated August 20, 2026 — 6:34am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose after the US Treasury Department announced a move that could ease pressure coming from the bond market. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estee Lauder, Target and other US companies also helped support Wall Street. The S&P 500 climbed 0.2 per cent for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 119 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite ticked 0.2 per cent higher. Wall Street’s benchmark index rose for its first gain in four days. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 6.50am AEST pointing to a rise of 28 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX fell for a sixth-straight session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.24¢. A busy day on the reporting season calendar is ahead, with Fortescue and Northern Star among companies due up. Australia’s unemployment figures for July will be released at 11.30am AEST. Financial markets have come under growing strain as Treasury yields charged higher through the summer on worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors. That makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments.



Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the US Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy. Longer-term yields are set instead by investors in the bond market, who decide how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.18 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. The relief could be short lived, some analysts warn. The amount of bonds the US Treasury is proposing to repurchase is a fraction of the overall total. “The boost to buybacks is also happening in a world of challenged Fed credibility,” according to strategists at BNP Paribas. Investors are questioning whether the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate soon to match the tough talk its chairman, Kevin Warsh, has been offering on getting inflation down toward its 2 per cent target. “We do not believe buybacks will be enough to offset a continued loss in Fed credibility,” the BNP Paribas strategists wrote in a report, calling them “necessary, but not sufficient.” On Wall Street, Moderna and Merck helped lead the market after they announced encouraging initial results from a study of a cancer vaccine they co-developed. The new drug showed better recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients who had a combination of it and Keytruda, a prescription immunotherapy drug made by Merck, than with Keytruda alone.



Moderna soared 177 per cent, while Merck jumped 12.6 per cent. The continuing parade of US companies reporting bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, meanwhile, continues to support stocks. Estee Lauder rallied 16.3 per cent after CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said a key measure of its revenue growth accelerated for a fourth straight quarter. It reported growth in revenue around the world, with the strongest in mainland China. The skin care company reported earnings per share of 39 cents, after excluding some restructuring and other one-time expenses. That’s up from just 9 cents a year earlier and was better than the 32 cents that analysts expected, according to FactSet. Such growth is imperative because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. And strong growth helps allay criticism that stock prices shot too high in their runs to records.



Target rose 4.3 per cent, Lowe’s added 2 per cent and homebuilder Toll Brothers climbed 4 per cent after they all reported better profits for the latest quarter than expected. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing They helped offset drops for some Big Tech stocks, which restrained the overall market. Broadcom fell 4.6 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom have been swinging sharply through the summer on worries that their stocks may have shot too high and that the AI frenzy may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce big-enough profits. All told, the S&P 500 rose 16.22 points to 7,707.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 119.65 to 53,463.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 41.38 to 26,331.09.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Asia and mixed in Europe. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 sank 3.2 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi, which has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings because of its heavy reliance on AI stocks, slumped 5.8 per cent. World.content:
Israel’s ambassador to Australia has been summoned for a rebuke after the country cleared its military of any criminal wrongdoing over an attack in Gaza that killed seven aid workers, including Australian Zomi Frankcom. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) decided there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct” in the strike on the World Central Kitchen (WCK) workers in April 2024 as they delivered humanitarian aid to a warehouse. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in a 2024 airstrike while delivering aid in Gaza with World Central Kitchen. The formal IDF decision came hours after Foreign Minister Penny Wong called for “full accountability” over the deaths, as she honoured Frankcom at an event in Canberra on Wednesday to launch a humanitarian award in her name. Wong released a strongly worded statement on Thursday morning, expressing Australia’s outrage and pointing out she learnt of Israel’s decision on World Humanitarian Day moments before it was announced – a fact that was “especially insulting to Zomi’s loved ones, humanitarians and all Australians”.



“This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect,” Wong said. “Democracies seek and accept higher standards. The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues.” The foreign minister added that she will call in Israel’s ambassador – a process where a diplomat is summoned for a formal warning or dressing down – and that Australia was considering its next steps. The outcome was one of five IDF reports issued on Wednesday into separate incidents. In one case, which made global headlines, five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab died in January 2024 after pleading to be rescued from an attack that had killed her aunt, uncle and three cousins. Hind Rajab, who was killed alongside her family in an Israeli strike in 2024. Family Handout via AP



The IDF ruled there should be a criminal investigation by the military police into the death of Rajab, her family members, as well as paramedics who sought to come to her aid. In a second case, the IDF decided there should also be a criminal investigation into an ambush by Israeli forces that killed 15 Palestinians, including medical personnel, as well as a United Nations employee in March 2025. The decision on Frankcom and her colleagues outraged WCK, which condemned the outcome and called for an independent inquiry into the airstrikes on the grounds that the Israeli military could not credibly investigate its own conduct. Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues died on April 1, 2024 when the vehicle they were travelling in was fired upon while delivering aid in Gaza. The IDF said its officers had “mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”.



It claimed that attempts were made to contact WCK representatives during “the approximately half-hour period in which the convoy vehicles were tracked on the understanding that they contained Hamas operatives”, but those attempts were unsuccessful. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘We have expressed sympathy’: Israeli ambassador declines to apologise for Zomi Frankcom killing The Israeli military said the presence of armed security to accompany the convoy “was not coordinated with IDF authorities” and the vehicles had deviated from the route arranged in advance, while several people were also mistakenly identified as armed persons. “Following review of all findings of the factual assessment, it was determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said. It added that there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation”.



Two Israeli officers were dismissed from their positions and three senior officers were formally reprimanded, according to the Israeli military. WCK said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024,” the aid organisation said in a statement. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.” Wong spoke in Canberra on Wednesday at a Parliament House event attended by Frankcom’s family to launch the Zomi Frankcom Humanitarian Award.



“Two years on from Zomi Frankcom’s death, the pain of her loss remains with us,” she said. “People like Zomi are rare, and their courage deserves to be celebrated. “I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues. Zomi and her family deserve justice.” Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong with Zomi Frankcom’s brother Mal Frankcom, pictured in September 2025. Dominic Lorrimer In a report released in July 2024, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found that “a significant breakdown in situational awareness” by the Israeli military caused the strike that killed Frankcom, adding he did not believe the charity workers were deliberately targeted.



The IDF said its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM) had reviewed approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the war, then transferred them for examination by the Military Prosecution. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas Rajab and her family were trapped in a vehicle under fire in Gaza City in January 2024, while she pleaded for help by phone with her cousin Layan Hamada beside her. The IDF concluded that in the hours shortly after the firing, following a telephone call to rescue authorities, the movement of a Palestine Red Crescent ambulance was coordinated for the purpose of evacuating the casualties. “However, according to the allegations raised, upon the ambulance’s arrival at the scene of the incident, a shell was fired toward it, resulting in the deaths of the two paramedics travelling in it,” the IDF said.



“Several days later, the bodies of the seven members of the Hamada family, including the bodies of Hind and Layan, were recovered from the vehicle. In addition, the bodies of the two paramedics were recovered from the ambulance. “It has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID). In light of this decision, no further details can be provided beyond the above with respect to the aspects arising from the FFAM’s review.” The 15 Palestinian paramedics were killed as they drove in the southern city of Rafah in March 2025. The IDF decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. On Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike killed nine Palestinians at a police station in Gaza, medics said.



Medics and police sources said several officers were among those killed at what the Hamas-led interior ministry said was the headquarters of the municipal police. Fifteen others were wounded. The Israeli military said it had struck Hamas militants who “operated from the civilian police station” to advance attacks against its troops. with Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Landmark’: New mRNA vaccine could prevent skin cancer from returning, companies say
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination ‘Landmark’: New mRNA vaccine could prevent skin cancer from returning, companies say Michael Erman and Julie Steenhuysen August 20, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Moderna and Merck said a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of recurrence and spread of melanoma in a late-stage trial, a major success in a new field of cancer treatment that sent Moderna’s shares surging more than 170 per cent. The companies tested the vaccine together with Merck’s immunotherapy drug Keytruda, a widely used melanoma treatment. Thousands of patients who have undergone surgery to remove high-risk melanoma tumours could benefit as soon as next year if regulators approve the vaccine, Moderna president Stephen Hoge said in an interview on Wednesday (US time). Cancer vaccine research in Moderna’s lab in Massachusetts. Bloomberg This is the first positive late-stage trial result for an mRNA cancer vaccine, which trains a patient’s immune system to fight tumours by targeting specific mutations in those cells, and the first such study to show that adding a treatment to Keytruda worked better than that therapy alone. Merck, Moderna and other companies are testing similar approaches against lung, breast and pancreatic cancers. Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, said the Moderna results could signal a new era for treating solid-tumour cancers.



“The positive hit here leads us into truly this next phase in immunotherapy,” Knudsen said. “This is an auspicious start – this is where things begin.” The results signalled a reversal of fortune for Moderna, which has struggled to generate new products beyond its COVID-19 vaccine and faced pushback over its mRNA technology from US President Donald Trump’s administration. The Moderna headquarters in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Bloomberg US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has criticised the safety and efficacy of mRNA vaccines and cut $US500 million ($702 million) in mRNA vaccine projects. Still, the National Cancer Institute has continued to fund trials of cancer vaccines, including those based on mRNA. Moderna shares surged to multiyear highs, adding about $US40 billion to the company’s market capitalisation. Merck climbed 12 per cent on hopes the vaccine would expand its prospects in cancer as Keytruda, once the world’s best-selling drug, faces patent expiration later this decade.



The vaccine – which is a personalised treatment – could be difficult to make and scale up commercially, although Hoge said Moderna was confident it could meet demand over the next few years. Related Article Updated

World markets ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results The companies did not provide detailed results, which they said they would share at an upcoming medical meeting. They do not yet have results on overall survival, a secondary endpoint in the trial that measures whether patients who receive a treatment live longer than those who do not. Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer. Interim results of the ongoing study, released on Wednesday, found the treatment, Intismeran, met both its primary target of reducing cancer recurrence and its secondary goal of preventing tumours from spreading to other parts of the body, compared with Keytruda alone.



When the vaccine is injected into a patient, the patient’s cells produce copies of mutations for the immune system to recognise and destroy. “This is the first time that we’ve seen really clinically significant, statistically significant improvements over checkpoints like Keytruda in this population, and it is the first time we’ve done that with an individualised treatment,” Hoge said. Merck said the companies were already in talks with regulators about the treatment. Hoge said, given the vaccine’s breakthrough therapy designation, it could be available as soon as next year. He called the result a landmark. The cancer treatment combines Merck’s Keytruda with a made-to-order mRNA vaccine from Moderna that is based on an analysis of mutations found in the patients’ own tumours. The trial enrolled 1137 high-risk patients with stage IIB-IV melanoma that had been surgically removed.



Volunteers were randomised to receive up to nine doses of Keytruda plus the personalised vaccine or Keytruda alone for about one year. The companies said no new safety signals have emerged in the trial. In January, the companies announced results of a mid-stage trial of the treatment showing that it reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 49 per cent after five years. Stephane Bancel, chief executive officer of Moderna. Bloomberg Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said on CNBC the companies had not decided on pricing, saying the data had only become available a couple of days ago. William Blair analyst Myles Minter said the interim results position both companies well to seek regulatory approval, while also reading positively for the vaccine’s studies in other types of cancer.



Last month, Barclays analysts said they expected the therapy could generate annual sales of about $US3 billion for treating melanoma by 2035. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise ahead of jobs data, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results Stan Choe Updated August 20, 2026 — 6:34am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose after the US Treasury Department announced a move that could ease pressure coming from the bond market. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estee Lauder, Target and other US companies also helped support Wall Street. The S&P 500 climbed 0.2 per cent for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 119 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite ticked 0.2 per cent higher. Wall Street’s benchmark index rose for its first gain in four days. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 6.50am AEST pointing to a rise of 28 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX fell for a sixth-straight session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.24¢. A busy day on the reporting season calendar is ahead, with Fortescue and Northern Star among companies due up. Australia’s unemployment figures for July will be released at 11.30am AEST. Financial markets have come under growing strain as Treasury yields charged higher through the summer on worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors. That makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments.



Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the US Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy. Longer-term yields are set instead by investors in the bond market, who decide how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.18 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. The relief could be short lived, some analysts warn. The amount of bonds the US Treasury is proposing to repurchase is a fraction of the overall total. “The boost to buybacks is also happening in a world of challenged Fed credibility,” according to strategists at BNP Paribas. Investors are questioning whether the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate soon to match the tough talk its chairman, Kevin Warsh, has been offering on getting inflation down toward its 2 per cent target. “We do not believe buybacks will be enough to offset a continued loss in Fed credibility,” the BNP Paribas strategists wrote in a report, calling them “necessary, but not sufficient.” On Wall Street, Moderna and Merck helped lead the market after they announced encouraging initial results from a study of a cancer vaccine they co-developed. The new drug showed better recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients who had a combination of it and Keytruda, a prescription immunotherapy drug made by Merck, than with Keytruda alone.



Moderna soared 177 per cent, while Merck jumped 12.6 per cent. The continuing parade of US companies reporting bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, meanwhile, continues to support stocks. Estee Lauder rallied 16.3 per cent after CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said a key measure of its revenue growth accelerated for a fourth straight quarter. It reported growth in revenue around the world, with the strongest in mainland China. The skin care company reported earnings per share of 39 cents, after excluding some restructuring and other one-time expenses. That’s up from just 9 cents a year earlier and was better than the 32 cents that analysts expected, according to FactSet. Such growth is imperative because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. And strong growth helps allay criticism that stock prices shot too high in their runs to records.



Target rose 4.3 per cent, Lowe’s added 2 per cent and homebuilder Toll Brothers climbed 4 per cent after they all reported better profits for the latest quarter than expected. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing They helped offset drops for some Big Tech stocks, which restrained the overall market. Broadcom fell 4.6 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom have been swinging sharply through the summer on worries that their stocks may have shot too high and that the AI frenzy may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce big-enough profits. All told, the S&P 500 rose 16.22 points to 7,707.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 119.65 to 53,463.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 41.38 to 26,331.09.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Asia and mixed in Europe. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 sank 3.2 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi, which has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings because of its heavy reliance on AI stocks, slumped 5.8 per cent.
