World.title: Space, the next frontier in NZ and global fight against wildfires
World.content:
Soon entire constellations of satellites dedicated to spotting wildfires will be circling the earth

A local data scientist is urging New Zealand to get on board - and the country is beginning to with a new national fire fuels map on its way

But a rural fire expert says the country first needs to get the basics right and manually fix gaps in wildfire data

How satellites are being used to fight wildfires Morning Report Download MP3 3m

In May a rocket carrying four wildfire detecting satellites took off in a project to set up a world-first - Greece's new Hellenic Fire System.

Greece is among several European countries currently ravaged by wildfires.

Its system is finding its feet. "We can have the information of starting fires very quickly, and this is something amazing, the early detection," global vice president of the International Association of Fire and Rescue Services Zisoula Ntasiou told PBS News.

"If we have more time we can save properties, we can save lives."

Last year eight similar fire-spotting satellites from the same German company OroraTech went up from Mahia via Rocket Lab.

A second initiative sent up three satellites last month for what the not-for-profit Earth Fire Alliance intends to be a 50-strong constellation that by 2029 has coverage across the earth with sweeps every 20 minutes.

The US - where New Zealand firefighters have headed to help battle the latest big blazes in the northwest and Canada - has this year expanded how it taps into commercial satellite systems. It has already been tapping military satellites more and more to fight fires.

The satellites use AI systems and much more precise thermal cameras than before to spot even very small fires through cloud and smoke.

A snapshot of wildfires burning in Canada and the United States this month. NASA / FIRMS US and Canada

NZ urged to join up

Dr Finlay Thompson of Dragonfly Data Sciences in Wellington urged New Zealand to join the global satellite efforts for which he sees wide benefits.

"The monitoring of impacts from disasters is wide, and what you need to do monitoring for fires is similar to what you need to do for monitoring for cyclones and earthquakes," Thompson said.

The government has a national space mission with an aim to put up a sovereign satellite.

DOC and FENZ firefighters working on the Little Giant fireground, Washington State. Supplied / Fire and Emergency

Thompson, though, who has helped satellite-map wildfire impacts in California, said a single satellite was limited and any sovereign one perhaps could be incorporated into a multinational web.

"It's much better for us to join in with consortia internationally ... it's much more cost effective and more useful for us to be part of that."

Satellite images of a wildfire in Portugal. European Space Imaging / Vantor

First fuel map

Getting ahead of fires after they start this way is one thing; getting ahead before ignition is another - and New Zealand is trying to do that.

The Bioeconomy Science Institute is about to hook up to a Nasa satellite to build the country's first fire fuel map showing where the most vulnerable farm, forest, scrub and grasslands are.

Fire scientist Shana Gross Supplied

Shana Gross is a fire scientist with the institute as well as a trained firefighter.

"We actually have a lot better tools and technology now too to make it easier," Gross said, explaining why this was not done years ago as priorities were juggled.

"There's more frequent satellites, there's better satellite products, there's better deep learning models to segment the fuel types.

"And so we'll have fuel types across the country and our intention is to update that maybe quarterly so that we capture those disturbances or changes in the landscape."

Some of the Kiwis who have been deployed to help with widespread wildfires in the US. Supplied / Fire and Emergency

First things first

But Murray Dudfield, who led national rural firefighting for over two decades and chairs the national institute of forestry's fire committee, favours the basics.

"We're relying on technology to give us the results that were done manually prior to 2017."

Back then the rural fire authorities provided reams of written records countrywide of all large wildfires, maybe 100 or 200 a year. Some of that data, such as around the land-use where fires broke out, had been lost after the authorities were incorporated into Fire and Emergency, Dudfield reported recently to the Forest Owners Association.

He believes satellites are not yet a substitute as they struggled to tell the difference between a wildfire and a controlled burnoff.

"Until we have a satisfactory solution with the satellite technology - and it will come at some point, I've got no doubts about that - but I think before that, we need to go back to the system we had prior to 2017."

Another veteran rural fire expert Alan Thompson said rural fire data had deteriorated significantly.

"There are lots of reasons for this happening but primarily it is a lack of commitment and action by FENZ as an urban-based organisation that has caused this."

He noted how official wildfire summary reports had been coming out later and later after the end of the fire season, from just a couple of months after it in 2019 to about two years after it recently, though the reports were meant to help regions prepare ahead of the following fire season.

New moves

However, some additional data is getting through: A new Wildfire Occurrence Database has just opened up to the public.

Fire and Emergency which declined an interview says it's committed to continual improvement.

Fenz's new fire mapping app. Supplied / Fire and Emergency

It had significantly improved the data it collects and was using a new fire mapping app, and sometimes drones too, it said.

"These technologies provide increasingly accurate information about wildfire extent."

Dudfield said not enough fire data was making it to those who needed it.

World.title: Man charged after hunting incident in Kawerau Island, Hauraki Gulf
World.content:
A man has been charged after a firearm was discharged in a hunting incident in Kawau Island in the Hauraki Gulf overnight.

Police said at 12.50am on Thursday emergency services responded to reports that a person had been injured after a firearm was discharged in bushland near Schoolhouse Bay Road.

One person was transported to hospital in a critical condition, police said.

A 44-year-old man has been charged with careless use of a firearm and will appear in North Shore District Court on Friday.

World.title: 21-year-old facing murder charge after body found in Rototuna
World.content:
A 21-year-old has been charged with murder after a body was found in Rototuna, north of Hamilton.

A police spokesperson said the man is due to appear in the Hamilton District Court on Thursday.

The spokesperson said the alleged offender and the dead person were known to each other and police are not looking for anyone else in connection with the case.

World.title: SkyCity reports 38 percent drop in profit for 2026 amid restructuring
World.content:
Casino operator SkyCity has reported a 38 percent drop in full year (FY26) net profit as it undergoes a restructuring.

"We are becoming a simpler, smarter, and more connected business , actioning further savings to deliver annualised benefits of $30m in FY27 and growing to total benefits of $70m in FY28," chief executive Jason Walbridge said.

"This is a strategic response to our evolving operating environment and the future direction of our business, including the regulation of online gambling."

The company recently announced a proposal to shed up to 200 roles, mainly within its Auckland precinct.

Key numbers for the 12 months ended June compared with a year ago:

Net profit $18.2m v profit $29.2m down 38%

Revenue $878.9m v $852.2m up 6.5%

Underlying profit $38m v $71.5m down 47%

Full year dividend nil v nil

Earnings per share 1.8 cents per share v 3.9cps down 54%

SkyCity did not provide an profit outlook with its report, but would update the market at the annual shareholders meeting in October.

"One-off costs from our cost-out programme will likely affect reported earnings," Walbridge said.

"Capital expenditure in FY27 is forecast to be in the range of $80m - $100m and this includes retention payments for the NZICC and is before any costs for online licences.

World.title: How many portfolios can one minister handle?
World.content:
A law professor says 11 portfolios for one minister would be "completely unsustainable" during a political term, but it's close enough to the election that it could work as a placeholder.

"It'll just be a case of keeping the car on the road rather than trying anything new."

University of Otago Law professor Andrew Geddis told RNZ it was "probably just the easiest and quickest thing to do" given the circumstances the prime minister was in last Wednesday.

He said in the normal course of governing - if it was at the start or the middle of a parliamentary term - it would "probably be completely unsustainable".

The fact there was less than three months until the election mean it was possible to do so as "placeholder" type role.

"But certainly, there is not going to be a huge amount of time for Paul Goldsmith to devote to each of his individual portfolios, let alone giving them all of the attention that they perhaps need."

University of Otago Law professor Andrew Geddis. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Goldsmith is now the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, Minister of Defence, Minister Responsible for the GCSB, and for the NZSIS, Minister of Justice, Minister for Media and Communications, Minister for Pacific Peoples, Minister for Public Service and Digitising Government, Minister for Space, Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations and Minister for Veterans.

The Spinoff published on Wednesday a suggestion for Goldsmith's new schedule, including drinking three cups of coffee on Monday at 1.30am.

It also suggested he "think briefly about art" between 2.30am-2.33am and between 6pm-7pm he should "Google 'how to get Ngāpuhi to sign Treaty settlement'". On Tuesday between 5pm-11pm it suggested getting "yelled at by Winston Peters".

Asked if the schedule was accurate, Goldsmith said it was not.

"I'm pleased to see satire and comedy are still a feature of the political landscape," he added.

Geddis said Goldsmith would be receiving regular updates from his public servants, "so he'll get a heads up" as to the matters that are occurring within those portfolios.

"Most of those updates will merely be informing him rather than asking for complicated decisions, and they certainly won't involve starting any new projects or any new policy development, given that we're so close to the election."

Geddis acknowledged some of the criticisms that New Zealand's executive government has "an awful lot of portfolios" with ministers in charge of them, "far more so than in some other countries".

And he said some portfolios are created "almost as vanity measures", so the government can show that it is "really concerned about a particular area, without it actually needing a minister's direct oversight".

"So space seems to have been created as a portfolio mainly, so ministers can be associated with the success of the space industry."

Some of the portfolios that had fallen in Goldsmith's lap "aren't going to require much work week to week anyway", he said.

"So the fact that you can put 11 of them onto a minister and the minister is deemed able to still function, might be an indication that we simply just have too many portfolios across government as a whole."

The workload increase comes as Goldsmith has confirmed he will be campaigning for the Epsom seat, after musing momentarily that he might contest the now free Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate, which Penk will no longer be contesting.

Epsom MP David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Epsom MP David Seymour was pleased with Goldsmith's new workload.

"I'm very happy with him being this busy. I think it's one of the most creative and innovative ways a National leader's distracted a National candidate for Epsom."

Seymour said Goldsmith could get a lot done with minimal effort, but Goldsmith said on Wednesday it might be like a "duck swimming across water".

"It might look like it's little effort, but their little legs are going frantically underneath the water."

But he has already missed one engagement, a meeting with his Australian and Japanese counterparts on his first day in the Defence role.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters suggested the issue could be resolved shortly.

"We'll take the defence portfolio. There's a defence minister in waiting. He's coming here very shortly. His name's Ron Mark."

National Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

National Minister Chris Bishop said it was not a matter of National not having enough talent to promote, but the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick suggested it was "kind of looking like" Luxon did not have anyone else he could trust to do the job.

But Luxon said he was a "safe pair of hands" and a "competent minister", with only a number of days to go before the election.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the amount of portfolios it was reasonable for a minister to have was dependent on the size of the portfolio and overall workload.

"If you're talking about Paul Goldsmith, it's ridiculous.

"Him doing all of the jobs that he's doing now, he clearly can't do justice to all of them - if you'll excuse the pun," Hipkins said about the justice minister.

"You're talking about justice, defence, broadcasting, security, and intelligence. These are big, meaty portfolios, and he's clearly not going to be able to do them justice."

World.title: Data centre build could create 5000 jobs, report says
World.content:
A new report on the potential growth of data centres in New Zealand says a large-scale construction programme could create about 5000 jobs, with a significant proportion in electrical and mechanical trades.

The report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) said New Zealand could capture up to $120 billion in economic activity from new data centres over the next decade if it moved quickly.

That is up from the group's earlier forecast of $70 billion in potential economic gains.

The new forecast is based on a larger future data centre build-out of 1 gigawatt (GW).

BCG said a construction programme of that scale could drive economic activity across New Zealand's supply chain, creating about 3500 jobs during the peak construction period.

It said about 60 percent of those roles would be in electrical and mechanical trades, while civil trades would account for a further 21 percent.

The report said that once operational, data centres typically sustain about one role for every megawatt of capacity, resulting in about 1000 ongoing jobs.

An early artist impression of Datagrid's data centre in Makarewa, north of Invercargill. LDR/SUPPLIED

BCG New Zealand managing director and partner Kelly Newton, said growing global demand for data centres opened up opportunities for New Zealand.

"Between New Zealand's natural advantages, renewables development, stable political environment, and growing investor interest, it has the opportunity to move quickly to capture its slice of the global data centre pie, worth approximately $120 billion in economic activity," Newton said.

Earlier this month, Contact Energy announced it was exploring plans with CDC Data Centres for a potential large-scale 250-megawatt data centre at Stratford in Taranaki.

Meanwhile, in Southland, Datagrid is preparing to build a large-scale data centre at Makarewa, north of Invercargill.

Data Centre development is not without controversy however.

Large builds have faced local opposition in the United States and the Greens have recently called for a one-year moratorium on data centre builds in New Zealand.

World.title: New Zealand netball exodus: Tracking every player heading overseas for 2027
World.content:
New Zealand's leading netballers are preparing to head offshore in unprecedented numbers as the future of the country's elite domestic competition remains uncertain.

This week will provide the clearest picture yet of the scale of the talent drain facing Netball New Zealand, after the contracting window for the Australian league opened on Monday.

According to netball officials, upwards of 15 players are expected to take up contracts overseas in 2027 - the vast majority bound for Australia's Suncorp Super Netball (SSN) competition, while three are understood to have deals lined up in the United Kingdom.

The expected exodus comes amid ongoing uncertainty over the future of the ANZ Premiership. Without a broadcast deal in place for next season, Netball NZ has been unable to provide any assurances there will be an elite domestic competition next year.

Follow the player movement below:

Former Silver Ferns skipper Ameliaranne Ekenasio has signed a one-year deal with the West Coast Fever in Australia. Michael Bradley Photography Ltd

Confirmed signings

Ekenasio joins West Coast Fever

Former Silver Ferns skipper Ameliaranne Ekenasio was the first of several new Kiwi players expected to announced they are joining the SSN this week, when it was confirmed on Wednesday she has signed a one-year deal with the West Coast Fever.

Ekenasio elected to step away from the Silver Ferns last year, saying she needed a break "for my mind, body and spirit".

The 35-year-old has stated in the past her desire to play in the Australian league and has undoubtedly been pursued by clubs across the Tasman in previous seasons.

But confronted with the possibility of no elite domestic competition in New Zealand next year, Ekenasio faced potential retirement unless she jumped across the ditch.

The confident long-range shooter will play alongside prolific Jamaican goal shooter Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard.

In a statement accompanying her signing, Ekenasio said she was excited by the opportunity to grow her game.

"Being able to play with Jhaniele will be special as well, that circle will be a lot of fun," she said.

"I'm someone who is all in and to be able to come over and experience a new environment is a privilege, I just want to work hard to be my best for Fever and play great netball."

Star defender Kelly Jackson will return for another year at the Queensland Firebirds. Marty Melville

Jackson back at Firebirds

The Queensland Firebirds will welcome back star defender Kelly Jackson for the 2027 Super Netball season.

The Silver Ferns defender returns to Brisbane after a stellar first campaign in purple, in which she swept the club's end of season awards, including being named most valuable player.

Firebirds' head coach Kiri Wills said securing Jackson's signature for another season was a huge result for the franchise.

"Kelly's impact in her first season with us was simply extraordinary," Wills said.

"To sweep our end-of-season awards in your debut year and then go on to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal with the Silver Ferns tells you everything about the calibre of player and person we have in Kelly Jackson."

Burger re-signs with Lightning

Silver Ferns skipper Karin Burger has signed for a second season with the Sunshine Coast Lightning.

The Lightning announced on Monday the world class defender had been retained after impressing in her maiden season at the Queensland franchise this season.

Burger will again pair up with Australian Diamonds defender Courtney Bruce in the Lightning defensive circle, forming one of the strongest defensive combinations in the league.

Unconfirmed

Star shooter Grace Nweke, whose decision to play in the SSN helped pave the way for other New Zealand players to explore opportunities in Australia, is on the move in 2027. The NSW Swifts confirmed over the weekend that Silver Ferns' linchpin would not be returning for a third season with the club.

Reports out of Australia suggest Nweke will join cross town rivals the Sydney Sirens, formerly known as the Giants, who have new owners at the helm.

Silver Ferns midcourter Maddy Gordon will also turn out for a new SSN club in 2027. Gordon's club, the Queensland Firebirds, announced on Tuesday the versatile midcourter was exiting the franchise after one season. She has been linked to a move to the Fever, where she will play alongside her former Central Pulse teammate, Ekenasio.

Midcourter Mila Reuelu-Buchanan is understood to have signed with the Melbourne Vixens for 2027. www.photosport.nz / Bruce White

There has been speculation in Australia that Mila Reuelu-Buchanan - one of the revelations of the Silver Ferns' Commonwealth Games campaign - will replace Gordon at the Firebirds. However, RNZ understands Reuelu-Buchanan has signed with this year's beaten finalists, the Melbourne Vixens.

Fellow Silver Ferns' midcourter Kimiora Poi, is understood to be joining the Firebirds, where she will link up with New Zealand coach Kiri Wills.

Poi previously had a brief stint in the SSN competition in 2019 when she played for the now defunct Collingwood Magpies as a temporary injury replacement player.

There will likely once again be a strong Kiwi contingent at the Firebirds, with Jackson's return confirmed, while former Silver Ferns shooter Te Paea Selby-Rickit is also expected to re-sign in 2027.

Also expected to return to her club in 2027 is Kate Heffernan, who was one of the stars of the Adelaide Thunderbirds' championship-winning run this year.

The versatile midcourter is understood to be joined in the Australian league next year by twin sister Georgia Heffernan, who is rumoured to have signed with the Lightning.

Georgia stamped her mark on the Ferns' goal attack bib in Glasgow, forming a strong combination with shooter Grace Nweke.

World.title: AFL Players Association labels Swans allegations 'very serious'
World.content:
The AFL Players Association (AFLPA) has added its voice to the chorus of organisations expressing concern over a sexual assault allegation at the centre of a scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans.

Multiple law-enforcement agencies yesterday told the ABC Victorian sex crime detectives were due to travel to Sydney as part of their investigation into the incident.

It follows some of the players involved speaking informally to police while they were still in Melbourne.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent following a complaint regarding players' behaviour during celebrations at the Pullman East Melbourne Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

AFLPA CEO James Gallagher issued a statement on Wednesday evening calling the allegation "very serious".

"Our thoughts are with the woman who brought this matter to the relevant authorities, and they should be afforded our respect, privacy and support," he said.

"The AFLPA acknowledges the impact this has had on our AFLW members, as well as recognise the effect on their families, industry staff, the football community and members of the public."

Sydney Swans players (clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Five players involved in the scandal — Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — issued a statement on Wednesday evening, saying they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved" and accepted the Swans' decision to suspend them for the rest of the season for failing to meet club standards.

It is not suggested that they are being accused of sexual assault, and no-one has been arrested or charged in relation to the alleged incident.

Noting the players' statement, Mr Gallagher said the AFLPA, the representative body for AFL and AFLW players, "acknowledges the accountability they've rightly taken and will continue to support them".

"We understand the police investigation is ongoing and any public discussion should be conducted with care," he added.

Investigation expanding over alleged hotel incident Sydney Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich explain the decision to suspend five players for the rest of the AFL season amid an investigation into an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel.

The AFLPA was just one of several organisations that spoke out yesterday expressing concern over the scandal, with club sponsors QBE and realestate.com.au issuing statements calling the allegations "serious" and saying they would wait for the outcome of the police investigation before commenting further.

Telstra, which the ABC understands has brand ambassador arrangements with two of the players involved, said those players would not participate in any ambassador activity while the police investigation was ongoing, adding that the arrangements would be reviewed after the investigation was complete.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn, a former Swans board member and the first female AFL commissioner, also spoke out, saying she was "shocked and troubled" by the allegations and "devastated" for all women affected by the alleged incident, including those not directly involved.

The Swans' decision to suspend five of their players for the rest of the season was welcomed by some advocates, with Respect Victoria CEO Helen Bolton calling the club's statement "clear and accountable".

Greens leader Larissa Waters similarly said it was good to see the club act, "but it's a disgrace that it took a national outcry before they did so".

"This is a serious issue that is bigger than one AFL club, and a serious response with consequences for the players involved is warranted," she wrote on social media.

"We need to challenge gender inequality and disrespect wherever it occurs, whether that's at a school, within an AFL club or at home."

The alleged incident has rocked the Sydney Swans and prompted the club to sanction five of its star players. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich yesterday stressed the decision to suspend the players was not directly related to the allegation being investigated by police, although they said they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare of the women involved.

The bans instead related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, they said, with Mr Pavlich adding the behaviour fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players".

In addition to spelling the end of the players' seasons, the club's sanctions mean the players will not be eligible for All Australian selection.

World.title: Kyrgios provisionally suspended after positive cocaine test in Spain
World.content:
Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has said he tested positive for cocaine on the Spanish island of Mallorca and has issued an apology.

In a statement on his Instagram, he announced he "made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it".

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios said.

"Above all I'm sorry to the kids who follow me.

" I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed with myself. "

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) issued a statement revealing Kyrgios had been "provisionally suspended" since August 4.

"31-year-old Kyrgios provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on 22 June 2026," it said.

"On 17 July 2026, a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine."

"Kyrgios, who reached a career-high world singles ranking of 13 in October 2016, has the right to appeal the provisional suspension, but has not done so to date," the ITIA said.

"As with all Tennis Anti-Doping Programme cases, ITIA support is available to Kyrgios.

"While suspended, Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association."

Nick Kyrgios has been open with his struggles with mental health in the past, including with depression and suicidal ideation. (Reuters: Amr Alfiky)

Kyrgios explained the incident came in the context of years "of injuries … both physically and mentally".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Kyrgios has spoken publicly about his previous struggles with mental health, telling the BBC in 2022 he struggled with alcohol and drug abuse, as well as depression and self-harm.

He has won seven ATP singles titles and the 2022 Australian Open doubles title, partnering with Thanasi Kokkinakis.

In July 2026, he lost in the first round of men's doubles at Wimbledon and later said it was probably his last appearance at the competition.

"I would probably say pretty confidently my last Wimbledon," Kyrgios said.

"It would be hard to see myself coming back here again and competing.

"That [2022] final was always going to be one of the better memories of my tennis career, but I just can't see myself getting back to anywhere near that level.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis, tennis chose me," Kyrgios said.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face.

" At times I've felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. "

He said the "good news" was his drug test failure and suspension "has given me a wake-up call" and said he would step away from social media and the public spotlight for the next 28 days.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family," he said.

"I'm sorry.

"I'll do the work and come back better."

World.title: 'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident
World.content:
Five Sydney Swans players who were stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards have issued an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

In a statement on behalf of Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner, the players said they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved".

The players were banned by the Swans for breaches of standards and expected behaviour after staying out late drinking and bringing women back to the team hotel after the game against Essendon on Sunday night.

"We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club," they said.

The five said that they accepted the club's sanction and apologised for the impact on those involved.

Earlier in the day, the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending the five star players proved their commitment to upholding standards at the club.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Victorian detectives head to NSW

Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate the alleged incident.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and none of the banned players has been formally interviewed by police, according to the club.

Sponsors speak out

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that police were investigating the matter.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation, it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

"I know the five players involved. They're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Loading...

Sydney's sanctions came after the club interviewed the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site, with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacts others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human, and for those who are in high-profile positions, understand that you being a good human matters, but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

WALLABIES SQUAD: Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Massimo de Lutiis, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw , Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (c), Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Dylan Pietsch, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

AP

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

AP

Tech.title: Nielsen is leaning more on wearables to hear what people are watching
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

In order to beef up its ability to accurately measure viewership data in the streaming era, Nielsen is moving forward with a plan to use more information gathered from its partners’ wearable devices.

Today, Nielsen announced “a number of key enhancements” that are being added to its data capturing process ahead of the upcoming fall TV season. As of August 31st, Nielsen’s co-viewing data will now include information obtained from smart-watch like gadgets that Neilsen’s research panelists wear in their homes. The Portable People Meter (PPM) Wearables — which Nielsen first began deploying nationally in 2016 to bolster its audio, local TV, and national audience measurements — are meant to be worn on the wrist while listening for audio from TV scenes, series, and films. The company says that users wearing the devices won’t need to go through the typical Nielsen log in process, and it believes that incorporating this technology into its processes will give it a better idea “of how many people are watching a given program.”

Building on its decision from earlier this year to adopt the Advertising Research Foundation’s (ARF) Device and Account Sharing (DASH) data into its methodology, Nielsen will use new DASH estimates that are based on more recent survey data. The company will also use data from two additional surveys in order to better estimate how many Spanish-speaking households are in its pool of panel participants. Nielsen is also updating the machine learning tool it uses to process information from data providers to assess the demographic makeup of individual households, which means. The firm noted that this last update should help “ensure the data is more representative and does not artificially skew toward older residents.”

Each of these new features makes it sound like Nielsen is taking even more stops to maintain its position as the industry standard for ratings capture at the time when people’s viewing habits have become much more fractured. The company also has to contend with the way the rise of streaming makes it difficult to accurately assess what people are watching. Being asked to keep Nielsen’s proprietary devices in their homes is nothing new for the company’s panel participants, but the push to wear listening wearables could strike some as a bit intrusive. But if this all really does lead to Nielsen capturing more reliable information, other firms might follow its example.

Tech.title: Google Gemini is getting a dedicated student hub
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As we’re gearing up for back-to-school season, Google is rolling out a new dedicated student hub in Gemini. It’s a one-stop repository for collecting research in a study notebook, creating flashcards, taking practice quizzes, and more. Google is also enhancing its study notebooks with support for graphs and images. It can even add test dates and deadlines to your Google Calendar based on your syllabus.

Google is also adding Deep Research to Gemini Live. You can ask Gemini to generate complicated research reports and talk through the results. If it’s taking a while, you can close the chat and lock your phone screen, and Gemini will let you know when your report is ready. In the coming weeks, it will also start rolling out a new feature for Lens in the Google mobile app that lets you take a photo of your study or worksheet and get explanations, help with complicated concepts, or even coaching if you’ve made a mistake.

Eligible students in the US can score one year of Google AI Pro for free, which includes 5TB of storage, Google Health Premium, higher usage limits on Gemini, and access to Gemini across Google apps. Students outside the US will have to make do with the slightly less comprehensive Google AI Plus sub, which comes with 400GB of storage and lower Gemini usage limits.

Tech.title: Watch Valve set up the Steam Frame in its own leaked videos
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Valve just leaked several new videos showing the Steam Frame’s unboxing, setup process, and various accessories. The videos apparently appeared on the ARM Steam client following an update, but they were “quickly pulled after that,” according to the Steam Hardware Updates account on X.

The Steam Frame is Valve’s virtual-reality headset that can stream games from a PC or play them locally. Valve first took the wraps off the headset last year, and it offers LCD screens with 2160 x 2160 resolution per eye, a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip, and an up to 110-degree field of view. But these leaked videos offer a closer look at what it might be like to unbox and set up the new device.

As shown in one of the videos, Valve shows how you can use the Steam Frame’s “pivot arms” to adjust the position of the headset, as well as how to insert a spacer beneath the face gasket if you wear glasses. Another video details how you can plug the wireless dongle into your PC or Steam Machine to stream games.

Though Valve previously said that it plans to release the Steam Frame this summer, it hasn’t yet shared an exact launch date. Still, that timeframe, these setup videos, and a recent 13-ton shipment of VR headsets could all indicate that a launch is right around the corner.

Tech.title: The wearable future is stuck in weird, experimental, existential limbo
Tech.content:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

For the past week, I’ve been testing the Google Pixel Watch 5. In many ways, it’s a typical, modern smartwatch. In others, it feels like one part of a wearable future that’s increasingly in flux. Everyone I’ve spoken to in wearable tech has roughly the same goal — soon, your tracker of choice will feature a helpful AI coach, “check engine” alerts that preventively flag hard-to-detect health conditions, and personalized health recommendations based on your lived experiences and needs.

That’s certainly what’s being pitched. But so far, it seems like most companies don’t know how exactly we’re going to get there.

AI coaches? Even the best ones are too chatty, fixate on one random detail you shared during setup, and require a ton of hand-holding. “Check engine” alerts can be useful and have been documented as saving lives. They can also spark health anxiety and the regulatory quagmire can be expensive to navigate. Personalized health holds great promise, but requires so much of your private data while also being subject to AI’s myriad shortcomings. Even now, most people think of wearable devices as fancy step trackers.

“Historically, wearables have been very focused on hardcore health enthusiasts,” Rishi Chandra, Google’s vice president of health and home, tells me at a roundtable of tech reporters in New York ahead of Made by Google. Usually, tech companies like to keep mum on future ideas and plans. But recently, Google seems eager to lay out its particular vision.

“There’s a huge market of people who are not thinking about their health every day. Today, wearable penetration is about 30 percent — 70 percent of the population has no notion of wearables,” Chandra adds.

Waraich says Google views “glanceble” interactions as lasting roughly seven seconds.

In other words, wearable tech is still in its early days with a lot of untapped potential. The smartwatch is not the end-all, be-all. The fact that wearables can also capture a vast array of personal data compounds that. That’s one reason why, during last year’s Made by Google event, Chandra and Sandeep Waraich, Google’s senior director of wearables, told me that the future of AI gadgets won’t just be a single device. It’ll be an entire ecosystem of diverse accessories.

Since that chat, I’ve already seen several signs supporting Google’s multi-wearable ecosystem thesis. Multiple companies have pivoted to AI glasses (or as Google calls it, “intelligent eyewear”). But we’ve also seen other wearable form factors start gaining steam. See: the horde of screenless Whoop dupes and smart rings. In the AI sphere, some wearable makers are eschewing the health tracking aspect altogether. Some smart jewelry startups like Vocci, Taya, and Sandbar envision rings and pendants as a way to record and transcribe your thoughts using AI.

These are not proven ideas. That there are so many different approaches is a pretty big indication that the entire industry is in the process of throwing wearable spaghetti at a wall, desperately hoping that something will stick and be the next smartphone. It’s enough to make a senior wearable reviewer excited — because yay! Weird experimental products — and also mad — because no! Weird experimental products that don’t work as advertised! Still, there’s a nugget of truth in this new search for new wearable form factors and use cases.

“Wearables are a great conduit for presence. And it goes both ways. As AI reaches you in a respectful way, and as you want to interact with it, these interactions will become more frequent, but also quicker and glanceable,” says Waraich, noting that Google views seven seconds as its current benchmark for any one wrist-based interaction. The question now is figuring out the ideal surface for each specific technological task. For example: What device should you use to check your calendar? Your phone, tablet, or laptop? Or, with the addition of the Proactive Assistance feature on the Pixel Watch 5, should it be your smartwatch?

A Google or Fitbit smart ring is not on the table right now. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

According to Chandra and Waraich, Google has had deep internal discussions about the pros and cons of various wearable form factors. Smart rings, for instance, are something that Google consistently gets asked about but won’t be pursuing in the short term.

“To be clear, we’re not closing the door on [smart rings],” Chandra says. “But our belief right now is that there’s so much headroom on a wrist-worn wearable … I think the Fitbit Air is going to have far bigger expansion opportunities given how simple and easy it is for everyone to use it.”

Okay, so Google just introduced the minimalist Fitbit Air and for now is passing on smart rings. Perhaps then the next step is an “Ultra” Pixel Watch as Samsung and Apple have done. Not so. When I ask, Waraich explains the current Pixel Watch is where Google sees its premium offerings. Chandra adds that the company is wary of spreading itself too thin.

Google certainly has a hypothesis of what wearable tech ought to be. It’s placing its bets through product launches and software updates, watching carefully to see how we — the wearable lab rats — react to specific ideas. The experiment continues.

Another wearable debate: whether it makes sense to add in microphones just because you can. For example, putting mics in something like the Fitbit Air so that it can also double as your AI memory — something akin to Amazon’s Bee device.

“At this point, it’s not a technology issue. It’s a user-sentiment, privacy issue. If you [add] a mic, it’s not just that it’s learning from you. It’s learning from the environment. So I think we’re being cautious about how to push that in the right way,” Chandra says, noting it’d have been easy for Google to stuff microphones into the Fitbit Air but the actual problem is whether doing so would add any customer value. “I don’t know yet if we have, as a tech industry, have figured out the right balancing act there.”

Having tested several AI wearables, my answer is a resounding hell no. As I’ve written on the site, this type of AI wearable tech often makes me feel like a spy. Similarly, I’ll simply point to the defunct Amazon Halo trackers, which not only tracked your emotions based on the tone of your voice but also created highly cursed, self-esteem-obliterating 3D models of your body to estimate fat percentages. Just because AI wearables can track new things doesn’t mean they should.

The Fitbit Air and other wrist-worn wearables, Google says, have more runway than other form factors. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

This problem also plagues smart glasses, as seen with the recent privacy backlash toward Meta’s “pervert glasses.” Some of that is Meta’s penchant for sticking its foot in it. Some of that, Google argues, is perhaps a matter of time and place. Perhaps, Chandra notes, people are more amenable to ambient computing — where your devices are always listening — inside the home instead of outside of it.

Even so, Google is committed to experimenting. What if, Waraich posited, the camera in smart glasses simply acted as a sensor without recording? As in, the glasses see what you see and can answer questions about your environment, but nothing gets recorded for posterity. In theory, this might mean the ability to automatically log your food without ever having to take a picture. A blind person might be able to ask an AI questions about their surroundings, and passersby wouldn’t have to worry that a photo of them exists in someone else’s camera roll.

To that, I say: Love the concept, good luck communicating how that’s different to the masses.

This is part of the existential problem facing my beat. How can any AI wearable be versatile enough to account for every individual’s privacy preferences and health journey? It’s easy enough to differentiate the hardware. Casual users? You get a Fitbit Air or Oura Ring. Tech nerds tired of their phones? Depending on your phone, I’ll point you to a Pixel Watch or Apple Watch. Oh, you’re entering an Ironman? I already know you’re wondering which flavor of Garmin or Coros suits you best.

But the software experience is a whole ’nother beast. Right now you can pick from multiple wearable form factors, but they all pretty much give you the same cluttered app and whap you over the head with data fatigue. That’s hardly a recipe for personalized health. I’ve shared over the course of several Optimizers that my current health journey relates to fixing my borked metabolism. That requires one set of advice. A cancer patient would need something wholly different. So would a hypochondriac or a young college athlete. Maybe you like a drill-sergeant-type coach. Or, if you’re like me, that type of tough love would make you want to throw up your hands. It’s already hard enough for people to learn how to be wise and judicious about their health, to accept limits and practice compassion without veering into overindulgence. How the hell can any one LLM achieve that wisdom? How can we expect one cluttered, unified software experience to meet the needs of an infinite number of individual needs?

AI is often seen as the key to data context and personalized health. It’s defintely a work in progress. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

I asked both Chandra and Waraich this. Both were optimistic that AI will one day get there, but it isn’t there currently. They acknowledged that this is a yearslong journey that will require lots and lots of work. That there are a lot of societal and cultural questions that’ll have to be debated internally and externally. After a decade, my wearable bullshit radar is strong, and since Wear OS 3, Google has genuinely welcomed a good wearable grilling whenever I (or other reporters) have offered frank feedback. I can’t say the same for every gadgetmaker on my beat.

I also can’t tell whether Google’s making all the right wearable bets with the Pixel Watch 5, Fitbit Air, or its AI coach. Maybe it’s a whiff to pass on smart rings. I still think I need to see more proof that an AI hardware ecosystem of diverse accessories is the ultimate move. I’ll give Google credit for being so candid about the multiple layers of privacy, culture, design, and tech logistics that go into the current era of wearable gadgets. That said, whenever I zoom out, I can’t help but feel like I’m caught in the proverbial hamster wheel. Testing each new smartwatch, smart ring, or smart glasses, I keep running toward this vaguely defined, AI-powered wearable future. I just don’t feel any closer to reaching it.

Tech.title: OpenAI hit the brakes. Now what?
Tech.content:
With a looming IPO, intense competition from Anthropic, and Chinese and open-weight rivals nipping at its heels, OpenAI has plenty of reasons to move fast. Instead, it hit the brakes.

On Tuesday, the company said it had slowed the pace of some AI development while it tightened security and safeguards. That included a two-week pause in reinforcement learning training on its “latest models intended for deployment,” and an ongoing delay to its “largest planned frontier RL run.”

The decision is a very public test of an idea AI safety advocates have pushed for for years: that companies should be willing to bow out of the AI race and slow things down when their safeguards fail to keep up with what they are building. But as the race around them continues, will slowing down accomplish anything?

“For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”

For all the talk of slowing down, OpenAI isn’t exactly standing still. The company said it is “pacing” development, a fuzzy and imprecise term that has nevertheless become part of the industry’s lexicon in recent months. In practice, the slowdown is narrowly scoped. OpenAI’s announcement says the pause only covers models meant for deployment while it beefs up security and monitoring before it runs the kind of tests where models may be capable of getting out and hacking real targets. It doesn’t necessarily mean there will be a significant slowdown of the company’s broader development.

From the outside, it’s hard to tell how sincere OpenAI is about stopping solely for the sake of safety, particularly when the company and senior staff have been so vocal about it. But the company’s commitment to safety has been called into question in recent months following a series of high-profile safety team departures and the disbanding of its preparedness team. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

There are good reasons to take OpenAI’s slowdown seriously. Experts who spoke to The Verge pointed to the costs of slowing down at a time of intense competition. Every delay gives rivals more time to catch up or extend their lead. “Due to the intensity of the AI race, everyone has an incentive to work at breakneck speed,” said Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and cofounder of Apollo Research, an AI safety research organization. “Voluntarily slowing down worsens your positioning in the race, so it’s not something that a lab would do lightly.”

The decision also broadly fits with OpenAI’s own published safety doctrine, its Preparedness Framework, as well as the safety frameworks of other AI companies, said Alan Chan, a research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI. “The basic principle is: Continue with development and/or deployment only when we have the mitigations that enable doing so with acceptable risk,” Chan said. As part of the new safety measures, OpenAI said it plans to review and “evolve” the framework — much of which dates back to 2023, when it was first published — to account for advances in its models.

There are also good reasons to believe the new safeguards will actually make OpenAI’s systems safer, at least in the short term, though experts cautioned that this is difficult to assess without more information. “These are good steps that, implemented well, are probably enough to prevent the current generation of agents from causing harm,” Adam Gleave, cofounder and CEO of AI safety organization FAR.AI, told The Verge. “The key question is how OpenAI will keep pace as capabilities increase.”

Gleave’s question points to a broader problem: If technical safeguards falter again, what then? Nothing required OpenAI to stop and take stock this time, which is what made its willingness to do so meaningful. But it also means there is nothing guaranteeing OpenAI — or any other AI company — will make the same choice next time.

“Pacing buys time, not safety… An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis.”

Relying on companies to make that call themselves is a precarious form of governance, particularly in an industry where, as Hobbhahn noted, there is every incentive to keep going. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, described self-policing as the structural problem at the heart of the current approach to AI safety. He argued it should be possible for governments to decide whether OpenAI or any other company should pause development of a technology deemed unsafe. “This is how most industries operate,” he said, pointing to drugs, construction, aircraft, and even restaurants as sectors with stronger regulatory oversight than AI.

Voluntary measures also risk the industry converging on the lowest common denominator. If slowing down imposes a cost, companies have an incentive to adopt only the measures their rivals are also willing to accept. That pressure becomes particularly acute as the race tightens. If OpenAI repeatedly slows down development while its competitors do not, it “will simply be replaced by Anthropic,” Moës argued. “For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”

Sustainable safety needs something stronger than voluntary action. Moës said government oversight could fill that void, as it does in other industries. Independent verification could play a part too. Chan said making sure companies actually implement safety measures will be especially important as technical mitigations like monitoring AIs becomes more expensive. Hobbhahn concurred: “It’s always hard to tell from the outside if a lab is sincere about pausing or safety more broadly, so having more evidence and an independent party to validate the claim is super important.”

Even a perfectly transparent pause is only useful if something actually happens during it. “Pacing buys time, not safety,” said Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. The point is to create breathing room for companies and governments to understand risks and respond appropriately. This would mean deciding what would trigger a slowdown — as well as what happens during one and conditions needed to end one — ahead of time. “An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis,” she said.

It’s possible OpenAI’s slowdown will set a precedent for the industry.
